author: john-hyde
fields.title: Portraits of Courage – Praying Hyde
fields.subtitle: The Life, Prayers, and Hidden Courage of a Missionary to the Punjab
fields.description: A Christian biography of John “Praying” Hyde (1865–1912), the American Presbyterian missionary to the Punjab remembered above all as a man of prayer. It follows him from an Illinois parsonage through slow, misunderstood years in India to the Sialkot Conventions, the soul-a-day years, and his death — keeping what the records show apart from the legend, and weighing his example under Scripture. Written with gratitude but not hagiography; all Scripture from the public-domain ASV (1901).

qa.question: What is the biography Praying Hyde about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of John Hyde (1865–1912), the American Presbyterian missionary to the Punjab known as “Praying Hyde.” It follows his life from a minister’s home in Illinois through twenty years in India — slow early years, the Punjab Prayer Union, the Sialkot Conventions, his long nights of intercession, and his death in 1912 — and draws out what his prayer life teaches under Scripture.

qa.question: Who was John Hyde?
qa.answer: John Nelson Hyde was a missionary of the Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. to the Punjab, in what is now Pakistan and north-west India, from 1892 until his death in 1912. Deaf, slow of speech, and shy, he became known for giving himself day and night to prayer, so that Punjabi villagers called him “the man who never sleeps,” and for his part in the revival that began at the Sialkot Convention in 1904–05.

qa.question: How does this book treat the legends about Praying Hyde?
qa.answer: It keeps them apart from the record. Almost everything vivid about Hyde comes from two devotional memoirs of 1923, so the book says which friend each story comes from, checks it against mission reports, church magazines, and a colleague’s obituary, and corrects what the popular accounts got wrong — such as the place of his death (Northampton, Massachusetts, not Clifton Springs) and the unverified “soul a day” totals.

qa.question: Did prayer really move Hyde’s heart?
qa.answer: That claim rests on a friend’s memory of one Calcutta doctor saying Hyde’s heart had shifted to the right side of his chest. The book tells the story as his friends told it, explains the ordinary medical causes of a right-sided heart, and leaves the miracle unclaimed — while being honest that his way of life did wear down his health.

qa.question: What was the Punjab Prayer Union?
qa.answer: A small covenant of Christian workers in the Punjab, begun around April 1904, in which Hyde was one of the moving spirits. Members answered five questions — beginning with prayer for quickening in their own lives — and promised half an hour of prayer each day, as soon after noon as possible, “till the awakening comes.” Its members saw it as the hidden root of the revival that followed.

qa.question: What can ordinary Christians learn from Hyde’s life?
qa.answer: Not his exact form of prayer, which his own friends warned against copying, but its spirit: preparing the messenger as well as the message, putting the Holy Spirit first, praying persistently for real people, giving thanks instead of accusing others even in prayer, putting on praise before feeling it, and loving the one still missing. Each chapter closes with reflection, and an appendix gathers twenty-five lessons.

qa.question: How is Scripture used in the book?
qa.answer: Every chapter opens with a passage from the American Standard Version (1901) that carries its theme, and further passages are woven through the story — the promises Hyde prayed, such as “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it,” and the texts his life illustrates. All quotations were checked against the ASV text.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning, reading in order: the preface and introduction explain the sources, Part One shows how an ambitious young man became an intercessor, Part Two follows the school of prayer he entered in the Punjab, and Part Three his last illness and legacy. The study guide in Appendix B suits a small group reading one chapter a week.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“What, could ye not watch with me one hour?”

— Matthew 26:40, ASV

The first volume of this series told the story of Watchman Nee, a Chinese church leader whose books travelled the world while he spent his last twenty years in prison. Courage in his case had a public shape. It stood before interrogators and refused to recant, and it paid for faithfulness with freedom.

The man in this second volume was never arrested. He never faced a hostile government. He was not martyred, and he preached no famous sermon that anyone troubled to write down. For most of twenty years he lived in the villages of the Punjab, travelled by ox cart and third-class railway carriage, ate what his Indian fellow workers ate, and spent a quite unreasonable part of his life on his knees, or flat on his face on the floor of a prayer room. The people among whom he worked gave him a name that has outlasted almost everything else about him: “the man who never sleeps.” English-speaking Christians gave him another. They called him Praying Hyde.

Why put such a man in a series called Portraits of Courage?

Because there is a courage that is harder to see than the courage of the prison cell, and in some ways harder to sustain. It is the courage to keep doing the hidden thing when the visible thing would be praised. It is the courage of a missionary who, with few converts to report and colleagues who thought him odd, decided that the answer was not to work harder in front of people but to wait longer before God. It is the courage to be misunderstood without defending yourself, to be passed over without resentment, and to be corrected by God in the middle of your own prayers. John Hyde had that courage. He was not born with it. The story of how he came by it is the story of this book.

Why a Book About Prayer Must Be Honest

There is a difficulty at the heart of any life of John Hyde, and it is better to name it on the first page than to hide it in an appendix. Hyde wrote very little. He kept no journal that has come down to us and published no book. Almost everything vivid that Christians know about him comes from two small books printed in 1923, eleven years after his death. One was compiled in India from the memories of two of his closest friends. The other was compiled in Ohio by a minister who had known his family. Both were written by people who loved him, for readers who wanted to pray more. Neither was written to answer a historian’s questions.

Since 1923 the story has been retold many times, and each retelling has tended to be a little more certain than the one before. Numbers have hardened. Dates have drifted. A doctor’s puzzled remark has become a medical miracle. A great deal of what is now repeated about Hyde as fact is really devotional memory handed from book to book.

This volume does not treat that tradition with contempt. The friends who remembered Hyde were honest people, and many of their memories are precise, local, and entirely believable. But it does treat the tradition as a tradition. Where the historical record is firm, this book says so plainly. Where a story rests on one friend’s recollection, it says that too. The record includes the seminary catalogue, the missionary magazines of his church, his colleagues’ reports, and the obituary a fellow missionary wrote in the spring of 1912. Where the popular accounts have simply got things wrong, as they have with the place of his death, this book corrects them without fuss.

This is not only a matter of scholarly tidiness. A book about prayer that exaggerates its evidence teaches readers, without meaning to, that prayer needs exaggerating. It does not. Hyde himself was uneasy with admiration. His friends recalled that he dreaded anyone copying him. He would disappear to pray when he thought people were looking at him rather than at Christ. The most fitting tribute to such a man is to tell the truth about him, and then to look past him to the One he looked at.

Scripture in This Book

As in the first volume, all Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901. The ASV belongs to the public domain. Its formal, careful English suits extended reflection on the biblical text. And it was published in the middle of Hyde’s own years in India, so it is an English Bible of his own generation.

Each chapter opens with a single passage that carries the chapter’s theme, and further passages are woven through the narrative. This is not decoration. Hyde’s friends remembered him with a Bible almost always open in his hands. When he knelt, his hands rested on it. When he prayed in the prayer room at Sialkot, he would take one promise and repeat it, word by word, until it seemed to fill the room. He took a verse such as “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm 81:10, ASV) and prayed it until the people around him could not forget it. A biography of such a man that did not keep returning to Scripture would miss the thing that shaped him most.

The verse at the head of this preface is the question Jesus asked in Gethsemane, when the three friends he had brought to pray with him had fallen asleep. Hyde’s friends believed he had heard that question addressed to himself, and had answered it with his life. Whether or not we are called to pray as he did, and this book will argue that most of us are not called to his particular form, the question is still addressed to us. It is asked gently, by a Lord who knows that “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41, ASV). The purpose of this book is to let John Hyde’s life put that question to us again.

fields.title: Introduction: One Man, Two Little Books, and a Legend
fields.body_html:
“prove all things; hold fast that which is good”

— 1 Thessalonians 5:21, ASV

A Name Before a Life

Many Christians know the name “Praying Hyde” long before they know anything else about the man. They meet it in a sermon illustration, or a paragraph in a book on prayer, or a quotation shared on a card: O God, give me souls, or I die! The name arrives already shining. It belongs, it seems, to a figure half in heaven, a man who prayed all night, who asked God for a soul a day and got them, whose heart was said to have been physically moved by the strain of intercession, and whose prayer turned an English evangelistic campaign from failure to triumph in an afternoon.

Some of that is true. Some of it is probably true. Some of it rests on nothing firmer than a single friend’s memory, written down ten years later. A little of it is simply wrong. Before we follow John Nelson Hyde from Illinois to the Punjab and back, it is worth pausing to ask where the name and the stories came from, and how much weight each of them can bear.

Two Little Books

Hyde died in February 1912. His friends in India were slow to write about him, and the most important of them waited almost ten years. He was the Rev. J. Pengwern Jones of the Welsh Presbyterian Mission in Sylhet. He edited a small monthly prayer circular called The Remembrancer for the Bengal and Assam Prayer Union. Jones had often meant to set down what he remembered of Hyde, and had always put it off. He believed the church “was not ready for such a record.” Then, around 1921, news came of fresh revival on the east coast of England and in the north of Scotland, and he found he could write at last. Month by month he published in The Remembrancer his reminiscences of Hyde. He described their first meeting in a prayer room at Ludhiana, the week they shared a tiny room in the hill station of Murree, the conventions at Sialkot, and Hyde’s last spring in Wales. A second series came from the Rev. R. McCheyne Paterson of the Punjab, Hyde’s closest companion in prayer. The articles were read, passed from hand to hand, and prayed over. In 1923 they were gathered into a small book by Captain E. G. Carré and published in Madras as A Present-Day Challenge to Prayer. Carré insisted that he had done nothing but arrange them. The reminiscences, he said, were given “practically word for word as they originally appeared.”

In the same year, on the other side of the world, a Presbyterian minister in Akron, Ohio, named Francis McGaw published a shorter book called Praying Hyde. McGaw had known the family for years. As a young minister he had eaten at their table in Carthage, Illinois, been with the family when Hyde’s mother died, and helped to conduct John’s own funeral. He described himself not as the author of his sketch but as “the compiler of material that others have so generously furnished.” That material came from Paterson and Jones in India, from Hyde’s sisters, from mission secretaries, and from others. Much of McGaw’s account of the Sialkot years comes from a narrator he leaves unnamed, “a brother” or simply “I”. Several of those passages match Paterson’s own reminiscences almost word for word, so the narrator is almost certainly Paterson, and this book usually calls him that. But it is an inference, and the book marks it where it matters.

These two books are the source of nearly every well-known story about John Hyde. Later biographies drew on them. Later sermons drew on the biographies. Over the following century the stories were retold with growing confidence, and sometimes with growing detail that no one had actually witnessed.

What Kind of Sources Are They?

It would be easy either to trust these books completely or to dismiss them. Both would be mistakes.

They are memoirs by friends. That means they are close to their subject. Jones shared a room with Hyde. Paterson prayed beside him through whole nights. McGaw knew his father well. Many of their details are small and odd in exactly the way real memories are: the heavy overcoat Hyde knelt in at Murree, the teenage servant who cried because his master would not eat, the glass of water he asked for instead of tea. These are not the inventions of a legend-maker.

But memoirs by friends are also shaped by love and by purpose. These books were written to make readers pray, and they say so. They rarely give dates. They sometimes place the same story in different settings. In one telling of the letter Hyde received on his voyage, he throws it “on the deck”; in another, “into a corner of the cabin.” They report numbers of converts without saying where the numbers came from. And they were written a decade after the events by people who, by their own account, were deeply moved by what they had seen. That is not a reason to disbelieve them. It is a reason to read them as what they are.

The Other Record

There is, happily, another record. It is quieter and duller, and it is precious for that very reason. Hyde was a missionary of the Presbyterian Church in the United States of America, and his church kept books.

The general catalogue of McCormick Theological Seminary records his birth, his college, his ordination, and his station. The women’s missionary magazine of his church, Woman’s Work for Woman, noted his sailings and his arrivals in its columns of missionary movements. The printed report of the Punjab Mission for 1907 describes the district he superintended and quotes his own summary of how village work should be done. And in April 1912 the church’s missionary magazine, The Assembly Herald, printed an obituary by his colleague H. D. Griswold. Griswold had shared a crowded convention dormitory with Hyde, and he wrote with an honesty that is a gift to any biographer. Hyde’s first ten years in India, Griswold said, were “steady, patient, but not especially fruitful.” He was “sometimes criticised by his brethren for the rigorous and ascetic nature of his piety.” He “had not the gifts of an organizer.” And yet, Griswold went on, “from few others have I ever heard such heart-searching and powerful messages.”

That record corrects the legend in places. Hyde did not die at the sanitarium in Clifton Springs, New York, as many books say. He died at his sister’s home in Northampton, Massachusetts. Sialkot, the town whose convention made him famous, was never his station. It belonged to a different Presbyterian mission, and he travelled there each year for the gathering. The celebrated figures of a soul a day and four hundred converts in 1908 appear in no mission report that has yet been found. The closest official figure is a note that 685 people were baptized in the Moga district, where Hyde had been “burying the good seed,” in 1910.

At other points the record quietly confirms the memoirs. The people really did call him “the man who never sleeps.” He really was slow of speech and for years was thought unlikely ever to speak the language really well. His last words really were spoken in Punjabi. And at Moga he really was, in Griswold’s phrase, “marvelously used of God … in bringing very many to decision and baptism.”

How This Book Will Proceed

The chapters that follow tell Hyde’s story in order, from his father’s pulpit in Illinois to his grave in the same town. Part One traces how an ambitious, awkward young man became an intercessor. Part Two looks closely at the school of prayer he entered in the Punjab: the prayer union, the conventions, the long nights, the hunger for souls, and the lessons in praise and humility that God taught him there. Part Three follows him through the breaking of his health to his death, and asks what his life leaves to the church.

Throughout, the book will try to let you hear which kind of source is speaking. When it says “Jones remembered,” or “in Paterson’s telling,” or “McGaw records,” it is not hedging for the sake of it. It is telling you how the story reached us. When it says that something is documented, it means that a record independent of the memoirs confirms it. When a story cannot be checked, it will usually still be told, because a friend’s careful memory is real evidence, but it will be told as a memory.

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s instruction to a young church excited about spiritual gifts and prophetic words: “prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21, ASV). Paul did not tell the Thessalonians to despise what they heard. In the verse before, he warned them, “despise not prophesyings” (1 Thessalonians 5:20, ASV). Nor did he tell them to swallow everything. He told them to test, and then to hold on hard to what survived the testing. That is the spirit in which this book approaches the life of John Hyde. What survives the testing is more than enough to humble and stir anyone who reads it.

fields.title: A Minister’s Son from Carthage
fields.body_html:
“Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he send forth laborers into his harvest.”

— Matthew 9:38, ASV

A Prayer Heard in a Parsonage

Long before anyone called John Hyde a man of prayer, he grew up listening to one.

His father, the Rev. Smith Harris Hyde, was a Presbyterian minister in western Illinois. For seventeen years he was pastor of the Presbyterian church in Carthage, the seat of Hancock County, a small prairie town with a courthouse, several churches, and a Lutheran college that had moved there in 1870. The picture of him that survives is warm. Herrick Johnson, a leading Presbyterian preacher and a professor at McCormick Seminary in Chicago, where John would one day study, knew the elder Hyde. Johnson described him as “of rare proportion and balance, a healthful soul, genial and virile, firm of conviction, of good scholarly attainment, of abundant cheer and bent on doing for God to the best of his ability.” Francis McGaw, then a young minister in the same presbytery, often ate at the family’s table. He remembered a courteous, loving husband and a father who was “firm yet sympathetic,” “commanding his household after him.”

McGaw remembered something else, and it is the thread from which this whole story hangs. Again and again he heard Dr. Hyde pray one particular prayer. He prayed it at the family altar, with his children around him, and he prayed it from the pulpit. It was the prayer Jesus told his disciples to pray when he looked at the crowds in Galilee: “The harvest indeed is plenteous, but the laborers are few. Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he send forth laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37-38, ASV). McGaw’s older English has Dr. Hyde asking the Lord to “thrust out laborers” into his harvest. The phrase is vigorous, almost violent, as though workers had to be pushed out of comfortable places toward the fields.

It is an extraordinary prayer for a father to pray with his own children listening. Most parents, even devout ones, pray for their children’s safety, health, and happiness, and keep a little distance from the prayer that might send those children far away. McGaw once heard a minister say, with some satisfaction, that his son would never follow him into the ministry, because the boy “knows too well the treatment a minister receives at the hands of the people.” Smith Hyde was not that kind of father. McGaw says he “magnified his office and rejoiced to give his sons up to a life of hardship and trial.” He prayed for labourers without adding the quiet clause, but not mine.

God answered the prayer in the parsonage itself. Two of the Hyde sons went into the ministry, and one of the daughters, for a time, into full-time Christian work. The son this book is about went to the other side of the world.

A Household of Six

John Nelson Hyde was born on 9 November 1865 at Carrollton, in Greene County, Illinois. The Civil War had ended that spring. He was one of six children who grew up in that home, three boys and three girls. The eldest brother, Edmund, was two years older than John. There was a third brother, Will, and there were three sisters: Mary, Gratia, and a sister who married a college professor in Northampton, Massachusetts. Sisters appear again and again at the edges of John’s story. He wrote them letters. A card to one of them survives from his last illness. And in the end it was a sister’s home in which he died.

Of his mother we know less than we would like, but what we know is consistent. McGaw calls her “sweet-spirited, gentle, music-loving, Christ-like.” Years later, walking the hills of north Wales with his friend Pengwern Jones, John talked about her a great deal. He told Jones that she had been the best singer he had ever heard, and “such a holy woman.” He also told him she had trained him carefully in the faith. Jones had the impression that the tired missionary, then forty-five and seriously ill, “just longed to go home to her.” She had died some years before. She was buried in Moss Ridge Cemetery at Carthage, where he would one day be laid beside her.

It was, in short, an ordinary devout Presbyterian home of the late nineteenth century, with a family altar, a praying father, and a mother who sang. There is nothing unusual in such a home. That is worth saying plainly, because it is easy to imagine that a man like Hyde must have come from somewhere extraordinary. He did not. He came from the kind of home that thousands of readers of this book grew up in, or are trying, with many failures, to build.

Faith That Is Handed Down

When Paul wrote to his young colleague Timothy, he reminded him of the soil his faith had grown in: “having been reminded of the unfeigned faith that is in thee; which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and, I am persuaded, in thee also” (2 Timothy 1:5, ASV). McGaw reached for the same comparison when he wrote about the Hydes. The point is not that faith is inherited like a family likeness. Paul is careful to say that he is “persuaded” it dwells in Timothy also. Each generation must believe for itself. But faith can be modelled, taught, prayed over, and made to look desirable in a home, and that is what the Hydes did.

The Old Testament law pictured this kind of teaching as woven into the ordinary hours of family life: “And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be upon thy heart; and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deuteronomy 6:6-7, ASV). A father who prays for the harvest every evening teaches his children something before they can explain it. The world has fields in it. The fields are God’s. There are not enough workers. And the right response to that is not first to organise, or to worry, but to pray.

John Hyde would spend his life living out that lesson, and he would take it further than his father ever did. But he did not invent it. He learned it on his knees in a parsonage in Illinois, from a man who meant what he prayed.

Carthage College and a Teacher’s Desk

John graduated from Carthage College in 1887, at twenty-one. Carthage was a small Lutheran college, and it drew its students mostly from the farms and small towns around. Later accounts say he graduated with honours and was at once offered a teaching post at the college. The seminary catalogue confirms only the essential outline: a Carthage degree in 1887, and then a period of teaching before he went on to study for the ministry.

What the young graduate was like inwardly, we know from an unexpected source: John himself, many years later, describing his younger self to Pengwern Jones with rueful honesty. He had decided as a youth, he said, to be a missionary. But he wanted to be a “good missionary,” and by that he meant a great one. “I wanted to shine as a great missionary,” he told Jones. He was, he admitted, “a little proud of the ‘B.A.’ after my name,” and determined to master whatever languages he would need, so that nothing should stand in the way of his success. “I loved the Lord and I wanted to serve Him,” he said, “but ‘self’ was at the foundation of my ambition.”

It is a disarming confession, and it matters for everything that follows. The man who would one day be remembered as an almost otherworldly intercessor did not begin that way. He began as a gifted, earnest, somewhat awkward young man who wanted to be admired for his devotion. Most people who take up Christian service begin with some mixture of real love for God and a strong wish to be significant. The difference between them is not usually where they start. It is whether they let God deal with the mixture.

A Death in the Family

In the autumn of 1889 John entered McCormick Theological Seminary in Chicago, the principal seminary of the Presbyterian Church in the Midwest. His elder brother Edmund followed him there a year later. Edmund had graduated from Lake Forest University in 1888, and he too was preparing for the ministry. He had joined the Student Volunteer Movement, the great wave of college students who were signing a pledge to serve overseas if God permitted. The movement’s watchword, the evangelization of the world in this generation, was being repeated on campuses across the country.

During one summer vacation Edmund went west to do Sunday school mission work in Montana. There he caught what McGaw calls “mountain fever.” A doctor advised him to go home to Illinois at once. He was too ill to travel safely, so they pinned his railway ticket and instructions for each conductor to the lapel of his coat and put him on the train. He was delirious before he reached home, but he arrived. A few days later he died. The seminary catalogue records the date simply: August 1891. He was about twenty-eight. He was buried at Moss Ridge.

John was at that point between his second and final years at seminary. He was already planning to preach. He had long thought vaguely about foreign missions. Now his brother, who had actually pledged himself to go, was dead before he could sail. McGaw says John “was deeply impressed by his brother’s death. There would be a break in the ranks on the foreign field, and he wondered if it were not God’s will for him to step into the gap.”

It is an old pattern in the history of missions: one worker falls, and another steps forward to take the place. It can be a noble instinct, and it can also be a confused one. A grieving young man may try to finish his brother’s story instead of discovering his own. John seems to have sensed that danger, for he did not decide at once. He carried the question for most of a year. The next chapter tells how it was finally settled.

The Prayer Behind the Answer

Before we leave the parsonage at Carthage, it is worth standing back to see what had happened there. A father had prayed for years that God would send labourers into the harvest. One son had offered himself and died. Another was now wondering whether he should go in his place. Within a year and a half, that second son would be on a ship bound for India, sent by his church, as a direct answer, although no one could yet see it, to a prayer said over and over in a small-town manse.

McGaw draws the obvious lesson with a preacher’s vigour. The great need of the church, he says, is not first for more training schools or better organisation. Christ has provided one method for securing labourers, and it is prayer. He puts Jesus’ command into a single stark sentence: “Look on the fields … they are white … the laborers are few … PRAY!” McGaw was writing in the 1920s. He was troubled that thousands of American churches were without pastors and millions of people overseas had never heard the gospel. He believed the cause was simple: “prayer closets are deserted, family altars are broken down, and pulpit prayers are formal and dead.”

We may think that diagnosis too simple. The reasons why churches lack workers are many and tangled. But McGaw is surely right about the order of things. Jesus did not first tell his disciples to go. He told them to pray, and only in the next chapter did he send them (Matthew 10:5, ASV). Prayer for labourers comes before the sending of labourers. And very often, as the Hyde family found, those who pray the prayer find that God answers it through them, or through their children.

That is worth pondering before we go further. Many Christian parents quietly hope that God will call someone else’s children to hard and distant places. Many Christian young people pray for the world while privately assuming that the answer will not involve them. The prayer at the head of this chapter is a dangerous prayer to pray honestly, because the Lord of the harvest may say, as he did in Carthage, I have heard you, and I will send one of yours.

For Reflection

John Hyde’s story does not begin with John. It begins with a father’s faithfulness, a mother’s quiet holiness, and a brother’s unfinished life. The courage of the later chapters grew from roots that were planted by others, in a home that was not remarkable except for its seriousness about God.

That should encourage anyone who feels that their own faithfulness is small and unseen. A father who prays the same prayer for twenty years may never know what it achieves. Smith Harris Hyde did not live to hear his son called “the Apostle of Prayer.” He simply prayed, and believed that the Lord of the harvest was listening. He was right.

fields.title: “It Is Settled”
fields.body_html:
“And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then I said, Here am I; send me.”

— Isaiah 6:8, ASV

Chicago, 1889

McCormick Theological Seminary stood on the north side of Chicago, in a city that was growing faster than almost any other on earth. When John Hyde arrived in the autumn of 1889 to begin his training for the ministry, Chicago had risen from the ashes of the great fire and was pushing out across the prairie. It was also full of new immigrants and packed with churches. D. L. Moody had opened his Bible institute there that very year, and the city was restless with religious energy. For a serious young man from a small Illinois town, it was a larger world.

The seminary’s course ran for three years. Students read Hebrew and Greek, church history, and systematic theology, and they preached practice sermons before professors who did not always hide their opinions. They also talked a great deal among themselves about where they would go. Some would take quiet country pulpits like the one Smith Hyde had filled in Carthage. Some would go to the growing cities. And a surprising number, in those years, were talking about going abroad.

The Volunteers

To understand why, one has to know a little about the Student Volunteer Movement. In the summer of 1886, at a conference for college students called by D. L. Moody at Mount Hermon, Massachusetts, one hundred young men had declared themselves willing, if God permitted, to become foreign missionaries. The idea spread from campus to campus with astonishing speed. Within a few years thousands of students had signed the volunteer declaration, and the movement’s watchword became famous: the evangelization of the world in this generation.

The watchword was bold, and later generations have criticised it for its confidence. But it did one thing very powerfully. It made the question of the mission field personal. A student could no longer think of foreign missions as something the church did through other people. The question pressed on each one: If God permits, am I willing to go? Edmund Hyde had faced that question and said yes. His death in the summer of 1891 left the same question lying on his brother’s desk.

John was not a stranger to the question. He later told Pengwern Jones that he had determined as a youth to be a missionary. But a youthful intention is not the same as a settled call, and it seems that in his seminary years the matter had become unsettled. Perhaps the pull of a comfortable American pastorate was stronger than he expected. Perhaps he doubted his own fitness, for he was slow of speech and a little hard of hearing, and knew it. Perhaps, having grown up in a minister’s home, he simply could not tell his own desires from other people’s expectations. Whatever the reason, Edmund’s death forced the issue, and John did not rush to settle it.

A Year of Wondering

McGaw says plainly that “the decision was not finally reached till the next year, his last in seminary.” That means John lived with the question for most of a year. He went back to classes in the autumn of 1891 grieving his brother and unsure of his road.

There is wisdom in that slowness. Grief can produce sudden vows, and sudden vows are not always from God. A young man who has just buried a brother may promise, in a rush of feeling, to take his brother’s place, and later find that he has built his life on an emotion rather than a call. John seems to have sensed this. He did not treat Edmund’s death as the answer. He treated it as the question.

Isaiah’s call, which stands at the head of this chapter, did not come out of nowhere either. It came “in the year that king Uzziah died” (Isaiah 6:1, ASV), after the death of a king who had reigned for over fifty years. Isaiah went into the temple in a time of loss and uncertainty, and there he saw the Lord “sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1, ASV). What moved him to volunteer was not the empty throne in Jerusalem. It was the throne in heaven that was not empty. And before he said “Here am I,” he said something else: “Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5, ASV). The call to go came to a man who had first been shown his own unfitness, and then cleansed.

That order matters, and we shall see it again and again in Hyde’s life. The ones God sends are rarely the ones who feel best qualified. They are the ones who have seen enough of God to stop pretending about themselves.

“Stay There Till the Question Is Settled”

The moment of decision, when it came, was undramatic. McGaw tells it in a few lines, and they have the feel of a story that a classmate told many times afterwards.

Late one Saturday night in his final year, John went to a classmate’s room. He asked him for all the arguments he could furnish on the question of the foreign field. He wanted, it seems, a debate. He wanted someone to set out the case for going and the case for staying, so that he could weigh them and reach a sensible conclusion.

His classmate refused. He told John that it was not argument he needed. What he should do, the classmate said, was go to his own room, get on his knees before God, and stay there till the question was settled.

John went. We do not know how long he knelt, or what he prayed, or whether he slept that night at all. We know only what happened the next morning. At chapel he found his classmate and said to him, “It is settled.” McGaw adds that “his shining face was enough to show which way the decision had been made.”

Later accounts have sometimes named the classmate. One modern reference work credits a fellow student, Burton Alva Konkle, with a decisive influence on Hyde’s call. Konkle was indeed in Hyde’s class at McCormick. But the early sources do not name the man in the story, and it is better to leave him as McGaw left him: a friend with the sense to refuse a request for arguments, and to send John to his knees instead.

What the Classmate Understood

The classmate’s advice is worth pausing over, because it holds in miniature the whole shape of John Hyde’s later life.

There is a proper place for arguments in Christian decisions. Scripture tells us to count the cost before we build a tower or go to war (Luke 14:28-31, ASV). It commends the counsel of many advisers. Hyde’s friend did not despise thinking. But he saw that John had reached the point where more arguments would not help. He had heard them all. He knew the needs of the world, the claims of his own country, the risks of India, and his own limitations. What he lacked was not information. He lacked a settled word from God, and a willingness to obey it whatever it turned out to be.

There is a kind of decision that can only be made alone before God. Jesus himself, before choosing the twelve apostles, “went out into the mountain to pray; and he continued all night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12, ASV). The psalmist heard God say, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10, ASV). Arguments keep a person busy, and they keep the final decision at arm’s length. Kneeling until something is settled means risking an answer one did not want.

That Saturday night in Chicago was, as far as we know, the first time John Hyde prayed his way through to a decision in that way. It would not be the last. Twenty years later his friends would watch him stay on his knees, sometimes for a whole day, sometimes for many nights, until some burden was lifted or some assurance given. The habit that made him famous began with a classmate who would not argue with him.

Mixed Motives, Real Call

It would be pleasant to report that John went to India with a pure heart, having laid aside all ambition on that Saturday night. He did not, and he said so himself. He told Pengwern Jones years later that when he boarded the ship he still wanted to be a “great missionary,” still counted on his abilities, and still had “self” at the foundation of his plans. The call was real, and it would be tested within days of his sailing. But he was not yet the man he would become.

This is a comfort, not a scandal. Very few people answer God’s call with entirely clean motives. Paul could even rejoice when some in Rome preached Christ “of envy and strife” rather than of goodwill, because “in every way … Christ is proclaimed” (Philippians 1:15, 18, ASV). God does not wait for our motives to be perfect before he sends us. He sends us, and then, very often, he purifies our motives on the way. A young man can say “Here am I; send me” with sincerity and a good deal of pride mixed together. What matters is that he means it enough to let God deal with the pride.

Ordination and Sailing

The records from here on are clear and precise. John Hyde graduated from McCormick Theological Seminary in the spring of 1892, having completed the full three-year course. On 26 April 1892 the Presbytery of Schuyler, in western Illinois, ordained him to the ministry of the Presbyterian Church. The Board of Foreign Missions of the Presbyterian Church in the United States of America appointed him to its mission in the Punjab, in the far north-west of British India. It was then still called the Lodiana Mission, after the town of Ludhiana where American Presbyterians had begun their work in 1834.

On his way east that autumn he called at the Chicago rooms of the women’s missionary board, which noted in its magazine that he had visited them “on his way to Lodiana.” The same issue listed him among the month’s departures in a single line: “Rev. John N. Hyde, to North India.” He had sailed from New York on 15 October 1892. He was twenty-six.

Behind him were a father who had prayed for labourers, a mother who had sung the faith into him, and a brother buried in Moss Ridge Cemetery. Ahead lay a language he would struggle to learn, a climate that would test his health, a people he would come to love more than his own life, and colleagues who would not understand him for years. Between the two, a few hours out of New York harbour, a letter was waiting for him. He did not know it yet, but it was the most important letter he would ever receive.

For Reflection

Many Christians carry an unsettled question for years: a call they half-believe in, a step they neither take nor abandon, a decision they keep reopening with fresh arguments. John Hyde’s classmate would give them the same advice he gave John: not more arguments, but time on their knees until the matter is settled.

This is not a promise that the answer will always be dramatic, or that the face will always shine the next morning. It is simply the recognition that some questions belong to God. They will not be answered until we are willing to hear his answer, and are willing to say, whatever it is, “Here am I.”

Then I said, Here am I; send me.” — Isaiah 6:8, ASV Chicago, 1889 McCormick Theological Seminary stood on the north side of Chicago, in a city that was growing faster than almost any other on earth. When John Hyde arrived in the autumn of 1889 to begin his training for the ministry, Chicago had risen from the ashes of the great fire and was pushing out across the prairie. It was also full of new immigrants and packed with churches. D. L. Moody had opened his Bible institute there that very year, and the city was restless with religious energy. For a serious young man from a small Illinois town, it was a larger world. The seminary’s course ran for three years. Students read Hebrew and Greek, church history, and systematic theology, and they preached practice sermons before professors who did not always hide their opinions. They also talked a great deal among themselves about where they would go. Some would take quiet country pulpits like the one Smith Hyde had filled in Carthage. Some would go to the growing cities. And a surprising number, in those years, were talking about going abroad. The Volunteers To understand why, one has to know a little about the Student Volunteer Movement. In the summer of 1886, at a conference for college students called by D. L. Moody at Mount Hermon, Massachusetts, one hundred young men had declared themselves willing, if God permitted, to become foreign missionaries. The idea spread from campus to campus with astonishing speed. Within a few years thousands of students had signed the volunteer declaration, and the movement’s watchword became famous: the evangelization of the world in this generation. The watchword was bold, and later generations have criticised it for its confidence. But it did one thing very powerfully. It made the question of the mission field personal. A student could no longer think of foreign missions as something the church did through other people. The question pressed on each one: If God permits, am I willing to go? Edmund Hyde had faced that question and said yes. His death in the summer of 1891 left the same question lying on his brother’s desk. John was not a stranger to the question. He later told Pengwern Jones that he had determined as a youth to be a missionary. But a youthful intention is not the same as a settled call, and it seems that in his seminary years the matter had become unsettled. Perhaps the pull of a comfortable American pastorate was stronger than he expected. Perhaps he doubted his own fitness, for he was slow of speech and a little hard of hearing, and knew it. Perhaps, having grown up in a minister’s home, he simply could not tell his own desires from other people’s expectations. Whatever the reason, Edmund’s death forced the issue, and John did not rush to settle it. A Year of Wondering McGaw says plainly that “the decision was not finally reached till the next year, his last in seminary.” That means John lived with the question for most of a year. He went back to classes in the autumn of 1891 grieving his brother and unsure of his road. There is wisdom in that slowness. Grief can produce sudden vows, and sudden vows are not always from God. A young man who has just buried a brother may promise, in a rush of feeling, to take his brother’s place, and later find that he has built his life on an emotion rather than a call. John seems to have sensed this. He did not treat Edmund’s death as the answer. He treated it as the question. Isaiah’s call, which stands at the head of this chapter, did not come out of nowhere either. It came “in the year that king Uzziah died” (Isaiah 6:1, ASV), after the death of a king who had reigned for over fifty years. Isaiah went into the temple in a time of loss and uncertainty, and there he saw the Lord “sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1, ASV). What moved him to volunteer was not the empty throne in Jerusalem. It was the throne in heaven that was not empty. And before he said “Here am I,” he said something else: “Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5, ASV). The call to go came to a man who had first been shown his own unfitness, and then cleansed. That order matters, and we shall see it again and again in Hyde’s life. The ones God sends are rarely the ones who feel best qualified. They are the ones who have seen enough of God to stop pretending about themselves. “Stay There Till the Question Is Settled” The moment of decision, when it came, was undramatic. He knew the needs of the world, the claims of his own country, the risks of India, and his own limitations. What he lacked was not information. He lacked a settled word from God, and a willingness to obey it whatever it turned out to be. There is a kind of decision that can only be made alone before God. Jesus himself, before choosing the twelve apostles, “went out into the mountain to pray; and he continued all night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12, ASV). The psalmist heard God say, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10, ASV). Arguments keep a person busy, and they keep the final decision at arm’s length. Kneeling until something is settled means risking an answer one did not want. That Saturday night in Chicago was, as far as we know, the first time John Hyde prayed his way through to a decision in that way. It would not be the last. fields.title: The Letter on the Ship
fields.body_html:
“If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?”

— Luke 11:13, ASV

Hours Out of New York

A long sea voyage in the 1890s was a strange suspension of life. For weeks a traveller had nothing to do and nowhere to go. One home had been left and the other not yet reached. McGaw, who had perhaps made such voyages himself, says of it that “the feet lifted up from off the dear homeland and not yet planted on the new homeland” gave “suggestion and opportunity for thoughtful meditation.” For John Hyde, in the autumn of 1892, the voyage became something more than that. It was the first great crisis of his spiritual life, and it began with the post.

We have two accounts of what happened, both claiming to come from Hyde himself. They agree on the essentials and differ in the details, which is roughly what we should expect from two tellings of the same story many years apart. It is worth reading them side by side.

The First Telling

The first comes from Francis McGaw. He says that Hyde afterwards described the incident “in an Indian publication,” and he quotes Hyde’s words directly:

My father had a friend who greatly desired to be a foreign missionary, but was not permitted to go. This man wrote me a letter directed in care of the ship. I received it a few hours out of New York harbor. He urged me to seek for the baptism of the Holy Spirit as the great qualification for mission work. When I had read the letter I crumpled it up in anger and threw it on the deck. Did this friend think that I had not received the baptism of the Spirit, or that I would think of going to India without this equipment? I was angry. But by and by better judgment prevailed and I picked up the letter and read it again. Possibly I did need something which I had not yet received.

Hyde goes on to say that for the rest of the voyage he “gave himself much to prayer” that he might “indeed be filled with the Spirit.” He wanted to know “by an actual experience” what Jesus meant when he said, in the words he quoted from the Revised Version, “Ye shall receive power, when the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be my witnesses … unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1:8). And he says, simply, that “these prayers on shipboard were finally answered in a marvelous way.”

The Second Telling

The second account comes from Pengwern Jones. Years later, when the two men had become close friends, Jones asked Hyde how he had come into his life of prayer. It was, Jones says, “very difficult to get him to speak about himself.” But Hyde understood that Jones was not merely curious, and he told him. Jones wrote the story down afterwards, and he was careful to say that he was giving it “as far as I can remember … in some such words.”

In Jones’s telling, Hyde began with his ambition, as we saw in the first chapter. He wanted to be a great missionary, and he was a little proud of his degree. Then he described the letter. When he went aboard the steamer at New York, he found in his cabin a letter in the handwriting of his father’s friend. “The words were not many,” he told Jones, “but the purport of them was this: ‘I shall not cease praying for you, dear John, until you are filled with the Holy Spirit.’”

“My pride was touched,” Hyde went on, “and I felt exceedingly angry and crushed the letter and threw it into a corner of the cabin and went up on deck in a very angry spirit. The idea of implying that I was not filled with the Spirit! I was going out as a missionary, and I was determined to be a good missionary, and yet this man implied that I was not fitted and equipped for the work!”

He paced the deck, he said, “a battle raging within.” He loved the writer and knew the holy life he led, “and down in my heart there was a conviction that he was right and that I was not fit to be a missionary.” After a while he went back to his cabin, got down on his knees to hunt for the crumpled letter, smoothed it out, and read it again, and then again. He was still annoyed, but “the conviction was gaining on me that my father’s friend was right and I was wrong.”

This went on, he said, for two or three days, “until I felt perfectly miserable.” At last, “in a kind of despair,” he asked the Lord to fill him with the Holy Spirit, “and the moment I did this the whole atmosphere seemed to clear up. I began to see myself, and what a selfish ambition I had.” It was “a struggle almost to the end of the voyage.” But long before the ship reached port he had made up his mind that, whatever the cost, he would be filled with the Spirit. Then came what he called the second climax. He was willing, he told the Lord, even to fail his language examinations in India. He was willing to be a missionary “working quietly out of sight.” He would do anything and be anything, “but the Holy Spirit I would have at any cost.”

Reading the Two Together

The differences between the accounts are small. In one the letter is handed to him a few hours out; in the other he finds it waiting in his cabin. In one he throws it on the deck; in the other he throws it into a corner of the cabin and then goes on deck. McGaw’s version is shorter, more restrained, and shaped for a public audience. Jones’s is longer and more intimate, the story as a man tells it to a friend in private conversation. Jones’s version also carries the most important detail. The letter did not only urge Hyde to seek the Spirit. It promised that the writer would keep praying until he did.

Both tellings agree on what matters. A letter from an older Christian implied that Hyde was not spiritually ready for the work he was going to do. Hyde’s first reaction was wounded pride. His second, after a struggle, was to admit that the letter was right. And the voyage became a time of seeking God that changed the direction of his life.

Who Wrote the Letter?

Neither account names the letter-writer, but they give three clues. He was a friend of Hyde’s father. He had greatly wanted to be a foreign missionary himself but had been prevented. And, in a small aside in the middle of Jones’s reminiscences, Jones adds in brackets: “I understand that this friend is the one who is preparing a short account of Hyde and especially of his prayer-life.”

The short account of Hyde’s prayer life that was being prepared in America at the time Jones was writing was Francis McGaw’s Praying Hyde. McGaw had known Smith Hyde well. His own mother had prayed for labourers for the mission field, and one of his brothers served as a missionary in India. If Jones’s information was right, then the friend who wrote the letter, and then kept his promise to pray, was McGaw himself. That would explain why his own account says so little about the letter-writer and so much about what the letter did. A modest man telling a story in which he plays a part will often leave himself out.

We cannot be certain. Jones says only “I understand,” and McGaw never claims the letter as his own. But it is a moving possibility. The man who compiled the book that made Hyde famous may have been the man whose prayers, thirty years earlier, set Hyde on his way.

The Wound of a Friend

Whoever wrote it, the letter was a risk. It is not easy to tell a young man on his way to the mission field, a new graduate newly ordained and full of hope, that he is not yet ready. Most of us, if we had such a thought about someone we loved, would keep it to ourselves, or dress it up so heavily that it lost its point. The letter-writer said it plainly and then promised to pray.

The book of Proverbs has a word for this: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are profuse” (Proverbs 27:6, ASV). A true friend will sometimes say what hurts. A false friend, or a merely polite one, will say only what pleases. Hyde’s first response was the natural one: he felt insulted. What makes him remarkable is not that he was angry but that he went back on his knees and looked for the letter he had thrown away. He let himself be corrected by someone who loved him.

That willingness would mark his whole life. Two decades later he would be corrected in the middle of his own prayer, rebuked by God for criticising a fellow pastor. The capacity to receive correction without defending oneself is one of the least glamorous and most important parts of Christian character. It began, for John Hyde, with a crumpled letter on a ship.

What Was He Asking For?

The letter used language that would be familiar to many Christians in the 1890s and strange to many today. Hyde was urged to seek “the baptism of the Holy Spirit” as the great qualification for missionary work, and to be “filled with the Spirit.” Among evangelicals of that generation such language was common. The Keswick Convention in England, the preaching of D. L. Moody and his associates, and a wide stream of writing on the “higher Christian life” all urged believers to seek a deeper experience of the Spirit’s power for holiness and service. Christians then, as now, disagreed about exactly how to describe that experience, and how it related to conversion.

This book will not try to settle those debates. What is clear from Scripture is the thing Hyde longed for. The Christian is commanded, “be not drunken with wine, wherein is riot, but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18, ASV). Jesus promised his disciples power for witness when the Spirit came upon them. And the verse at the head of this chapter gives the simplest possible instruction for receiving him: ask. “If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?” (Luke 11:13, ASV).

Hyde asked. He asked in anger at first, then in misery, then “in a kind of despair,” and finally with the settled resolve of a man who would rather fail every examination in India than go on without the Spirit’s help. It is worth noticing what he did not do. He did not demand a particular sensation or sign. He did not decide in advance what the answer should look like. He asked to be filled, confessed the selfish ambition he now saw in himself, and offered to be anything God wanted, even an unnoticed worker “quietly out of sight.”

That last phrase is almost a prophecy. John Hyde spent much of the rest of his life out of sight, in prayer rooms, in village huts, and on his face on the floor while others preached. The young man who had wanted to shine was given, instead, the grace to be hidden. It was the answer to his prayer.

Not the End of the Story

It would be tidy to end the chapter here, with the ship coming into harbour and a transformed missionary stepping ashore. But Hyde himself did not tell it that way. In Jones’s account, the voyage was only the beginning. Within days of arriving in India, Hyde met a question at an open-air meeting that went deeper than the letter had. It showed him that there was still something in his own life that the gospel he had come to preach had not dealt with.

The letter had humbled his pride. The next test would search his conscience. That is the subject of the next chapter.

For Reflection

Two things in this story deserve attention. The first is the letter-writer’s courage: to say a hard thing to someone he loved, and then, most important of all, to commit himself to pray until it came true. We would all be the poorer if such friends were rare.

The second is Hyde’s response. Pride throws the letter away. Grace goes back on its knees to look for it. Most of us have had letters, conversations, sermons, or rebukes that we crumpled up in anger. Some of them were wrong, and deserved to be thrown away. But some of them were from God, and are still lying in the corner of the cabin, waiting to be smoothed out and read again.

It is worth noticing what he did not do. He did not demand a particular sensation or sign. He did not decide in advance what the answer should look like. He asked to be filled, confessed the selfish ambition he now saw in himself, and offered to be anything God wanted, even an unnoticed worker “quietly out of sight.” That last phrase is almost a prophecy. John Hyde spent much of the rest of his life out of sight, in prayer rooms, in village huts, and on his face on the floor while others preached. The young man who had wanted to shine was given, instead, the grace to be hidden. It was the answer to his prayer. Not the End of the Story It would be tidy to end the chapter here, with the ship coming into harbour and a transformed missionary stepping ashore. But Hyde himself did not tell it that way. In Jones’s account, the voyage was only the beginning. Within days of arriving in India, Hyde met a question at an open-air meeting that went deeper than the letter had. It showed him that there was still something in his own life that the gospel he had come to preach had not dealt with. The letter had humbled his pride. The next test would search his conscience. That is the subject of the next chapter. For Reflection Two things in this story deserve attention. The first is the letter-writer’s courage: to say a hard thing to someone he loved, and then, most important of all, to commit himself to pray until it came true. We would all be the poorer if such friends were rare. The second is Hyde’s response. Pride throws the letter away. Grace goes back on its knees to look for it. Most of us have had letters, conversations, sermons, or rebukes that we crumpled up in anger. Some of them were wrong, and deserved to be thrown away. But some of them were from God, and are still lying in the corner of the cabin, waiting to be smoothed out and read again.

fields.title: The Sin That Had Not Been Taken Away
fields.body_html:
“Therefore let us also, seeing we are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us”

— Hebrews 12:1, ASV

Arrival

John Hyde reached India at the end of 1892, at the start of the cool season in the north. From the coast he travelled up-country by rail to the Punjab, the land of five rivers in the north-west of British India, where his church had worked for nearly sixty years. It was a land of wheat fields and canal villages, of mud-walled towns and Sikh temples, mosques and Hindu shrines. Along the roads moved bullock carts, camels, and the occasional missionary on a pony. The languages he would need were Urdu, the common tongue of the towns and of educated conversation, and Punjabi, the language of the villages. He knew neither.

For his first days he stayed, as new missionaries usually did, with an older colleague, a man Hyde later described simply as “a brother of some experience.” Almost at once, “on one of the first few days” in India, something happened that he never forgot. Years afterwards he told Pengwern Jones about it, immediately after telling him about the letter on the ship, as though the two belonged together. They did.

A Question at an Open-Air Meeting

The older missionary took him out to an open-air service in the town. In the Punjab of those days this was a common method. The preacher would take his stand in a bazaar or at a crossroads, perhaps with a helper or two to sing, and speak to whoever would stop and listen. Hyde could not understand a word. But someone told him what the subject was: the missionary was speaking about Jesus Christ as the real Saviour from sin.

When the address was over, a respectable-looking man in the crowd stepped forward. He spoke good English, and he asked the missionary a direct question: had he himself been saved from sin in the way he was describing?

We do not know how the older missionary answered. The story is not about him. It is about the young man standing silently beside him, who suddenly found that the question had gone straight into his own heart. “If the question had been asked me,” Hyde told Jones, “I would have had to confess that Christ had not fully saved me, because I knew that there was a sin in my life which had not been taken away.”

The thought appalled him. Here he was, newly arrived to proclaim to others that Christ was a perfect Saviour, and he could not honestly say that Christ had delivered him. “I realized,” he said, “what a dishonour it would be on the Name of Christ to have to confess that I was preaching a Christ that had not delivered me from sin, though I would be proclaiming to others that He was a perfect Saviour.”

The Unnamed Sin

Hyde never told Jones what the sin was, and Jones never asked, or if he asked, never recorded the answer. Hyde used the language of the verse that stands at the head of this chapter: it was “the sin that so easily beset me.” It was a single, particular, recurring failure that he knew well, and it had followed him, it seems, all the way to the Punjab.

It is natural to want to know what it was, and wise not to guess. Every Christian who reads this story will probably find their own besetting sin coming to mind, and that is the point. Hyde’s silence on the matter is itself a kind of mercy to his readers. Had he named it, some would have thought, “Well, that is not my problem.” Unnamed, it becomes a mirror.

The writer to the Hebrews assumes that every Christian has such a sin. He does not say “lay aside the sin, if you happen to have one.” He speaks of “the sin which doth so easily beset us” (Hebrews 12:1, ASV), as a runner might speak of a heavy cloak that wraps around the legs and trips him every time he tries to run. The sin that besets us is not the dramatic fall we would never contemplate. It is the familiar one. It knows our weak places and our tired hours, and we have half made our peace with it.

“One of Two Things”

Hyde went back from the meeting to his room, shut himself in, and had it out with God. What he told Jones about that hour is uncompromising.

“I told the Lord that it must be one of two things,” he said. “Either He must give me victory over all my sins, and especially over the sin that so easily beset me, or I must return to America and seek there for some other work. I said that I could not stand up to preach the Gospel until I could testify of its power in my own life.”

It is easy to misread this as a kind of bargaining with God, or an ultimatum. It was not. It was a young man refusing to live a divided life. He had come to India to proclaim a Saviour from sin. If that Saviour could not save him, then he had no business preaching. And if the Saviour could save him, then there was no reason to put up with the besetting sin any longer. Either the gospel was true in his own life or he would go home. He would not do the one thing that hypocrisy would have made easy: carry on preaching while quietly keeping the sin.

Paul warned his young colleague Timothy: “Take heed to thyself, and to thy teaching. Continue in these things; for in doing this thou shalt save both thyself and them that hear thee” (1 Timothy 4:16, ASV). Notice the order: first thyself, then thy teaching. Paul applied the same discipline to himself: “I buffet my body, and bring it into bondage: lest by any means, after that I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Corinthians 9:27, ASV). Hyde had not read these verses for the first time that evening, but for the first time they were addressed to him personally, by a stranger’s question in a Punjabi street.

“He Did Deliver Me”

Hyde stayed in his room “for some time,” he said, “facing the question, and realized how reasonable it was.” And then: “The Lord assured me that He was able and willing to deliver me from all sin, that He had planned work for me in India. He did deliver me and I have not had a doubt of this since. I can now stand up without hesitation to testify that He has given me victory, and I love to witness to this and to tell all of the wonderful faithfulness of Christ my Lord, my Saviour.”

Jones never forgot Hyde’s face as he told the story. There was, he said, “that inexpressibly sad look when he spoke of his sin, and that wonderful smile of his when he referred to the faithfulness of Christ.” The two expressions together are a good summary of Christian experience. Sin is never a trivial matter, even when it has been forgiven and overcome, and a Christian who can speak of past sin without any sorrow has perhaps not understood it. But the last word belongs to the faithfulness of Christ, and it is spoken with a smile.

Scripture holds out the same promise that Hyde discovered: “For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14, ASV). It is not a promise that we will never be tempted, or even that we will never stumble. It is a promise about dominion, about who is in charge. The besetting sin need not be master. Paul, crying out “Wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me out of the body of this death?”, answered his own question at once: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24-25, ASV).

A Caution and a Comfort

Hyde’s testimony, as Jones recorded it, is very strong. He said the Lord was able to deliver him “from all sin,” and that he had not doubted it since. Readers from different Christian traditions will hear such language differently. Some will hear it as an overstatement of what is possible in this life. Others will hear it as a plain statement of what grace can do. Both should also hear the balancing word of the apostle John. John writes, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”, and then, in the next breath, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:8-9, ASV).

The rest of Hyde’s life suggests that his victory in 1892 was a real beginning, not a finished work. McGaw’s sources describe him at the first Sialkot Convention in 1904, twelve years later, still speaking to the men of the convention about “some of the desperate conflicts that he had had with sin and how God had given him victory.” One close friend went so far as to say that until that convention Hyde, though truly “born of God,” had still been “a babe in Christ.” Paterson, who knew him best, said Hyde would regularly search himself in prayer for what was hindering God’s work, confess what he found, and ask again for grace. None of that contradicts the story of the open-air meeting. It simply shows that deliverance from a besetting sin is the start of a road, not the end of one.

There is a comfort in that. Many Christians have had some decisive moment of surrender or deliverance, and then have been bewildered to discover that the struggle with sin was not over. They wonder whether the first experience was real. Hyde’s life suggests that it can be entirely real and still only a beginning. The writer to the Hebrews, having told us to lay aside the sin that besets us, immediately adds, “and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.” Laying aside the weight is not the end of the race. It is what makes running possible.

Preacher and Practice

One more thread in this story is worth drawing out. The man who asked the question at the open-air meeting was not hostile. He was, Hyde says, “respectable-looking,” educated, and apparently in earnest. He had heard the missionary claim that Christ saves from sin, and he wanted to know whether the claim was true of the man making it. It was a fair question. Indian listeners in the Punjab of the 1890s asked it of missionaries often, sometimes sharply. They saw very clearly the gap between the Christianity preached in the bazaar and the Christianity practised in some European bungalows, clubs, and cantonments.

Hyde spent the next twenty years answering that man’s question with his life. Much of what made him influential in India was the plain evidence that he believed what he preached, and lived it. He shared the food and houses of his Indian fellow workers. He gave away his clothes. He prayed through the night. He refused to defend himself against unkind treatment. In his later years an Indian enquirer, who had secretly been sent to watch him and find his faults, went back to the men who sent him and reported that Hyde had none. That story is told later in this book, and like many such stories it probably grew in the telling. But the reputation behind it was earned. And it began here, with a young missionary who could not bear to preach a Saviour he had not yet fully trusted.

For Reflection

There are two ways to deal with a besetting sin in the life of a Christian worker. One is to keep working, keep preaching, and keep the sin, managing the tension as best one can. The other is Hyde’s way: to bring the matter to God as a question of integrity, and to refuse to go on until it is dealt with. The first way is common, and it is quietly destructive. The second is costly, and it is the only way to preach with a clear conscience.

Not everyone who reads this is a preacher. But every Christian is a witness, and every witness will one day meet, in some form, the question the stranger asked in the Punjab: Has this Saviour you speak of saved you? Hyde’s answer, after a hard hour on his knees, was yes. It can be ours.
