fields.title: Slow of Speech and Hearing
fields.body_html:
“And Jehovah said unto him, Who hath made man’s mouth? or who maketh a man dumb, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? is it not I, Jehovah? Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt speak.”

— Exodus 4:11-12, ASV

Not a Remarkable Missionary

If the story of John Hyde were a legend, it would move straight from the ship and the open-air meeting to triumph. A young man is filled with the Spirit and set free from sin, and he goes out at once to win the Punjab. That is not what happened, and every early witness is honest about it.

“At the first,” McGaw writes, “John Hyde was not a remarkable missionary.” His colleague H. D. Griswold, writing the obituary in 1912, was blunter still. Hyde’s first ten years in India, he said, “were marked by steady, patient, but not especially fruitful service.” Ten years is a long time. It is the whole career of many missionaries, who go out young, serve a single term or two, and come home. If Hyde had been one of them, no one would ever have written a book about him.

The reasons for those slow years were partly outside his control. The work in the villages of the Punjab was hard and slow for everyone. But some of the reasons lay in Hyde himself, and his friends named them with affection and without pretending.

“He Seemed Not to Hear”

Hyde was slow of speech. McGaw’s informants remembered that “when a question or a remark was directed to him he seemed not to hear, or if he heard he seemed a long time in framing a reply.” Part of the reason was physical. “His hearing was slightly defective,” McGaw says, “and this it was feared would hinder him in acquiring the language.” Pengwern Jones, who knew him in his last years, says without qualification that “Mr. Hyde himself was deaf.” The deafness seems to have grown worse with time. In his final spring in Britain he told an elderly woman that he could rarely hear anything at all when he went to church.

He was also, by temperament, quiet and withdrawn. Paterson, his closest friend, wrote that Hyde “was not naturally a bright and happy man. On the contrary he was in himself inclined to be morose, retiring, shy and silent.” McGaw’s sources describe a disposition “gentle and quiet” that seemed “to be lacking in the enthusiasm and zeal which a young missionary should have.” Some colleagues, Jones heard, thought him “a morose, melancholy person.”

There was one thing about him that everyone noticed. “He had a wonderful pair of blue eyes,” McGaw writes. “They seemed to search into the very depth of your inmost being, and they seemed also to shine out of the soul of a prophet.” People who could not hear much from him found themselves being looked at, and remembered it.

It is a strange picture of a missionary: a young man who was hard of hearing and slow to answer, shy by nature, and sent to learn two languages in a hurry and preach in them to crowds. If a mission board today were selecting candidates by aptitude, it might well have turned him down.

“Who Hath Made Man’s Mouth?”

Moses made the same objection when God called him. “Oh, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exodus 4:10, ASV). It was a reasonable complaint. Moses was being sent to argue with Pharaoh and to lead a nation, and his gifts did not seem to fit the task.

God’s reply, which stands at the head of this chapter, does not deny the problem. It goes behind it. “Who hath made man’s mouth? or who maketh a man dumb, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? is it not I, Jehovah?” The limitations Moses was worried about were not accidents that had escaped God’s notice. They were part of the man God had made and was now sending. And the promise that followed was not “I will make you eloquent” but “I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt speak.”

Paul, who had his own weakness to carry, learned the same lesson in a different form. When he pleaded for his “thorn in the flesh” to be removed, the answer was, “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness.” And Paul drew the conclusion: “Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest upon me” (2 Corinthians 12:9, ASV). He reminded the Corinthians that he had come to them “not with excellency of speech or of wisdom,” but “in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling,” so that their faith “should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:1, 3, 5, ASV).

Hyde’s deafness and slowness of speech were never removed. He was deaf to the end. What changed was not the weakness but what God did through it.

“First Things First”

New missionaries in the Punjab were expected to give their first years mainly to language study, working with a munshi, a language teacher, and sitting examinations set by the mission. One later reference work says Hyde began his study at Dehra Dun, in the hills north of the plains. Wherever it began, it did not go as the mission expected.

McGaw tells the story with evident relish. Hyde started on the language work, “but later neglected it for Bible study. He was reprimanded by the committee, but he replied: ‘First things first.’ He argued that he had come to India to teach the Bible, and he needed to know it before he could teach it.”

It is easy to admire this story too quickly. From the committee’s point of view, a new missionary who was already hard of hearing and slow of speech, and who then neglected his language study, was a real worry. They were right to be concerned. A missionary who cannot speak the language of the people will never reach them, however well he knows his Bible in English. Hyde was not wholly right, and later in life he may well have admitted it.

But he was not wholly wrong either. He had grasped something the committee was in danger of forgetting. The purpose of learning Urdu and Punjabi was to speak about God’s word, and a man who knew the words of a language but not the Word of God would have nothing to say in it. “Seek ye first his kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you” (Matthew 6:33, ASV). McGaw adds, and it is an important addition, that Hyde “did not neglect language study” altogether. He simply refused to let it crowd out the Scriptures. And “God by his Spirit wonderfully opened up the Scriptures to him.”

The psalmist prayed, “Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law” (Psalm 119:18, ASV). That was the prayer of Hyde’s early years in India. He could hardly hear the people around him, and he could not yet speak to them. So he gave himself to listening to God.

A Tongue Loosed

For years the outcome looked doubtful. Griswold remembered that during Hyde’s first decade “it was thought that his command of the vernacular of the Punjab would never be of the best.” Then something changed. “The baptism of the Spirit and the fire of love,” Griswold wrote, “loosed his tongue and gave him free utterance.”

By the end of his life Hyde was recognised as an effective speaker in three languages. The Indian Witness, a Methodist weekly, called him “an acceptable speaker in Urdu, Punjabi and in English,” and added that “it was always the man of holiness and power back of an address which made it indeed a message.” McGaw’s sources went further, saying that he became “a correct and easy speaker” and could hold audiences of hundreds of Indians spellbound. Jones, who did not know Urdu well himself, reported what Urdu speakers told him: that Hyde “spoke the language well, if anything a little highflown, using the book-language more than the colloquial.” That is a lovely detail. It is exactly what one would expect of a man who had learned his Urdu partly through long hours with an Urdu Bible.

Isaiah has a verse that could stand over this part of Hyde’s life: “The Lord Jehovah hath given me the tongue of them that are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him that is weary: he wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as they that are taught” (Isaiah 50:4, ASV). The tongue of the taught comes from the ear of the taught. Hyde’s friends noticed that he rose very early, morning after morning, to pray and read. The words that later reached so many came out of those hours of listening.

Misunderstood

The slow years had another cost. Hyde’s way of life puzzled his colleagues, and for a long time many of them did not approve.

Jones first met him around 1906, at a conference of the Punjab Mission in Ludhiana. Afterwards Jones talked with several of the missionaries about him and found “that he had been misunderstood by them.” They had not approved of “the way he spent so much of his time in prayer.” Griswold confirms that Hyde “was sometimes criticised by his brethren for the rigorous and ascetic nature of his piety, for the way in which he seemed to deny to the flesh even its just claims.” Some thought him impractical. It did not help that, as Griswold also said, “he had not the gifts of an organizer.” In a mission that depended on schools, accounts, committees, and careful administration, a man who prayed all night and forgot his meals did not always look like an asset.

Years later Jones asked Hyde whether he had realised, in those early years, that his colleagues disapproved of him. Hyde smiled, Jones says, “that sweet smile which one can never forget,” and answered: “Oh, yes, I knew it, but they did not understand me, that was all, they never intended to be unkind.” Jones added: “There was not one atom of bitterness as far as I could see.”

It is a small exchange, and it tells us a great deal. Hyde knew he was criticised. He did not pretend otherwise. But he refused to interpret his colleagues’ disapproval as malice. He assumed the best about them: they did not understand, and they did not mean to hurt him. That habit of charitable interpretation would be tested far more severely before his life was over. Here it already shows its roots.

Home for a Season

In the spring of 1901 Hyde went home to America on his first furlough. The women’s missionary magazine of his church recorded his arrival at New York on 15 May 1901, “from Ferozepore,” with a forwarding address at Prairie City, Illinois. He had been in India eight and a half years. McGaw saw him that year and did not see him alive again.

The furlough seems to have been partly for his health. When he sailed back from New York on 17 September 1902, the magazine noted that he and another returning missionary had “been doing much visiting,” and added the hope that they were “in more vigorous health than when they came home.” During that year he had spoken at the annual meeting of the Presbyterian women’s board of the Northwest, held in Omaha, stepping in when another missionary could not come.

He sailed back to India in September 1902 as he had left it: a faithful, quiet, somewhat misunderstood missionary with modest results. He was a few weeks short of thirty-seven. Nothing in the mission records of that year would suggest that the next ten years would be any different from the first. Many Christians carry some limitation they wish God would remove: a slowness of speech, a weakness of body, a shy temperament, a lack of the gifts their work seems to need. John Hyde carried several of these at once. They were not removed. He remained deaf and never became an organizer. By nature he remained more inclined to silence than to talk.

What God did instead was to give him the tongue of the taught, a loosened tongue fed by a listening ear. And he gave him the grace to be misunderstood for ten years without bitterness. If your first ten years of faithful service have been “steady, patient, but not especially fruitful,” John Hyde’s story does not promise that the next ten will be different. But it does show that such years are not wasted. They may be the soil in which everything else is growing.

Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt speak.” — Exodus 4:11-12, ASV Not a Remarkable Missionary If the story of John Hyde were a legend, it would move straight from the ship and the open-air meeting to triumph. A young man is filled with the Spirit and set free from sin, and he goes out at once to win the Punjab. That is not what happened, and every early witness is honest about it. “At the first,” McGaw writes, “John Hyde was not a remarkable missionary.” His colleague H. D. Griswold, writing the obituary in 1912, was blunter still. Hyde’s first ten years in India, he said, “were marked by steady, patient, but not especially fruitful service.” Ten years is a long time. It is the whole career of many missionaries, who go out young, serve a single term or two, and come home. If Hyde had been one of them, no one would ever have written a book about him. The reasons for those slow years were partly outside his control. The work in the villages of the Punjab was hard and slow for everyone. But some of the reasons lay in Hyde himself, and his friends named them with affection and without pretending. “He Seemed Not to Hear” Hyde was slow of speech. McGaw’s informants remembered that “when a question or a remark was directed to him he seemed not to hear, or if he heard he seemed a long time in framing a reply.” Part of the reason was physical. “His hearing was slightly defective,” McGaw says, “and this it was feared would hinder him in acquiring the language.” Pengwern Jones, who knew him in his last years, says without qualification that “Mr. Hyde himself was deaf.” The deafness seems to have grown worse with time. In his final spring in Britain he told an elderly woman that he could rarely hear anything at all when he went to church. He was also, by temperament, quiet and withdrawn. Paterson, his closest friend, wrote that Hyde “was not naturally a bright and happy man. On the contrary he was in himself inclined to be morose, retiring, shy and silent.” McGaw’s sources describe a disposition “gentle and quiet” that seemed “to be lacking in the enthusiasm and zeal which a young missionary should have.” Some colleagues, Jones heard, thought him “a morose, melancholy person.” There was one thing about him that everyone noticed. “He had a wonderful pair of blue eyes,” McGaw writes. “They seemed to search into the very depth of your inmost being, and they seemed also to shine out of the soul of a prophet.” People who could not hear much from him found themselves being looked at, and remembered it. It is a strange picture of a missionary: a young man who was hard of hearing and slow to answer, shy by nature, and sent to learn two languages in a hurry and preach in them to crowds. If a mission board today were selecting candidates by aptitude, it might well have turned him down. “Who Hath Made Man’s Mouth?” Moses made the same objection when God called him. “Oh, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exodus 4:10, ASV). It was a reasonable complaint. Moses was being sent to argue with Pharaoh and to lead a nation, and his gifts did not seem to fit the task. God’s reply, which stands at the head of this chapter, does not deny the problem. It goes behind it. “Who hath made man’s mouth? or who maketh a man dumb, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? is it not I, Jehovah?” The limitations Moses was worried about were not accidents that had escaped God’s notice. They were part of the man God had made and was now sending. And the promise that followed was not “I will make you eloquent” but “I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt speak.” Paul, who had his own weakness to carry, learned the same lesson in a different form. fields.title: The Punjab He Entered
fields.body_html:
“but God chose the foolish things of the world, that he might put to shame them that are wise; and God chose the weak things of the world, that he might put to shame the things that are strong; and the base things of the world, and the things that are despised, did God choose, yea and the things that are not, that he might bring to nought the things that are”

— 1 Corinthians 1:27-28, ASV

The Land of Five Rivers

It is impossible to understand John Hyde’s life without understanding the place where he spent it, and the people among whom he worked. The devotional books about him say little about either. They move quickly from the prayer room to the next prayer room, and the Punjab appears only as a backdrop of villages and heat. But the Punjab was not a backdrop. It was a real society, going through one of the most remarkable religious movements in the modern history of India, and Hyde’s prayers and preaching belonged to that movement.

The Punjab takes its name from five rivers, the tributaries of the Indus, that cross its broad plain from the Himalayas toward the south-west. In Hyde’s day it was a province of British India. Most of it now lies in Pakistan, and part in India. It was a land of farming villages, of wheat and cotton and sugar cane, fed increasingly by great new irrigation canals. Its people were Muslims, Hindus, and Sikhs, with a very small number of Christians. And like the rest of Indian society, its villages were ordered by caste.

Two Missions, One Field

Hyde belonged to the Punjab Mission of the Presbyterian Church in the United States of America. American Presbyterians had arrived in Ludhiana in 1834, and the mission had been known for most of its history as the Lodiana Mission. By Hyde’s time it had stations in a string of towns across the eastern Punjab: Ludhiana, Jagraon, Ferozepore, Jullundur, Lahore, Kasur, and others. The seminary catalogue sums up Hyde’s entire career in a single line: “miss. Ferozepore, India, ‘92–’12.” Ferozepore, now Firozpur, on the Sutlej river near today’s border between India and Pakistan, was his home station. From it, and later from Ludhiana, he worked the villages of the surrounding districts.

Another American Presbyterian body, the United Presbyterian Church of North America, had its own mission farther north and west, centred on the town of Sialkot. It is important to keep the two apart, because many books about Hyde blur them. Sialkot, whose convention would make Hyde famous, was never his station. It was the United Presbyterians’ town. Hyde travelled there each year for the convention and was a guest on their ground. The two missions were friendly and cooperated closely, and the Church of Scotland also worked nearby. But they were different churches with different missionaries, and the great movement toward Christ that shaped the region began in the United Presbyterian field.

A Lame Man Named Ditt

That movement began with a man who would never have appeared in any account of India’s leaders.

His name was Ditt. He lived in a village near Mirali, some thirty miles from Sialkot, and he earned a meagre living by buying hides in the neighbourhood and selling them on at a small profit. The United Presbyterian missionary Andrew Gordon described him as “a dark little man, lame of one leg, quiet and modest in his manner, with sincerity and earnestness well expressed in his face.” He belonged to the community then called the Chuhras. These were landless labourers, sweepers, and scavengers, at the very bottom of the Punjab’s caste order and treated as untouchable by those above them. The name itself was used with contempt and is today regarded as a slur. Their descendants make up much of the Christian community of Pakistan and the Indian Punjab.

Ditt heard the gospel from a Christian convert of higher caste, and around 1873 he asked the Rev. Samuel Martin to baptize him. Then he did something the missionaries had rarely seen. He did not ask to stay at the mission compound, as converts often did when their families cast them out. He went home. His relatives were furious. Gordon records his sister-in-law’s curse: “One of your legs is broken already; so may it be with the other.” Ditt answered, “Very well, my brethren; if it pleases you, you may oppose me and load me with reproaches and abuse; but your opposition will never induce me to deny Christ.”

In August 1873, three months after his own public confession, Ditt walked the thirty miles to Sialkot, lame as he was, with his wife, his daughter, and two neighbours, to present them for baptism. The following February he brought four more men. They too went straight home. The gospel began to pass from family to family and village to village along the lines of kinship, in the ordinary conversations of people whom no one else had ever thought worth converting.

A People Movement

What followed is known to historians as a mass movement or people movement. Over the next fifty years hundreds of thousands of people from the Chuhra community across the Punjab turned to Christ. They came not usually one by one, as missionaries had expected converts to come, but in families and groups. Each group decided together.

The numbers are striking. The census of the Punjab counted 3,912 Indian Christians in 1881. By 1901 there were 38,513. By 1911, the year Hyde left India for the last time, there were 163,994. The membership of the United Presbyterian mission alone grew from a few hundred in the late 1870s to over 24,000 by 1911, and its whole Christian community to more than 46,000. Hyde’s own mission shared in the movement. In the year he died its magazine reported two thousand baptisms “among low caste converts” in a single year.

The missionaries did not all welcome this. Some worried that people were coming for the wrong reasons: for the dignity and protection the church seemed to offer, or in hope of help, land, or education. The Punjab’s census superintendent in 1911, Pandit Harikishan Kaul, thought the movement was driven mainly by the converts’ desire for “enhanced dignity and social status.” Some missionaries worried that converts were baptized with too little instruction. A later study noted that Ditt himself “was baptized without instruction.” Others worried that a church made up almost entirely of the poorest and least educated people could never support itself or lead itself. These were serious questions, and serious people argued about them.

But others, and John Hyde was among them, saw in the movement something the apostle Paul would have recognised at once. The verse at the head of this chapter was written to a church in Corinth that had few prominent members: “not many wise after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called” (1 Corinthians 1:26, ASV). God, Paul says, deliberately chose “the base things of the world, and the things that are despised,” to shame the proud. The gospel had always gone first to the poor. Jesus announced his ministry with the words, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me to preach good tidings to the poor” (Luke 4:18, ASV). James asked his readers, “Did not God choose them that are poor as to the world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he promised to them that love him?” (James 2:5, ASV).

Hyde’s District

We have, unusually, an official picture of the work Hyde was doing in the middle of this movement. It comes from the printed report of the Punjab Mission for 1907.

Until the spring of that year or the one before (the report says “until April last”), the village work of the Ludhiana station “was solely in the hands of Rev. J. N. Hyde.” The district was then reorganised into four circles, each under a missionary with an Indian evangelist or pastor living in the central town. Hyde was made superintendent of the Moga circle, a district of 275 villages. The resident evangelist was an Indian worker named Jalal Masih. Missionaries travelled by rail where they could and by horse or two-wheeled cart in the remoter places. Luggage went by village ox cart. The aim was to visit every village at least once a year.

The same report summarises Hyde’s own observations on the people he was reaching, and they are among the few independent records we have of his views. Practical interest in religion, the report gives his testimony, was “limited almost entirely to the low castes. Only one convert came from another class. He was a Sikh.” The work among the low castes “advances generally along the lines of relationship,” from family to family, as it had in Ditt’s village. The farmers who employed the low-caste labourers often opposed the work, from fear “that if the low castes become Christians, they will refuse to serve them as they have done.” Yet Hyde also saw something hopeful among the higher castes. According to the report, he testified that “the better classes are drawn toward Christianity, being convinced that the religion which can elevate the lower classes must be the true religion. They see in Christians love not seen in their own.”

The report also records his testimony about what the gospel did in the lives of converts: “an immediate change in their conduct. They are more truthful, more patient, cease to worship idols, some of them become prayerful in their homes and endure persecution for Christ’s sake.”

Finally, the report quotes Hyde directly on how village work should be done. It is short enough to memorise, and it is worth doing so:

Begin the day in prayer and praise with your helpers. Then divide and go to the various parts of the town. Follow up inquirers and Christian converts in their places of work. Preach and baptize on the spot. Every time we visit a convert, we try to leave some lesson or some influence on his life.

There is nothing mystical in these sentences. They are practical instructions from a working evangelist. But the first sentence holds the key to everything else: begin the day in prayer and praise.

Among the Despised

The devotional sources add warmth to this official outline. One of McGaw’s informants, who once attended one of Hyde’s conventions for Christians, remembered how Hyde would meet his village converts as they arrived and embrace them “in Oriental style, laying his hand first on one shoulder and then on the other.” He did the same to Christians “of the lowest caste,” and he persuaded others to do likewise. The same witness thought it Hyde’s “strong point. Love won him victories.”

To understand why this mattered, we need to remember what caste meant in the Punjab of 1900. Members of the higher castes would not eat with Chuhras, touch them, or take water from their hands. Some missionaries unconsciously carried their own racial and social distances into their relations with converts. A European missionary publicly embracing a low-caste village Christian was making a statement that everyone present understood. Jones remembered that at the conventions it was often “Gulla, the sweeper” who carried a plate of curry and rice to Hyde in the prayer room. One of his Indian evangelists remembered sharing a village mud house with him, and Jones heard that Hyde “lived with them, he ate and slept with them.”

Paul told the Galatians, “There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28, ASV). In the Punjab that verse had a sharp edge. The church that grew from Ditt’s village was a church of the despised. And the missionaries who served it well were those who did not merely preach to them but lived among them as brothers. Griswold, writing Hyde’s obituary, singled this out: he would be greatly missed “by humble village preachers with whom he lived as a brother.”

Opposition

The movement also provoked resistance. In the same years, reforming Hindu organisations were growing in the Punjab. The most active was the Arya Samaj, founded in 1875. It worked hard to win low-caste communities back from Christianity and Islam, and sometimes it saw particular missionaries as threats. Jones later heard from an Indian doctor that the Arya Samaj had been troubled by Hyde’s influence and by the number of people baptized under his preaching. It had tried to find a fault in his life that it could publish. That story belongs to a later chapter. It is mentioned here only to show that Hyde’s work was not carried on in a vacuum. It was part of a contest for the souls, and the loyalties, of the poorest people in the Punjab.

For Reflection

The prayers of John Hyde, which this book will now begin to follow closely, were not prayers for an abstraction called “India.” They were prayers for particular villages full of particular people, most of them poor, many of them despised by their neighbours, and all of them precious to God. When he later cried, “Father, give me these souls, or I die,” he was thinking of faces he knew.

That is worth remembering whenever we are tempted to think of prayer as a spiritual exercise detached from the real world. Hyde’s prayer life grew up in the middle of one of the great people movements in Christian history. Its fruit was counted in baptisms in the villages of the Moga district, among people whom the world thought least likely to matter. God still chooses such people. Our prayers should follow his choosing.

A People Movement What followed is known to historians as a mass movement or people movement. Over the next fifty years hundreds of thousands of people from the Chuhra community across the Punjab turned to Christ. They came not usually one by one, as missionaries had expected converts to come, but in families and groups. Each group decided together. The numbers are striking. The census of the Punjab counted 3,912 Indian Christians in 1881. By 1901 there were 38,513. By 1911, the year Hyde left India for the last time, there were 163,994. The membership of the United Presbyterian mission alone grew from a few hundred in the late 1870s to over 24,000 by 1911, and its whole Christian community to more than 46,000. Hyde’s own mission shared in the movement. In the year he died its magazine reported two thousand baptisms “among low caste converts” in a single year. The missionaries did not all welcome this. Some worried that people were coming for the wrong reasons: for the dignity and protection the church seemed to offer, or in hope of help, land, or education. The Punjab’s census superintendent in 1911, Pandit Harikishan Kaul, thought the movement was driven mainly by the converts’ desire for “enhanced dignity and social status.” Some missionaries worried that converts were baptized with too little instruction. A later study noted that Ditt himself “was baptized without instruction.” Others worried that a church made up almost entirely of the poorest and least educated people could never support itself or lead itself. These were serious questions, and serious people argued about them. But others, and John Hyde was among them, saw in the movement something the apostle Paul would have recognised at once. The verse at the head of this chapter was written to a church in Corinth that had few prominent members: “not many wise after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called” (1 Corinthians 1:26, ASV). God, Paul says, deliberately chose “the base things of the world, and the things that are despised,” to shame the proud. The gospel had always gone first to the poor. Jesus announced his ministry with the words, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me to preach good tidings to the poor” (Luke 4:18, ASV). James asked his readers, “Did not God choose them that are poor as to the world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he promised to them that love him?” (James 2:5, ASV). Hyde’s District We have, unusually, an official picture of the work Hyde was doing in the middle of this movement. It comes from the printed report of the Punjab Mission for 1907. Until the spring of that year or the one before (the report says “until April last”), the village work of the Ludhiana station “was solely in the hands of Rev. J. N. Hyde.” The district was then reorganised into four circles, each under a missionary with an Indian evangelist or pastor living in the central town. Hyde was made superintendent of the Moga circle, a district of 275 villages. The resident evangelist was an Indian worker named Jalal Masih. Missionaries travelled by rail where they could and by horse or two-wheeled cart in the remoter places. Luggage went by village ox cart. The aim was to visit every village at least once a year. The same report summarises Hyde’s own observations on the people he was reaching, and they are among the few independent records we have of his views. Practical interest in religion, the report gives his testimony, was “limited almost entirely to the low castes. Only one convert came from another class. He was a Sikh.” The work among the low castes “advances generally along the lines of relationship,” from family to family, as it had in Ditt’s village. The farmers who employed the low-caste labourers often opposed the work, from fear “that if the low castes become Christians, they will refuse to serve them as they have done.” Yet Hyde also saw something hopeful among the higher castes. According to the report, he testified that “the better classes are drawn toward Christianity, being convinced that the religion which can elevate the lower classes must be the true religion. They see in Christians love not seen in their own.” The report also records his testimony about what the gospel did in the lives of converts: “an immediate change in their conduct. They are more truthful, more patient, cease to worship idols, some of them become prayerful in their homes and endure persecution for Christ’s sake.” Finally, the report quotes Hyde directly on how village work should be done. It is short enough to memorise, and it is worth doing so: Begin the day in prayer and praise with your helpers. Then divide and go to the various parts of the town. Follow up inquirers and Christian converts in their places of work. Preach and baptize on the spot. Every time we visit a convert, we try to leave some lesson or some influence on his life. There is nothing mystical in these sentences. They are practical instructions from a working evangelist. But the first sentence holds the key to everything else: begin the day in prayer and praise. Among the Despised The devotional sources add warmth to this official outline. One of McGaw’s informants, who once attended one of Hyde’s conventions for Christians, remembered how Hyde would meet his village converts as they arrived and embrace them “in Oriental style, laying his hand first on one shoulder and then on the other.” He did the same to Christians “of the lowest caste,” and he persuaded others to do likewise. The same witness thought it Hyde’s “strong point. Love won him victories.” To understand why this mattered, we need to remember what caste meant in the Punjab of 1900. Members of the higher castes would not eat with Chuhras, touch them, or take water from their hands. Some missionaries unconsciously carried their own racial and social distances into their relations with converts. A European missionary publicly embracing a low-caste village Christian was making a statement that everyone present understood. Jones remembered that at the conventions it was often “Gulla, the sweeper” who carried a plate of curry and rice to Hyde in the prayer room. One of his Indian evangelists remembered sharing a village mud house with him, and Jones heard that Hyde “lived with them, he ate and slept with them.” Paul told the Galatians, “There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28, ASV). In the Punjab that verse had a sharp edge. The church that grew from Ditt’s village was a church of the despised. And the missionaries who served it well were those who did not merely preach to them but lived among them as brothers. Griswold, writing Hyde’s obituary, singled this out: he would be greatly missed “by humble village preachers with whom he lived as a brother.” Opposition The movement also provoked resistance. In the same years, reforming Hindu organisations were growing in the Punjab. The most active was the Arya Samaj, founded in 1875. It worked hard to win low-caste communities back from Christianity and Islam, and sometimes it saw particular missionaries as threats. Jones later heard from an Indian doctor that the Arya Samaj had been troubled by Hyde’s influence and by the number of people baptized under his preaching. It had tried to find a fault in his life that it could publish. That story belongs to a later chapter. It is mentioned here only to show that Hyde’s work was not carried on in a vacuum. It was part of a contest for the souls, and the loyalties, of the poorest people in the Punjab. For Reflection The prayers of John Hyde, which this book will now begin to follow closely, were not prayers for an abstraction called “India.” They were prayers for particular villages full of particular people, most of them poor, many of them despised by their neighbours, and all of them precious to God. When he later cried, “Father, give me these souls, or I die,” he was thinking of faces he knew. That is worth remembering whenever we are tempted to think of prayer as a spiritual exercise detached from the real world. Hyde’s prayer life grew up in the middle of one of the great people movements in Christian history. Its fruit was counted in baptisms in the villages of the Moga district, among people whom the world thought least likely to matter. God still chooses such people. Our prayers should follow his choosing.

fields.title: Preparing the Messenger
fields.body_html:
“And it came to pass in these days, that he went out into the mountain to pray; and he continued all night in prayer to God.”

— Luke 6:12, ASV

The Man Who Never Sleeps

Somewhere in the Punjab, at some point in his middle years, the people began to call John Hyde by a new name. Griswold recorded it in the obituary: “He was mystical in temperament, and used to give himself day and night to prayer. So much so that he was called, by the people, ‘the man who never sleeps.’”

It was not a literal description. Hyde did sleep, though his friends agreed that he slept remarkably little and often in odd places. Jones once watched him, in a crowded prayer room, go aside into a corner and throw himself on the floor to sleep, and then spring up again when the prayer began to flag. But the name captured something the people around him had noticed. At whatever hour of the night they passed his room, there seemed to be a light burning, and a man on his knees or on his face.

How did this begin? The later legend tends to present Hyde as a man of prayer from the start, as though he stepped off the boat already praying through the night. His friends knew otherwise. The whole nights of prayer came later, and they began, as far as we can tell, in the most ordinary way imaginable: with a talk he had not finished preparing.

A Sleepless Night of Preparation

Jones asked Hyde once how the Lord had taught him to spend whole nights in prayer. Hyde told him a story that has a pleasing lack of drama.

Some time before, he said, he was due to give a Bible reading at a Bible school one morning. He had not had enough time to prepare it, so he stayed up the whole night working on it. The message was ready by morning, and the talk went well enough. But afterwards a thought came to him. He had spent a night getting the message ready. Was there not a need to get himself ready too? “Would not a night of prayer and praise be a good preparation for a real blessing the following day?”

Jones was sure it was “the Holy Spirit’s suggestion.” That night Hyde remained in prayer the whole night. He “enjoyed it so much that he repeated it the following night.” Others heard of it and joined him, some for part of the time and some for the whole night. The practice that would make him famous had begun.

Hyde did not stop preparing his talks. Jones insists that he “was always careful in his preparation for his Bible readings, sermons or Convention addresses.” But from then on he often said something that Jones never forgot: “the preparation of the Messenger was quite as important as the preparation of the message.”

Two Kinds of Preparation

That sentence deserves to be written over the desk of every preacher, teacher, and Christian worker. Most of us who speak about God put almost all our effort into the message: its structure, its illustrations, its accuracy, its application. That work matters, and Hyde did not despise it. But the message is only half of what happens when someone speaks for God. The other half is the messenger, the state of the heart that the words come through.

Paul expressed the same double concern when he told Timothy, “Take heed to thyself, and to thy teaching” (1 Timothy 4:16, ASV). And the apostles in Jerusalem, when they were being pulled into administration, protected both halves: “But we will continue stedfastly in prayer, and in the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4, ASV). Notice the order. Prayer comes first, and then the ministry of the word.

Jesus himself is the supreme example. The verse at the head of this chapter describes the night before he chose the twelve apostles: “he went out into the mountain to pray; and he continued all night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12, ASV). The next morning he called his disciples and chose the twelve. Mark records another morning, after a crowded day of healing: “in the morning, a great while before day, he rose up and went out, and departed into a desert place, and there prayed” (Mark 1:35, ASV). If the Son of God prepared himself in prayer for the work of the next day, it is hard to see how his servants can do without it.

“Morning by Morning”

Hyde’s nights of prayer attracted attention, and later writers have tended to make them the whole story. But his friends describe something more steady and more imitable: a daily discipline of early rising, Scripture, and prayer.

Griswold, describing Hyde’s last years at Moga, wrote that “the early morning would be given up to prayer and Bible study, and then being armed with the whole armour of God, Mr. Hyde and his fellow workers would go forth to do valiant battle for the Lord.” Jones, who shared a room with him for a week, noticed that Hyde was “on his knees long before I was up in the morning, though I was up with the dawn.” He also saw that Hyde “would also light the lamp several times in the night and feast on some passage of the word and then have a little talk with the Master.” A friend in Calcutta, lying awake with an illness in a room across the passage, watched Hyde’s electric light flash on at twelve, at two, at four, and at five. From five o’clock it stayed on until sunrise.

This was not a technique. It was a relationship with a God who, as Isaiah says, “wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as they that are taught” (Isaiah 50:4, ASV). The Calcutta friend was so struck by what he saw that he began to ask God to wake him too. At first he woke at two in the morning, and later at four, “with striking regularity.” He had always claimed exemption from night watches because he was too tired. Now he found it a joy.

The Bible Always Open

Jones noticed one more thing about the way Hyde prayed, and it may be the most important of all. “His Bible was always in his hand,” Jones wrote, “even when we had our morning cup of tea, he regaled me with manna from the Word. When he knelt to pray, the dear old Book was always open before him and his hands rested on it. Face to face with the Lord and resting on the promises.”

Hyde’s prayer was not a flight into vague spiritual feeling. It was anchored in Scripture. He prayed God’s promises back to God, as the psalmists and prophets did. When he prayed at the conventions he would take a single phrase of Scripture and repeat it slowly, with long pauses, until those around him felt that God had heard. The long nights were full of Bible reading. The lamp he lit several times a night was lit to read by.

Here Hyde was in line with every great intercessor of Scripture. Daniel, before his great prayer of confession, had been reading Jeremiah: “I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years … for the accomplishing of the desolations of Jerusalem” (Daniel 9:2, ASV). Then he “set my face unto the Lord God, to seek by prayer and supplications” (Daniel 9:3, ASV). The Word showed him what to pray for. Prayer that is fed by Scripture has somewhere to stand.

A Voice from 1896

We are fortunate to have a few paragraphs from a talk Hyde gave in these middle years, and it lets us hear how he spoke to others about the life he was learning. In 1896 the Student Volunteer Movement held a series of conferences for students in India, at Jaffna, Bombay, Lahore, Lucknow, Calcutta, and Madras. The American missions leader John R. Mott was present at Lahore, and Hyde gave an address there titled “The Life on Wings.” It was printed that year in Madras in a small volume of conference addresses. More than twenty-five years later an Indian Christian found a stained copy in a Calcutta second-hand bookshop. The bookseller would not take payment for it because it was spoiled, and part of the address was reprinted in the memoirs of 1923.

The surviving extract is about discouragement. There are times in Christian work, Hyde told the students, when “Satan seems to have struck a hard blow at the work, and one is fighting against discouragement.” At such times he found strength in a passage from the story of King Asa, which he quoted in the older wording, “The Lord is with you while ye be with him”, and which the ASV renders, “Jehovah is with you, while ye are with him” (2 Chronicles 15:2, ASV). The worker who knows he has not forsaken the Lord knows that the Lord has not forsaken him, and “with this promise he can say to Satan: ‘Wait and see who will have the victory.’” Hyde then quoted Asa’s prayer before battle, which the ASV renders: “Jehovah, there is none besides thee to help, between the mighty and him that hath no strength: help us, O Jehovah our God; for we rely on thee, and in thy name are we come against this multitude” (2 Chronicles 14:11, ASV).

Out of such prayer, Hyde went on, “when strength comes and one rests in the word ‘Father,’ there comes to one an experience in which he feels as it were on wings.” He took his title from Isaiah: “but they that wait for Jehovah shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles” (Isaiah 40:31, ASV). And then he asked the students a direct question: “My friend, can you say that word ‘Father’?”

He ended with the problem of fruitlessness, a problem he knew from the inside after four years of slow work. He told an old sermon story about a Scottish minister whose elders complained that only one person had joined the church in a whole year, and that one a boy. The boy, the story goes, became the great missionary Robert Moffat. It is the kind of anecdote whose details no one has ever been able to trace, and Hyde probably told it as he had heard it. The lesson he drew from it was his own. “The harvest of faithful work is sure. It may be, however, we have wanted results instead of wishing that needy souls might have life, and that Christ might see of the travail of His soul and be satisfied. Have we ever wept for souls? Have you? Have I?”

That last question, Have I?, is the voice of a man who was still learning what he taught. Within a decade he would be weeping for souls in a way that his friends found almost frightening. In 1896 he was only beginning to ask.

Not a Method but a Master

It would be easy to turn this chapter into a programme: rise early, read your Bible with your hands on it, pray through the night before important days. Hyde’s friends were anxious to prevent exactly that. Jones remembered how often Hyde told him “that he was afraid of following the example of men, and he dreaded lest any one should try to follow his example.” Jones begged his own readers to follow Hyde’s prayer life and prayer spirit, “but not necessarily in the ‘form’ that he manifested it.” Many Christians, he pointed out, could not physically do what Hyde did. But every Christian can make prayer “their very breath.”

That warning will matter more and more as this book goes on, because Hyde’s body paid a heavy price for his way of praying. For now it is enough to notice where it began. It did not begin with a heroic resolution to pray all night. It began with a man who noticed that he had spent a whole night preparing a message and none preparing himself, and who decided that this was the wrong way round.

For Reflection

Most of us are more comfortable preparing messages than preparing ourselves. Messages can be finished, and they can be checked and improved. Preparing the messenger is slower and less visible. It means time before God, with the Word open and the heart exposed.

John Hyde did not stop preparing his talks. He simply refused to believe that a well-prepared talk was enough. “The preparation of the Messenger is quite as important as the preparation of the message.” Whatever work God has given us, whether preaching, teaching, parenting, nursing, managing, or writing, the principle holds. The one who does the work needs preparing too, and only God can do it.

fields.title: The Half-Hour Rule
fields.body_html:
“I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem; they shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that are Jehovah’s remembrancers, take ye no rest, and give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.”

— Isaiah 62:6-7, ASV

Before the Fire

Revivals are usually remembered for their public moments: crowded meetings, weeping congregations, confessions, conversions, songs that go on past midnight. Those moments are real, and later chapters will describe several of them. But the people who were closest to the awakening that came to the Punjab in the years after 1904 were insistent that its public moments were not its beginning. The United Presbyterian mission’s own history, first published in 1909, said that the revival “had its springs in hidden resources of prayer that reached back several years.”

McGaw put it more vividly. “In every revival,” he wrote, “there is a divine side and a human side.” In the Welsh revival of 1904, which was then being reported across the Christian world, the divine side seemed to dominate. There was “no organization and very little preaching.” The Sialkot revival was different. It was, McGaw insisted, “just as certainly sent down from heaven,” but it came through human means: “organization … a certain amount of definite planning, and … seasons of long continued prayer.” He quoted the American evangelist Charles Finney, who had famously argued that revival is no more a miracle than a crop of wheat. It comes, that is, when people use the means that God has appointed.

The chief of those means, in the Punjab, was a small and very ordinary organisation called the Punjab Prayer Union.

A Union of the Willing

Carré’s book dates the beginning of the Prayer Union to “about April, 1904.” It was begun, the memoir says, by “a few souls” on whom “the burden of united prayer for Revival had been heavily laid.” Hyde was “one of the moving spirits.” Later books have sometimes called him its founder, but the early sources do not claim that, and it is fairer to say what they say. He was one of a small group of missionaries in the Punjab who, in the spring of 1904, agreed to pray together for an awakening, and who invited others to join them.

The Union was not an institution in any grand sense. It had no buildings and, as far as we know, no staff. It was a covenant among individuals, held together by a simple pledge and an annual meeting each spring. The sources do not list its members. They seem to have come from more than one mission, and to have included Indian workers as well as missionaries. What united them was a shared conviction that the church in the Punjab needed a fresh work of God, and that the first thing to do about it was to ask him.

Five Questions

The only surviving text of the Union’s pledge is the one McGaw printed in 1923. He says its principles were “stated in the form of questions which were signed by those becoming members.” There were five:

1. Are you praying for quickening in your own life, in the life of your fellow-workers, and in the Church?

2. Are you longing for greater power of the Holy Spirit in your own life and work, and are you convinced that you cannot go on without this power?

3. Will you pray that you may not be ashamed of Jesus?

4. Do you believe that prayer is the great means for securing this spiritual awakening?

5. Will you set apart one-half hour each day as soon after noon as possible to pray for this awakening, and are you willing to pray till the awakening comes?

It is worth reading these slowly, because their order is carefully thought out.

The first question begins with the member’s own life before it turns to anyone else’s. The prayer is for quickening “in your own life,” then in “your fellow-workers,” and only then “in the Church.” No one could join the Union in order to pray for other people’s revival while exempting themselves.

The second question asks about longing and about helplessness. It is not enough to think that more of the Holy Spirit’s power would be a good thing. The member is asked whether he is “convinced that you cannot go on without this power.” That is the language of desperation, not of improvement. Jesus said, “Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled” (Matthew 5:6, ASV). The Union was for the hungry.

The third question is the most surprising. After asking members to pray for power, it asks them to pray “that you may not be ashamed of Jesus.” It is a humbling prayer for missionaries to pray, people who had crossed the world for the sake of Christ. But the authors of the pledge knew their own hearts. It is quite possible to work for Jesus for years and still flinch from naming him plainly before those who despise him. Jesus warned that “whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of man also shall be ashamed of him, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels” (Mark 8:38, ASV). Paul could say, “I am not ashamed of the gospel: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Romans 1:16, ASV). The Prayer Union asked its members to pray for that boldness.

The fourth question is about conviction: “Do you believe that prayer is the great means for securing this spiritual awakening?” It does not say the only means. The members went on preaching, teaching, and organising. But it says the great means. Prayer is not the thing one does when all else has failed. It is the first thing.

And the fifth question is the practical heart of the whole covenant: half an hour each day, as soon after noon as possible, “till the awakening comes.”

Why Half an Hour, and Why Noon?

It is striking how modest this commitment was. The Union did not ask its members to pray all night, or to fast for weeks, or to give up their work. It asked for thirty minutes a day. A busy missionary with schools to run and villages to visit could keep it. So could a village pastor or a schoolteacher. So, today, could almost anyone reading this book.

The choice of noon was probably practical too. In the Punjab the heat of the day brought most outdoor work to a halt. In many households the middle of the day was already a time to withdraw indoors. But the choice also had a deeper logic. A fixed hour meant that members all over the province would be praying at roughly the same time, each in his own place, but together. The psalmist wrote, “Evening, and morning, and at noonday, will I complain, and moan; and he will hear my voice” (Psalm 55:17, ASV). Daniel, even under threat of death, “kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime” (Daniel 6:10, ASV). Peter went up on the housetop to pray “about the sixth hour,” that is, at noon, and there received the vision that opened the church to the Gentiles (Acts 10:9, ASV).

Set times of prayer are not a substitute for praying at all times. But they are a scaffold. They protect prayer from being crowded out by the urgent. The half-hour at noon was a promise kept daily, and a small promise kept daily can outlast a great resolution made once.

“Till the Awakening Comes”

The most demanding part of the fifth question is its last clause. The member did not promise to pray for a season, or until the next annual meeting, or until he felt he had done his share. He promised to pray “till the awakening comes.”

That is the language of Isaiah’s watchmen, the verse at the head of this chapter. God sets watchmen on the walls of Jerusalem who “shall never hold their peace day nor night.” And he tells them something astonishing: “ye that are Jehovah’s remembrancers, take ye no rest, and give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.” God commands his people not to let him rest. He invites persistence. He wants to be reminded of his promises until he keeps them.

Jesus taught the same thing in a parable: “And he spake a parable unto them to the end that they ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luke 18:1, ASV). The widow in the parable kept coming to the unjust judge until he gave in. If even an unjust judge yields to persistence, Jesus asks, “shall not God avenge his elect, that cry to him day and night?” (Luke 18:7, ASV).

Isaiah 62 became something like the motto of Hyde’s circle. McGaw says that at the 1905 convention the words of that passage “were burned into his brain as a command from God.” The circular that Pengwern Jones edited for the Bengal and Assam Prayer Union was called The Remembrancer, evidently after the same verse. The intercessors in the prayer rooms at Sialkot spoke of themselves as “watchmen” and “the Lord’s remembrancers.” They took the passage literally. Their business was to keep reminding God, day and night, of what he had promised to do.

A Season of Prayer Across India

The Punjab Prayer Union was not alone. In the same years, groups of Christians in many parts of India began to pray together for revival, often stirred by news from Wales. In January 1905 Pandita Ramabai called the young women of her Mukti mission near Poona to pray for an outpouring of the Spirit. By June hundreds were meeting twice a day, and at the end of that month revival broke out among them. In the Khasi Hills of Assam, where Welsh Presbyterian missionaries worked, an awakening was already spreading from village to village by the middle of 1905. It was the Khasi revival that Pengwern Jones had come to describe at Ludhiana when he first met Hyde.

In January 1906 The Missionary Review of the World surveyed what was happening. It listed Sialkot alongside Mukti, Assam, and other places where “God is mightily working.” It also noticed something they had in common: the revivals “followed closely upon the formation of Prayer Circles.” There is no record that Hyde had any direct link with Mukti or the Khasi Hills. They were parallel movements of the same season. But they tell the same story. Before the fire came, people had been gathering the wood.

The Spring Meetings

Each spring the members of the Punjab Prayer Union held an annual meeting. According to McGaw’s informant, the leaders prepared for it with “much time in prayers and fastings and all night watching.” At the meeting itself they looked to God “for guidance during the coming year.”

The spring meeting of 1905 left a deep mark on those who attended. “God laid on our hearts,” one of them wrote, “the burden of a world plunged in sin. We were permitted to share to some extent in the sufferings of Christ.” Carré’s account describes the same meeting: “all felt the great burden of the Indian Church, and her need of Revival, so very keenly as to be inexpressible in words.” The leaders attributed that burden largely to Hyde’s teaching about “the fellowship of Christ’s sufferings”, the idea that intercessors are invited to share, in some small measure, in the grief of Christ over sin. We will return to that theme, and to its dangers, in a later chapter. Here it is enough to notice that the Prayer Union was not only a scheme for organised prayer. It became a school in which a handful of missionaries and Indian workers learned to feel what God feels about the church and the world.

And its members were convinced that it was the spring meeting of 1905 that prepared the way for the great convention that autumn.

For Reflection

The Punjab Prayer Union asked very little: five honest questions and half an hour a day. It is easy to overlook, because it was so ordinary. But its members believed it was the hidden root of everything that followed.

That should hearten anyone who longs for revival in their own church or town and feels powerless to bring it about. Few of us can pray as John Hyde prayed. Almost any of us could answer those five questions honestly and keep a half-hour at noon. The Union’s pledge could be signed today, in any church, by any small group of Christians who are willing to begin with their own lives, to admit that they cannot go on without the Spirit’s power, to pray not to be ashamed of Jesus, and to keep praying till the awakening comes.
