fields.title: Sialkot: “Is the Holy Spirit First?”
fields.body_html:
“But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall bear witness of me: and ye also bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning.”

— John 15:26-27, ASV

A Convention for the Deepening of the Spiritual Life

In the late summer of 1904, a few months after the Punjab Prayer Union began, missionaries and Indian Christian workers gathered at Sialkot for a new kind of meeting. It was not a business conference, of which the missions had many. It was a “convention for the deepening of the spiritual life,” in the spirit of the great Keswick Convention in England. For several days the participants would study the Bible, pray, and seek a fresh experience of God for themselves. The host was the United Presbyterian mission, whose headquarters were in Sialkot. The organiser who made everything run, as Jones later recalled, was a Dr. Gordon, who fed and housed hundreds of people with such calm that the accounts “balanced to a pice.” For a time its chairman was the Rev. John Forman. The sources differ over who first proposed the gathering. McGaw names Hyde, R. McCheyne Paterson, and George Turner as the three on whose hearts God “laid a great burden of prayer” for it. The United Presbyterian missionary W. B. Anderson, according to McGaw, chaired the committee that established it. No independent record settles the matter. Griswold’s careful phrase is the safest: Hyde was “very closely associated with that great annual gathering” from its beginning in 1904.

The Sialkot Convention continues to this day, more than a century later, in Pakistan. It began as a small gathering, mostly of missionaries. Carré’s book remembers that the blessing came in stages. In 1904 it was the missionaries who were most deeply affected. In 1905 it reached “our Pastors and elders.” By 1906 it had spread “to Christians generally and reached outside congregations all over Northern India.”

1904: “I Must Not Lose This Vision”

Hyde came to the first convention to lead Bible studies. One missionary remembered that he spoke on “the length and breadth and height and depth of the love of God,” an echo of Paul’s prayer in Ephesians 3:18. But the most remembered moment of that first convention was not one of Hyde’s Bible readings. It was an evening when he arrived late.

McGaw’s source, a fellow missionary, told the story. The night before, Hyde had come to his study at about half past nine and started a conversation about “the value of public testimony,” that is, about whether Christians should speak openly of what God had done for them. They argued until after one in the morning. The next evening Hyde was due to lead a meeting for men in the tent on the mission compound. The men gathered on the mats and began to sing. Hyde did not come. They sang several hymns more. At last he came in, very late, sat down on the mat in front of them, and was silent for a long time. Then he stood up and said quietly:

Brothers, I did not sleep any last night and I have not eaten anything to-day. I have been having a great controversy with God. I feel that he has wanted me to come here and testify to you concerning some things that he has done for me, and I have been arguing with him that I should not do this. Only this evening a little while ago have I got peace concerning the matter and have I agreed to obey him, and now I have come to tell you just some things that he has done for me.

He spoke for fifteen or twenty minutes, “very quietly and simply,” about “some of the desperate conflicts that he had had with sin and how God had given him victory.” Then he sat down, bowed his head, and said, “Let us have a season of prayer.” The men lay on their faces on the mats in the Indian manner of prayer. For a long time, the witness remembered, “man after man rose to his feet to pray,” and there was “such confession of sin as most of us had never heard before and such crying out to God for mercy and help.” Several lives, he said, were “wholly transformed through the influence of that meeting.”

It is worth noticing what the controversy with God had been about. It was not whether to preach, or what to preach. It was whether Hyde would be honest in public about his own struggles. He had argued against it all night, as many Christian leaders would, for reasons that sound very respectable: it might seem self-centred, or unseemly, or might damage his authority. God won the argument. And the confession of the leader opened the way for the confession of others.

Something also happened within Hyde himself at that convention. One of his dearest friends wrote that until then, although Hyde was a child of God, he had never been “compelled to tarry at his Jerusalem till he was endued with power from on high.” At Sialkot in 1904, while he was speaking to his fellow missionaries about the work of the Holy Spirit, “God spoke to his own soul.” Griswold, who was there, remembered what Hyde said at the close of the convention: “Oh, I must not lose this blessing.” McGaw’s source remembered it as, “I must not lose this vision.” Whichever words he used, Griswold adds the verdict of the next eight years: “he never did lose it, but went on from strength to strength, and from glory to glory.”

Carré’s book preserves one more remark from that first convention, spoken by a leader whom it does not name: “Either we missionaries receive Power from on high now, or let us all take the first steamer home, for we are otherwise unfit for this task.” It is the same logic as Hyde’s hour in his room in 1892, now spoken by a whole group. They would have the gospel’s power in their own lives, or they would stop pretending.

1905: The Second Convention

The convention of 1905 is the one that everyone remembered. We have an unusually full record of it, including an official report written by the United Presbyterian mission within a few years and published in its history in 1909. That report is precious, because it is independent of the devotional books about Hyde. It does not mention him by name at all. It gives all the glory to the Holy Spirit, which is exactly what Hyde would have wanted.

The convention ran from 25 August to 3 September 1905. Nearly three hundred people attended. Most were Indian workers, men and women, and there were missionaries from the United Presbyterian, Scottish, and American Presbyterian missions. It lasted ten days. “Many prayers had been going up for this convention,” the report says. “In the Home land some had been praying for it, while in India very definite prayer had been made.”

A programme had been carefully prepared, and it included a series of morning Bible readings about the Holy Spirit. According to the memoirs, Hyde was the one appointed to give them.

“Is the Holy Spirit First?”

Hyde’s subject for those morning readings was the passage at the head of this chapter: “when the Comforter is come … he shall bear witness of me: and ye also bear witness” (John 15:26-27, ASV). The memoirs preserve the heart of what he said. The Holy Spirit, he insisted, is the true witness to Christ. He alone was present at every event of Jesus’ life: his birth, his baptism, his preaching, his miracles, his death, and his resurrection. So he alone can testify to them with full authority. Human witnesses are secondary. Our part is to bear witness in his strength and behind him, never in his place.

Then Hyde turned the point on his hearers. McGaw’s source preserved the questions he asked:

Is the Holy Spirit first in your pulpits, pastors? Do you consciously put him in front and keep yourselves behind him, when preaching? Teachers, when you are asked hard questions do you ask his aid as a witness of all Christ’s life? He alone was a witness of the incarnation, the miracles, the death and the resurrection of Christ. So he is the only witness!

Carré’s account adds that when Hyde asked the pastors “who was first and foremost in their pulpits, they themselves, or the Divine Teacher and Guide into all the truth,” there was not, in the writer’s judgement, “a single preacher who was not convicted of this sin.”

The teaching was not new with Hyde. Carré says that on this point he was following one of his own teachers, the Rev. D. Lytle of the United Presbyterian mission. Lytle had insisted that Indian churches would become self-supporting and self-propagating in the apostolic way only when “the Baptism of the Holy Spirit and then the constant infilling of the Holy Spirit, received its true place in the heart and life of the Christian community.” The apostolic churches, Lytle used to say, “put first things first.” Hyde had said the same thing to his mission committee a decade earlier, when they scolded him for studying his Bible instead of his grammar.

“He Has Given Me No Message”

What happened next is told in three sources, and they agree in substance, though McGaw’s order of events differs slightly from the mission report’s.

The official mission report says simply: “A series of morning addresses were to have been given about the Holy Ghost. Only one was delivered. After that, He came Himself in great power, and all learned from Him.” It continues: “When the one who had been appointed to give the addresses came in, the second morning, and said quietly, ‘I thank God, He has given me no message for you to-day,’ surprise was written on some faces. The chairman moved aside and said, ‘The Holy Ghost is leader of this meeting.’ Each morning meeting was left in this way and the liberty was not abused.”

McGaw’s account, from his unnamed informant (almost certainly Paterson), tells the same scene from Hyde’s side: “The next morning Mr. Hyde was not allowed to give any further teaching. The chairman came down from his seat and declared the meeting to be in the hands of God’s Spirit.” The next morning again, Hyde said that he had no fresh message from God. And Carré’s book adds: “when John Hyde intimated that he had no other message to give, the Chairman was led to leave each meeting to the guidance of the Holy Spirit — surely that was the direct result of this teaching!”

The unnamed speaker in the official report was, all but certainly, John Hyde. And the story fits his teaching with an almost uncomfortable neatness. He had spent one morning urging the pastors to put the Holy Spirit first in their pulpits and themselves behind. The next morning he did it himself. He had nothing to say, and he said so, and he sat down. A man who needed to be seen as a great speaker could not have done that. The young missionary who had wanted to shine could not have done it. The man who had prayed on the ship to be willing to work “quietly out of sight” now did it gladly, in front of three hundred people.

The Days That Followed

The official report describes what came next. The morning meetings “usually continued two and three hours.” There was deep conviction of sin from the start: “It was a time of intense mental agony.” One day was remembered as “the day of great confession,” when people “with trembling in every limb, stood obedient to His voice, confessing openly as He bade.” After that, the report says, “the cloud seemed to lift and the sunshine came and flooded the place, and joy was depicted on many countenances.” A room was set aside for prayer, and “after the first or second day this place was not empty, day or night.” An aged Indian minister, bitterly opposed to the public confessions, fell on his face in the prayer room and cried, “Oh, how I have sinned! O God, have mercy on me!” On the last Sunday there was no sermon and no leader. Someone announced the thirtieth Psalm, and it was sung three times over, the old minister himself calling for it again. The 148th Psalm, “Praise ye Jehovah,” became the song of the convention, sung day and night.

McGaw’s sources add scenes from inside the prayer room. They remember Hyde there day and night. At one point he was told by God to do something, and he went and obeyed, but he came back weeping and confessed that he had obeyed unwillingly: “Pray for me, brethren, that I may do this joyfully.” When he returned from obeying a second time, he entered the hall and repeated three words in Urdu and three in English, three times over: “Ai Asmani Bap,” “O Heavenly Father.” The writer struggled for a way to describe what followed. It was, he said, “as if a great ocean came sweeping into that assembly.”

One of the most moving memories comes from a missionary who went to comfort a Punjabi Christian sobbing in the prayer room. The man had seen, he said, a vision of “thousands of souls in this land of India being carried away by the dark river of sin.” The missionary put his arms around him and said, “The blood of Jesus Christ cleanseth us from all sin.” The man’s face lit up: “Thank God, Sahib.” The words the missionary quoted are from John: “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanseth us from all sin” (1 John 1:7, ASV). The grief of that convention was real, but it was never allowed to end in grief.

For Reflection

The heart of the 1905 convention was not a great sermon. It was a speaker who stepped back. The official report and the devotional memoirs, written for different purposes, agree that the turning point came when the appointed teacher had nothing to say, and the chairman gave the meeting to the Holy Spirit.

Most Christian gatherings today are carefully planned, and there is nothing wrong with planning. The 1905 programme was carefully prepared too. But Hyde’s question still presses: Is the Holy Spirit first? Do we consciously put him in front and keep ourselves behind him? It is easy to agree with that in theory. It is quite another thing to stand before a waiting crowd and say, “I thank God, He has given me no message for you to-day.”
fields.body_text: “But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall bear witness of me: and ye also bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning.” — John 15:26-27, ASV A Convention for the Deepening of the Spiritual Life In the late summer of 1904, a few months after the Punjab Prayer Union began, missionaries and Indian Christian workers gathered at Sialkot for a new kind of meeting. It was not a business conference, of which the missions had many. It was a “convention for the deepening of the spiritual life,” in the spirit of the great Keswick Convention in England. For several days the participants would study the Bible, pray, and seek a fresh experience of God for themselves. The host was the United Presbyterian mission, whose headquarters were in Sialkot. The organiser who made everything run, as Jones later recalled, was a Dr. Gordon, who fed and housed hundreds of people with such calm that the accounts “balanced to a pice.” For a time its chairman was the Rev. John Forman. The sources differ over who first proposed the gathering. McGaw names Hyde, R. McCheyne Paterson, and George Turner as the three on whose hearts God “laid a great burden of prayer” for it. The United Presbyterian missionary W. B. Anderson, according to McGaw, chaired the committee that established it. No independent record settles the matter. Griswold’s careful phrase is the safest: Hyde was “very closely associated with that great annual gathering” from its beginning in 1904. The Sialkot Convention continues to this day, more than a century later, in Pakistan. It began as a small gathering, mostly of missionaries. Carré’s book remembers that the blessing came in stages. In 1904 it was the missionaries who were most deeply affected. In 1905 it reached “our Pastors and elders.” By 1906 it had spread “to Christians generally and reached outside congregations all over Northern India.” 1904: “I Must Not Lose This Vision” Hyde came to the first convention to lead Bible studies. One missionary remembered that he spoke on “the length and breadth and height and depth of the love of God,” an echo of Paul’s prayer in Ephesians 3:18. But the most remembered moment of that first convention was not one of Hyde’s Bible readings. It was an evening when he arrived late. McGaw’s source, a fellow missionary, told the story. The night before, Hyde had come to his study at about half past nine and started a conversation about “the value of public testimony,” that is, about whether Christians should speak openly of what God had done for them. They argued until after one in the morning. The next evening Hyde was due to lead a meeting for men in the tent on the mission compound. The men gathered on the mats and began to sing. Hyde did not come. They sang several hymns more. At last he came in, very late, sat down on the mat in front of them, and was silent for a long time. Then he stood up and said quietly: Brothers, I did not sleep any last night and I have not eaten anything to-day. I have been having a great controversy with God. I feel that he has wanted me to come here and testify to you concerning some things that he has done for me, and I have been arguing with him that I should not do this. Only this evening a little while ago have I got peace concerning the matter and have I agreed to obey him, and now I have come to tell you just some things that he has done for me. He spoke for fifteen or twenty minutes, “very quietly and simply,” about “some of the desperate conflicts that he had had with sin and how God had given him victory.” Then he sat down, bowed his head, and said, “Let us have a season of prayer.” The men lay on their faces on the mats in the Indian manner of prayer. For a long time, the witness remembered, “man after man rose to his feet to pray,” and there was “such confession of sin as most of us had never heard before and such crying out to God for mercy and help.” Several lives, he said, were “wholly transformed through the influence of that meeting.” It is worth noticing what the controversy with God had been about. It was not whether to preach, or what to preach. It was whether Hyde would be honest in public about his own struggles. He had argued against it all night, as many Christian leaders would, for reasons that sound very respectable: it might seem self-centred, or unseemly, or might damage his authority. God won the argument. And the confession of the leader opened the way for the confession of others. Something also happened within Hyde himself at that convention. One of his dearest friends wrote that until then, although Hyde was a child of God, he had never been “compelled to tarry at his Jerusalem till he was endued with power from on high.” At Sialkot in 1904, while he was speaking to his fellow missionaries about the work of the Holy Spirit, “God spoke to his own soul.” Griswold, who was there, remembered what Hyde said at the close of the convention: “Oh, I must not lose this blessing.” McGaw’s source remembered it as, “I must not lose this vision.” Whichever words he used, Griswold adds the verdict of the next eight years: “he never did lose it, but went on from strength to strength, and from glory to glory.” Carré’s book preserves one more remark from that first convention, spoken by a leader whom it does not name: “Either we missionaries receive Power from on high now, or let us all take the first steamer home, for we are otherwise unfit for this task.” It is the same logic as Hyde’s hour in his room in 1892, now spoken by a whole group. They would have the gospel’s power in their own lives, or they would stop pretending. 1905: The Second Convention The convention of 1905 is the one that everyone remembered. We have an unusually full record of it, including an official report written by the United Presbyterian mission within a few years and published in its history in 1909. That report is precious, because it is independent of the devotional books about Hyde. It does not mention him by name at all. It gives all the glory to the Holy Spirit, which is exactly what Hyde would have wanted. The convention ran from 25 August to 3 September 1905. Nearly three hundred people attended. Most were Indian workers, men and women, and there were missionaries from the United Presbyterian, Scottish, and American Presbyterian missions. It lasted ten days. “Many prayers had been going up for this convention,” the report says. “In the Home land some had been praying for it, while in India very definite prayer had been made.” A programme had been carefully prepared, and it included a series of morning Bible readings about the Holy Spirit. According to the memoirs, Hyde was the one appointed to give them. “Is the Holy Spirit First?” Hyde’s subject for those morning readings was the passage at the head of this chapter: “when the Comforter is come … he shall bear witness of me: and ye also bear witness” (John 15:26-27, ASV). The memoirs preserve the heart of what he said. The Holy Spirit, he insisted, is the true witness to Christ. He alone was present at every event of Jesus’ life: his birth, his baptism, his preaching, his miracles, his death, and his resurrection. So he alone can testify to them with full authority. Human witnesses are secondary. Our part is to bear witness in his strength and behind him, never in his place. Then Hyde turned the point on his hearers. McGaw’s source preserved the questions he asked: Is the Holy Spirit first in your pulpits, pastors? Do you consciously put him in front and keep yourselves behind him, when preaching? Teachers, when you are asked hard questions do you ask his aid as a witness of all Christ’s life? He alone was a witness of the incarnation, the miracles, the death and the resurrection of Christ. So he is the only witness! Carré’s account adds that when Hyde asked the pastors “who was first and foremost in their pulpits, they themselves, or the Divine Teacher and Guide into all the truth,” there was not, in the writer’s judgement, “a single preacher who was not convicted of this sin.” The teaching was not new with Hyde. Carré says that on this point he was following one of his own teachers, the Rev. D. Lytle of the United Presbyterian mission. Lytle had insisted that Indian churches would become self-supporting and self-propagating in the apostolic way only when “the Baptism of the Holy Spirit and then the constant infilling of the Holy Spirit, received its true place in the heart and life of the Christian community.” The apostolic churches, Lytle used to say, “put first things first.” Hyde had said the same thing to his mission committee a decade earlier, when they scolded him for studying his Bible instead of his grammar. “He Has Given Me No Message” What happened next is told in three sources, and they agree in substance, though McGaw’s order of events differs slightly from the mission report’s. The official mission report says simply: “A series of morning addresses were to have been given about the Holy Ghost. Only one was delivered. After that, He came Himself in great power, and all learned from Him.” It continues: “When the one who had been appointed to give the addresses came in, the second morning, and said quietly, ‘I thank God, He has given me no message for you to-day,’ surprise was written on some faces. The chairman moved aside and said, ‘The Holy Ghost is leader of this meeting.’ Each morning meeting was left in this way and the liberty was not abused.” McGaw’s account, from his unnamed informant (almost certainly Paterson), tells the same scene from Hyde’s side: “The next morning Mr. Hyde was not allowed to give any further teaching. The chairman came down from his seat and declared the meeting to be in the hands of God’s Spirit.” The next morning again, Hyde said that he had no fresh message from God. And Carré’s book adds: “when John Hyde intimated that he had no other message to give, the Chairman was led to leave each meeting to the guidance of the Holy Spirit — surely that was the direct result of this teaching!” The unnamed speaker in the official report was, all but certainly, John Hyde. And the story fits his teaching with an almost uncomfortable neatness. He had spent one morning urging the pastors to put the Holy Spirit first in their pulpits and themselves behind. The next morning he did it himself. He had nothing to say, and he said so, and he sat down. A man who needed to be seen as a great speaker could not have done that. The young missionary who had wanted to shine could not have done it. The man who had prayed on the ship to be willing to work “quietly out of sight” now did it gladly, in front of three hundred people. O God, have mercy on me!” On the last Sunday there was no sermon and no leader. Someone announced the thirtieth Psalm, and it was sung three times over, the old minister himself calling for it again. fields.title: The Prayer Room
fields.body_html:
“I am Jehovah thy God, Who brought thee up out of the land of Egypt: Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.”

— Psalm 81:10, ASV

“Come With Me to the Prayer Room”

Pengwern Jones never forgot the first time he met John Hyde.

It was at Ludhiana, probably in 1906, at the annual meeting of the American Presbyterian mission in the Punjab. Jones, a Welsh missionary from Sylhet in Assam, had been invited to speak about the revival in the Khasi Hills. He travelled all night by train from Allahabad and arrived early in the morning, tired, and anxious about the address he was to give at four o’clock that afternoon. Someone took him to have tea with the delegates, and across the table he was introduced to a quiet American missionary. Hyde’s only words were, “I want to see you, I shall wait for you at the door.”

He was waiting at the door. “Come with me to the Prayer Room,” he said, “we want you there.” Jones was not sure whether it was a request or a command, but he felt he had to go. He protested that he had travelled all night, that he was tired, and that he had to speak at four. He went anyway.

There were half a dozen people in the room. Hyde went down on his face on the floor. Jones knelt, and “a strange feeling crept over me.” Several people prayed, and then Hyde prayed, and Jones remembered very little after that except the sense that “I was in the presence of God Himself and had no desire to leave the place.” People came and went. Meals were forgotten. His tiredness disappeared, and so did his anxiety about the talk. They had gone into the room at about eight in the morning. At half past three Hyde got up, and Jones found that they were the only two left.

“You are to speak at 4 o’clock,” Hyde said. “I shall take you to have a cup of tea.” Jones said Hyde must need some refreshment too. “No,” Hyde answered, “I do not want any, but you must have some.” They washed hastily, had a cup of tea each, and Hyde walked Jones to the door of the hall. There he took his hand and said: “Go in and speak, that is your work. I shall go back to the Prayer Room to pray for you, that is my work. When the service is over, come into the Prayer Room again and we shall praise God together.”

Jones spoke through an interpreter, and afterwards could not remember what he had said. But before the meeting ended the Indian interpreter was so overcome that he could not go on, and another had to take his place. “I know the Lord spoke that night,” Jones wrote. “He spoke to me, and spoke to many.” When it was over he went back to the prayer room. Hyde asked no questions about how the service had gone. “He seemed to know it all,” Jones wrote, “and how he praised the Lord.”

“That is your work … that is my work.” Those two sentences explain the prayer room better than any description of it. Hyde did not think prayer was more important than preaching, or that preachers were less spiritual than intercessors. He thought they were two parts of one work, and he had come to believe that his own part was the hidden one.

How the Prayer Room Began

At the Sialkot Conventions there were two prayer rooms, one for men and one for women. Prayer went on in them, Jones says, “day and night, without intermission,” from the first day of the convention until two or three days after it ended. Two or three experienced Christians were always present to help anyone who needed it. Sometimes someone led in prayer as at an ordinary meeting. Sometimes there was silence. Sometimes little groups formed around a particular need. Missionaries brought anxious enquirers there to be prayed for and helped.

Jones believed that the prayer room “was the work of the Holy Spirit through Hyde.” It was Hyde, he said, “that spent the first nights on the watch-tower,” joined almost from the start by McCheyne Paterson. We have seen that the official report of 1905 describes the same room, “not empty, day or night” after the first day or two. Whatever the precise origins, the prayer room became the heart of the convention. Jones remembered a missionary attending for the first time who came to him on the third day to complain. The convention was on the wrong lines, he said. The leaders ought to be on the platform, not hiding in the prayer room all day. Two days later the same man came back with a beaming face. “Do you know,” he said, “I have found out the secret of this Convention — it is that Prayer Room. I never saw anything like it.”

Thirty Days

The most famous claim about the prayer room concerns the preparation for one of the early conventions. McGaw, following Paterson, says that before one of the first conventions “Hyde and Paterson waited and tarried one whole month before the opening day. For thirty days and thirty nights these godly men waited before God in prayer.” George Turner joined them after nine days, “so that for twenty-one days and twenty-one nights these three men prayed and praised God for a mighty outpouring of his power.”

A friend in Calcutta, quoted by McGaw, dated this vigil to 1906, “when the Convention was opened for the first time to all Christians.” He had heard of it from Turner. When the two men were alone, he pressed Turner for details. Turner was very reluctant to say anything. “I cannot go into details,” he said, “but it was a time in the Mount with God.”

We should read this story carefully. It comes from people who loved the three men and were not present for the whole month. It should not be pictured as thirty days of unbroken kneeling. The prayer probably went on alongside the ordinary needs of life, and it may have included times of rest and work. But there is no reason to doubt its substance. Three missionaries set apart a month before the convention to wait on God together, and Turner’s refusal to talk about it is itself a mark of authenticity. People who have truly been “in the Mount with God” are usually slow to describe it.

“Wide, Lord, Wide”

What did Hyde actually do in the prayer room? Jones and McGaw both describe it, and their pictures match.

The prayer room at Sialkot was in the Scottish church. Some of the seats were moved aside and a carpet was laid over the open space. Sometimes there were hundreds of people in it, sometimes only two or three. “Right on his face on the ground is Praying Hyde,” Jones wrote, “this was his favourite attitude for prayer.” Hyde would utter a petition, then wait. After a little time he would repeat it, and wait again, “and this many times until we all feel that that petition has penetrated into every fibre of our nature, and we feel assured that God has heard.”

Jones remembered one prayer above all. Hyde was praying the verse at the head of this chapter: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm 81:10, ASV). “I think he repeated the word ‘wide’ scores of times with long pauses between,” Jones wrote. “‘Wide, Lord.’ ‘Wide.’ ‘Open wide.’ ‘Wide.’”

It is worth reading the verse in its setting. God speaks through the psalmist to Israel, reminding them that he brought them out of Egypt and offering them more than they have dared to ask. And then he mourns: “But my people hearkened not to my voice; and Israel would none of me” (Psalm 81:11, ASV). The tragedy of the psalm is not that God was unwilling to fill his people but that they would not open their mouths. Hyde’s long repetition of the word “wide” was a prayer that the church in the Punjab would not make that mistake. He was asking God to enlarge their expectation, so that they might receive what he was ready to give.

Another way Hyde prayed struck people just as deeply. He would simply address God by name, over and over. Jones heard him say, “Oh, Father! Father!” and felt that “even before he asked anything … the Father knew what he was going to ask for.” A missionary woman who knelt near him at a convention in Jubbulpore never forgot hearing him plead, “Jesus — Jesus — Jesus!” It seemed to her, she said, “as if a baptism of love and power came over me.”

Dancing for Joy

It would be a mistake to imagine the prayer room as a place of unbroken gloom. Jones describes what often happened when Hyde finished praying. Perhaps half a dozen people would be sobbing. Hyde would go to one of them and others to the rest. With his arm around the man’s neck, he “speaks but little but his well-worn Bible is used,” and before long the two men would stand up together with smiles. Then Hyde would begin to sing the old hymn, “’Tis done, the great transaction’s done.” And “he is so full of joy that his whole body begins to move, he claps his hands and then his feet begin to move, and look, he begins to dance for joy and others join him until the whole place rings with God’s praises.”

That picture of a shy, deaf, formerly morose Presbyterian missionary dancing for joy on a carpet in a Scottish church in the Punjab does more than any argument to correct the idea that Hyde was a gloomy ascetic. His prayer was often agonised. But it ended in praise, and it was full of joy.

Hidden Places and Unused Beds

Sometimes Hyde wanted to be alone even at the convention. Jones heard of him climbing into the church belfry. There, in the dark, high above the others, he prayed aloud, and people below heard the echo of his voice and knew he must not be disturbed.

His bed was a small tragedy of the convention. Hyde’s “boy,” as Jones calls him, was a lad of about sixteen whom Hyde had taken into his home and his heart. He brought his master’s bedding to Sialkot and made his bed carefully. It was never used during the convention. More than once Jones saw Hyde, when the prayer room was full, go aside into a corner and throw himself on the floor to sleep. Yet if the room began to empty and the prayer began to flag, “he somehow seemed to know it and was up immediately.” He rarely came to meals. Sometimes the boy, or a friend, or Gulla the sweeper would carry a plate of curry and rice to the prayer room, and Hyde would eat it in a corner. “How his ‘boy’ used to cry,” Jones remembered, “because he would not eat properly and would not go to bed to sleep.” It is a tender detail. It is also, as later chapters will show, a warning.

A friend in the prayer room noticed a small exchange during the 1905 convention. The lunch bell rang, and Hyde whispered, “Father, is it thy will that I go?” There was a pause. Then he said, “Thank you, Father,” rose with a smile, and went to lunch. It is easy to smile at such a story, but it shows that Hyde’s abstinence was not a rule. He did not stay in the prayer room because he despised food. He went to lunch when he believed he should.

Every Tent a Bethel

Jones noticed that Hyde prayed not only for the meetings but for everything connected with them. While the organisers were putting up the tents, arranging the cooking, and laying on the water supply, Hyde and his companions were already on the ground in prayer. As soon as the great marquee was erected, Hyde and his party entered it to dedicate it to the Lord, “to make the spot a real Bethel where God would meet with His people.” When the dining tent went up, they went there too, so that God could use even the mealtimes for blessing. Jacob, waking at Bethel, said, “Surely Jehovah is in this place; and I knew it not” (Genesis 28:16, ASV). Hyde wanted every corner of the convention ground to be a place where people could say that.

Jones believed the prayers were answered even at the tables. He never heard gossip in the dining tent at Sialkot. Indians and Europeans ate together, often sitting on the floor. People in spiritual trouble would go to a meal together to talk it over. When someone found peace with God, a hymn or an Indian bhajan would break out, and “in an instant the whole place is full of praise,” with the servers, the waiters, and the diners all singing.

And when the convention ended, the praying did not. While others pulled down the tents, the prayer room parties stayed behind to pray that the fruit would last. Paterson always said that the time for the most earnest prayer is immediately after a meeting. As Jones put it, it is then that the birds come to devour the seed.

“Let Us Meet Together to Pray”

The prayer room was also where the convention’s hardest disagreements were settled.

At the first convention Jones attended, there was a crisis over public confession of sin. At the previous convention, some shocking confessions had been made by missionaries and Indian workers. Some people were outraged and wanted the committee to forbid public confession, or at least to separate men and women so that such things were not said in mixed meetings. They demanded a meeting to debate the question. The committee’s reply was, “Let us meet together to pray over the matter.” The objectors refused. It was useless, they said, to pray until the question had been decided. One young man thumped the table in rage and shouted, “I’ll smash the whole Convention.”

Jones talked quietly with Hyde, who was on the committee. He was struck by how “tender, loving” and “sane” Hyde was through it all. Hyde said that the committee had never called for confessions, and that it was the Holy Spirit who had moved people to confess. To make rules about it, he thought, even to set apart special meetings for confession, would be “taking the matter out of the Holy Spirit’s hand.” He believed the sin behind many of the confessions was far more common among Christians than anyone had imagined, and he said gently, “Some men, I fear, are guilty and are afraid that the Holy Spirit will compel them to confess.” Yet he spoke of the objectors with tenderness, and his face, Jones said, “was full of joy for he knew that victory was assured.”

Victory came in the prayer room. The objectors went there, meaning to argue. They found Hyde and other committee members praying, and were welcomed so warmly that they knelt and prayed too. After a while Paterson spoke quietly, showing that no one on the committee had ever urged public confession: “All that the Committee desired was implicit obedience to the Holy Spirit.” The objectors agreed that they wanted the same. Someone began to praise God, all joined in singing, “and the Prayer Room became once more a Praise Room.” Jones said he learned that day that the best way through a church quarrel is often to “keep quiet in a corner, praying that the Holy Spirit might come and reveal His Will.” He tried it many times afterwards, and found that it worked.

For Reflection

The early church met in an upper room, and the Acts of the Apostles says they “with one accord continued stedfastly in prayer” (Acts 1:14, ASV). When they prayed again after their first persecution, “the place was shaken wherein they were gathered together; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spake the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31, ASV). Hyde’s friends believed they had seen something of that in the prayer room at Sialkot.

Very few churches have a prayer room that is never empty. But any church can decide that preaching and praying are two parts of one work, and that someone should always be doing the hidden part. “Go in and speak, that is your work. I shall go back to the Prayer Room to pray for you, that is my work.” Who is doing that work for your church, or for you? And is there someone for whom you could do it?

How the Prayer Room Began At the Sialkot Conventions there were two prayer rooms, one for men and one for women. Prayer went on in them, Jones says, “day and night, without intermission,” from the first day of the convention until two or three days after it ended. Two or three experienced Christians were always present to help anyone who needed it. Sometimes someone led in prayer as at an ordinary meeting. Sometimes there was silence. Sometimes little groups formed around a particular need. Missionaries brought anxious enquirers there to be prayed for and helped. Jones believed that the prayer room “was the work of the Holy Spirit through Hyde.” It was Hyde, he said, “that spent the first nights on the watch-tower,” joined almost from the start by McCheyne Paterson. We have seen that the official report of 1905 describes the same room, “not empty, day or night” after the first day or two. Whatever the precise origins, the prayer room became the heart of the convention. Jones remembered a missionary attending for the first time who came to him on the third day to complain. The convention was on the wrong lines, he said. The leaders ought to be on the platform, not hiding in the prayer room all day. Two days later the same man came back with a beaming face. “Do you know,” he said, “I have found out the secret of this Convention — it is that Prayer Room. I never saw anything like it.” Thirty Days The most famous claim about the prayer room concerns the preparation for one of the early conventions. McGaw, following Paterson, says that before one of the first conventions “Hyde and Paterson waited and tarried one whole month before the opening day. For thirty days and thirty nights these godly men waited before God in prayer.” George Turner joined them after nine days, “so that for twenty-one days and twenty-one nights these three men prayed and praised God for a mighty outpouring of his power.” A friend in Calcutta, quoted by McGaw, dated this vigil to 1906, “when the Convention was opened for the first time to all Christians.” He had heard of it from Turner. When the two men were alone, he pressed Turner for details. Turner was very reluctant to say anything. “I cannot go into details,” he said, “but it was a time in the Mount with God.” We should read this story carefully. It comes from people who loved the three men and were not present for the whole month. It should not be pictured as thirty days of unbroken kneeling. The prayer probably went on alongside the ordinary needs of life, and it may have included times of rest and work. But there is no reason to doubt its substance. Three missionaries set apart a month before the convention to wait on God together, and Turner’s refusal to talk about it is itself a mark of authenticity. People who have truly been “in the Mount with God” are usually slow to describe it. “Wide, Lord, Wide” What did Hyde actually do in the prayer room? Jones and McGaw both describe it, and their pictures match. The prayer room at Sialkot was in the Scottish church. Some of the seats were moved aside and a carpet was laid over the open space. Sometimes there were hundreds of people in it, sometimes only two or three. “Right on his face on the ground is Praying Hyde,” Jones wrote, “this was his favourite attitude for prayer.” Hyde would utter a petition, then wait. After a little time he would repeat it, and wait again, “and this many times until we all feel that that petition has penetrated into every fibre of our nature, and we feel assured that God has heard.” Jones remembered one prayer above all. Hyde was praying the verse at the head of this chapter: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm 81:10, ASV). “I think he repeated the word ‘wide’ scores of times with long pauses between,” Jones wrote. “‘Wide, Lord.’ ‘Wide.’ ‘Open wide.’ ‘Wide.’” It is worth reading the verse in its setting. God speaks through the psalmist to Israel, reminding them that he brought them out of Egypt and offering them more than they have dared to ask. And then he mourns: “But my people hearkened not to my voice; and Israel would none of me” (Psalm 81:11, ASV). The tragedy of the psalm is not that God was unwilling to fill his people but that they would not open their mouths. Hyde’s long repetition of the word “wide” was a prayer that the church in the Punjab would not make that mistake. He was asking God to enlarge their expectation, so that they might receive what he was ready to give. Another way Hyde prayed struck people just as deeply. He would simply address God by name, over and over. Jones heard him say, “Oh, Father! Father!” and felt that “even before he asked anything … the Father knew what he was going to ask for.” A missionary woman who knelt near him at a convention in Jubbulpore never forgot hearing him plead, “Jesus — Jesus — Jesus!” It seemed to her, she said, “as if a baptism of love and power came over me.” Dancing for Joy It would be a mistake to imagine the prayer room as a place of unbroken gloom. Jones describes what often happened when Hyde finished praying. Perhaps half a dozen people would be sobbing. Hyde would go to one of them and others to the rest. With his arm around the man’s neck, he “speaks but little but his well-worn Bible is used,” and before long the two men would stand up together with smiles. Then Hyde would begin to sing the old hymn, “’Tis done, the great transaction’s done.” And “he is so full of joy that his whole body begins to move, he claps his hands and then his feet begin to move, and look, he begins to dance for joy and others join him until the whole place rings with God’s praises.” That picture of a shy, deaf, formerly morose Presbyterian missionary dancing for joy on a carpet in a Scottish church in the Punjab does more than any argument to correct the idea that Hyde was a gloomy ascetic. His prayer was often agonised. But it ended in praise, and it was full of joy. Hidden Places and Unused Beds Sometimes Hyde wanted to be alone even at the convention. Jones heard of him climbing into the church belfry. There, in the dark, high above the others, he prayed aloud, and people below heard the echo of his voice and knew he must not be disturbed. His bed was a small tragedy of the convention. Hyde’s “boy,” as Jones calls him, was a lad of about sixteen whom Hyde had taken into his home and his heart. He brought his master’s bedding to Sialkot and made his bed carefully. It was never used during the convention. More than once Jones saw Hyde, when the prayer room was full, go aside into a corner and throw himself on the floor to sleep. Yet if the room began to empty and the prayer began to flag, “he somehow seemed to know it and was up immediately.” He rarely came to meals. Sometimes the boy, or a friend, or Gulla the sweeper would carry a plate of curry and rice to the prayer room, and Hyde would eat it in a corner. “How his ‘boy’ used to cry,” Jones remembered, “because he would not eat properly and would not go to bed to sleep.” It is a tender detail. It is also, as later chapters will show, a warning. A friend in the prayer room noticed a small exchange during the 1905 convention. The lunch bell rang, and Hyde whispered, “Father, is it thy will that I go?” There was a pause. Then he said, “Thank you, Father,” rose with a smile, and went to lunch. It is easy to smile at such a story, but it shows that Hyde’s abstinence was not a rule. He did not stay in the prayer room because he despised food. He went to lunch when he believed he should. Every Tent a Bethel Jones noticed that Hyde prayed not only for the meetings but for everything connected with them. While the organisers were putting up the tents, arranging the cooking, and laying on the water supply, Hyde and his companions were already on the ground in prayer. As soon as the great marquee was erected, Hyde and his party entered it to dedicate it to the Lord, “to make the spot a real Bethel where God would meet with His people.” When the dining tent went up, they went there too, so that God could use even the mealtimes for blessing. Jacob, waking at Bethel, said, “Surely Jehovah is in this place; and I knew it not” (Genesis 28:16, ASV). Hyde wanted every corner of the convention ground to be a place where people could say that. Jones believed the prayers were answered even at the tables. He never heard gossip in the dining tent at Sialkot. Indians and Europeans ate together, often sitting on the floor. People in spiritual trouble would go to a meal together to talk it over. When someone found peace with God, a hymn or an Indian bhajan would break out, and “in an instant the whole place is full of praise,” with the servers, the waiters, and the diners all singing. And when the convention ended, the praying did not. While others pulled down the tents, the prayer room parties stayed behind to pray that the fruit would last. Paterson always said that the time for the most earnest prayer is immediately after a meeting. As Jones put it, it is then that the birds come to devour the seed. “Let Us Meet Together to Pray” The prayer room was also where the convention’s hardest disagreements were settled. At the first convention Jones attended, there was a crisis over public confession of sin. At the previous convention, some shocking confessions had been made by missionaries and Indian workers. Some people were outraged and wanted the committee to forbid public confession, or at least to separate men and women so that such things were not said in mixed meetings. They demanded a meeting to debate the question. The committee’s reply was, “Let us meet together to pray over the matter.” The objectors refused. It was useless, they said, to pray until the question had been decided. One young man thumped the table in rage and shouted, “I’ll smash the whole Convention.” Jones talked quietly with Hyde, who was on the committee. He was struck by how “tender, loving” and “sane” Hyde was through it all. Hyde said that the committee had never called for confessions, and that it was the Holy Spirit who had moved people to confess. To make rules about it, he thought, even to set apart special meetings for confession, would be “taking the matter out of the Holy Spirit’s hand.” He believed the sin behind many of the confessions was far more common among Christians than anyone had imagined, and he said gently, “Some men, I fear, are guilty and are afraid that the Holy Spirit will compel them to confess.” Yet he spoke of the objectors with tenderness, and his face, Jones said, “was full of joy for he knew that victory was assured.” Victory came in the prayer room. The objectors went there, meaning to argue. They found Hyde and other committee members praying, and were welcomed so warmly that they knelt and prayed too. After a while Paterson spoke quietly, showing that no one on the committee had ever urged public confession: “All that the Committee desired was implicit obedience to the Holy Spirit.” The objectors agreed that they wanted the same. Someone began to praise God, all joined in singing, “and the Prayer Room became once more a Praise Room.” Jones said he learned that day that the best way through a church quarrel is often to “keep quiet in a corner, praying that the Holy Spirit might come and reveal His Will.” He tried it many times afterwards, and found that it worked. For Reflection The early church met in an upper room, and the Acts of the Apostles says they “with one accord continued stedfastly in prayer” (Acts 1:14, ASV). When they prayed again after their first persecution, “the place was shaken wherein they were gathered together; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spake the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31, ASV). Hyde’s friends believed they had seen something of that in the prayer room at Sialkot. Very few churches have a prayer room that is never empty. But any church can decide that preaching and praying are two parts of one work, and that someone should always be doing the hidden part. “Go in and speak, that is your work. I shall go back to the Prayer Room to pray for you, that is my work.” Who is doing that work for your church, or for you? And is there someone for whom you could do it?

fields.title: “Give Me Souls, or I Die”
fields.body_html:
“My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you—”

— Galatians 4:19, ASV

A Week at Murree

In the summer of 1907 a group of missionaries went up to Murree, a hill station in the foothills of the Himalayas on the road to Kashmir. They went to escape the heat of the plains, which in June can make work nearly impossible. Several of them had been leaders in the Sialkot prayer room, and as the weeks passed they arranged to set aside a week or ten days for waiting on God together. Others heard of it and came. Pengwern Jones was among them. He called it “the most wonderful week of my life.”

They stayed with the Rev. and Mrs. McCheyne Paterson. Jones shared a tiny room with Hyde, and he recorded what he saw with the eye of an affectionate roommate. Hyde, he says, was “very full of humour which was under perfect control.” In the company of people who shared his prayer life, “the sad burdened features relaxed … and his face was lit up with joy.” The conversation at meals was lively and uplifting. But Hyde’s place at the table was often empty. “We knew where he was,” Jones wrote. “No one enjoyed the company of men and women more than he did, but Jesus came first.” When Jones went to bed, Hyde was on his knees, wrapped in a heavy overcoat against the mountain cold. When Jones woke at dawn, Hyde was on his knees again. Sometimes he stayed there the whole day.

Then, at some point in that week, a particular burden came upon him. It was not for the Punjab villages but for the English visitors in the hill station, the officials, officers, and their families who crowded Murree in the hot season. For two or three days Hyde did not go to bed or come down to meals. The food sent up to his room came back untouched. Several times he came and knelt by Jones’s bed, asking him to help him carry the burden in prayer. On the Saturday night he was “in great agony,” and Paterson and Jones stayed up with him. Jones thought of Jacob wrestling at the ford of the Jabbok, saying, “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me” (Genesis 32:26, ASV). Yet in Hyde’s determination, he said, “there was such deep humility, such loving pleading.”

At two o’clock in the morning there was a knock at the door. Paterson whispered to Jones that it was probably his wife, reminding them to go to bed. It was not. It was a servant with a letter from a woman staying at the largest hotel in Murree, asking whether the missionaries would hold a service for Europeans in the hotel drawing room. The servant had been sent miles in the wrong direction and had struggled to find anyone at night who could direct him. That was why he came at two in the morning. Hyde heard them reading the letter, jumped up from his knees, and said, “That is the answer to my prayers, I know now that the Lord has heard me.”

The service was held. It was not large, and “from a human standpoint” it was not a success. Hyde, who had stayed in his room to pray, or rather, Jones says, to praise, was not at all disappointed. “He said that it was all in the Lord’s Hand and He knew how to carry on His work.” At least one person from the hotel came to the evening service in the Scottish church, and Hyde was there, his face so full of joy “that it was contagious.”

The story has none of the grand numbers that later books love. A burden, a night of agony, a knock at two in the morning, a small and unimpressive service, one person who came back. But it shows the pattern of Hyde’s intercession in these years very clearly. It began with a burden he did not choose. It continued in prayer that was costly to his body. It ended in an assurance that God had heard, and in a joy that did not depend on visible results.

“Souls or I Die”

The cry for which Hyde is best known belongs to the following summer. McGaw’s account, from the friend who was Hyde’s host that summer (very probably Paterson, though McGaw does not name him), describes Hyde’s stay in the hills in 1908. He had a separate room on the hillside, a little apart from the house. He came, they said, “for a very real intercession with his Master.” It was evident to everyone that he was “bowed down with sore travail of soul.” He missed many meals. When Paterson went to his room he would find him “lying as in great agony, or walking up and down as if an inward fire were burning in his bones.”

When Paterson begged him to come and eat, Hyde would look at him, smile, and say, “I am not hungry.” Paterson understood: “there was a far greater hunger eating up his very soul, and prayer alone could satisfy that.” And in the room on the hill, day after day, his hosts heard him pleading for the people of his district, “with sobs — dry choking sobs, that showed how the depths of his soul were being stirred.” The burden of his prayers was always the same: “Father, give me these souls or I die!”

That is the form in which McGaw records it. Later writers have varied the words. “O God, give me souls or I die!” appears in McGaw’s own preface, and other versions have spread from book to book. The exact wording cannot be fixed. What matters is the shape of the cry, and that is not in doubt.

It is worth noticing where the shape comes from. The words echo, perhaps deliberately, an ancient cry of longing in Genesis. When Rachel saw that she had no children, “she said unto Jacob, Give me children, or else I die” (Genesis 30:1, ASV). Hyde’s village converts were his children in the faith. The fruitlessness of his early years had taught him what it meant to long for them. And the language of spiritual birth runs all through the New Testament. The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s cry to the churches of Galatia: “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you” (Galatians 4:19, ASV). Isaiah had promised that “as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children” (Isaiah 66:8, ASV).

What Is Travail in Prayer?

The word “travail” means the labour of childbirth. Applied to prayer, it describes a kind of intercession that is not calm or detached. It involves the whole person, body included. The one who prays feels the need of others as though it were his own pain, and cannot rest until it is relieved.

Scripture gives many examples. Moses pleaded for Israel after the golden calf and offered to be blotted out of God’s book in their place. Jeremiah wished his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears, so that he could weep day and night for his people. Paul wrote to the Romans, “I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were anathema from Christ for my brethren’s sake” (Romans 9:2-3, ASV). That passage was on Hyde’s mind throughout these summers. McGaw’s informant, apparently Hyde’s host in the hills in 1907, remembered that Hyde’s last message before he left was on those very verses. When he finished, “how we all broke down!”

Above all there is Gethsemane. Jesus said to his three friends, “My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: abide ye here, and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38, ASV). Paterson believed that in those summers Hyde had heard the Lord say to him, “Abide ye here and watch with Me,” and had stayed.

The Fellowship of His Sufferings

Paterson and Hyde spoke often, in these years, of “the fellowship of Christ’s sufferings,” a phrase from Paul: “that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings” (Philippians 3:10, ASV). Hyde would quote another verse that puzzles many readers: “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and fill up on my part that which is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body’s sake, which is the church” (Colossians 1:24, ASV). And Paterson remembered his preoccupation with the thought “that our Lord still agonizes for souls,” that the risen Christ, who “ever liveth to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25, ASV), still bears their burdens with them.

This theme needs careful handling, and Hyde’s friends did not always handle it carefully. Scripture is clear that Christ’s sacrifice for sin was once for all, complete, and unrepeatable. He cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30, ASV). No intercessor adds anything to the atonement, and nothing is “lacking” in Christ’s work of redemption. When Paul speaks of filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions, he is not talking about the cross as payment for sin. He means the sufferings that Christ’s body, the church, must still undergo as it carries the gospel to the world. Those sufferings Christ counts as his own: “Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” (Acts 9:4, ASV). The intercessor is invited to share, in a small way, in the Lord’s grief over the world and his longing for its salvation. He is not invited to share in the Lord’s work of paying for it.

Some of the language in the memoirs goes further than this. It speaks of Hyde being given “the privilege of drinking of the Master’s cup,” and of a friend of his who seemed to tread “the winepress of the wrath of God against sin all alone.” Such phrases are the overflow of devotion and should not be pressed into theology. But at its heart the idea is sound and deeply biblical. When we pray for others, we are not persuading a reluctant God to care about them. We are being drawn into a care he already has. The Spirit himself, Paul says, “maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Romans 8:26, ASV). Hyde’s groans in the room on the hillside were, in his friends’ understanding, a small echo of those.

“It Is Not Our Broken Heart”

There is a danger here, and Paterson saw it. If intercession is measured by how much the intercessor suffers, then prayer becomes a kind of spiritual athletics. Those who can stay up longest and weep most will be counted the best at it, and ordinary Christians will despair.

McGaw preserves a conversation from the end of one of the conventions that addresses this directly. A Christian was praying aloud, asking God for “Thy heart of love for sinners, Thy broken heart for their sins, Thy tears with which to admonish night and day.” Then he went on, “But, O Lord, I feel so cold. My heart is so hard and dead. I am so lukewarm!” A friend interrupted him. “Why are you looking down at your poor self, brother? Of course your heart is cold and dead. But you have asked for the broken heart of Jesus, his love, his burden for sin, his tears. Is he a liar? Has he not given what you asked for? Then why look away from his heart to your own?”

Paterson drew the lesson clearly: “It is not our broken heart, it is God’s we need. It is not our sufferings, it is Christ’s we are partakers of. It is not our tears with which we should admonish night and day — it is all Christ’s. The fellowship of his sufferings is his free gift — free for the taking in simple faith, never minding our feelings.”

This is an important corrective. The burden that Hyde carried was not something he manufactured. It was given. And the secret of his prayer life, Paterson insisted, was not his own effort but Christ’s intercession: “I confess my ever failing prayers … and plead his never failing intercession.”

Not a Hermit

One more detail from the summer of 1908 deserves to be remembered. For all the intensity of those weeks, Hyde did not become a recluse. His host’s children loved “Uncle John,” who had often played with them, and they greeted him with smiles. They seemed to understand that this was “no time for play,” and were hushed and gentle in his presence. Yet “there was nothing of the hermit about him,” Paterson wrote. “People were more than ever attracted to him, and freely asked for his prayers. He always had leisure to speak to them of spiritual things, and entered even more patiently than ever into their trials and disappointments.”

That is the test of genuine intercession. Prayer that makes a person impatient with the people he prays for, or too spiritual to be interrupted, has gone wrong somewhere. Hyde’s prayer made him more available, not less.

For Reflection

Few of us will pray as Hyde prayed in the hills in 1907 and 1908, and later chapters will ask honestly whether he himself should have prayed quite so hard. But all of us can ask whether we have ever longed for the salvation of others as Rachel longed for children, or as Paul longed for his people. We can ask whether we have ever prayed for them until it cost us something.

And if our hearts feel cold, Paterson’s word is for us. We are not asked to produce a broken heart. We are invited to ask for Christ’s, and to trust that he gives it, “never minding our feelings.”
