This theme needs careful handling, and Hyde’s friends did not always handle it carefully. Scripture is clear that Christ’s sacrifice for sin was once for all, complete, and unrepeatable. He cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30, ASV). No intercessor adds anything to the atonement, and nothing is “lacking” in Christ’s work of redemption. When Paul speaks of filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions, he is not talking about the cross as payment for sin. He means the sufferings that Christ’s body, the church, must still undergo as it carries the gospel to the world. Those sufferings Christ counts as his own: “Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” (Acts 9:4, ASV). The intercessor is invited to share, in a small way, in the Lord’s grief over the world and his longing for its salvation. He is not invited to share in the Lord’s work of paying for it. Some of the language in the memoirs goes further than this. It speaks of Hyde being given “the privilege of drinking of the Master’s cup,” and of a friend of his who seemed to tread “the winepress of the wrath of God against sin all alone.” Such phrases are the overflow of devotion and should not be pressed into theology. But at its heart the idea is sound and deeply biblical. When we pray for others, we are not persuading a reluctant God to care about them. We are being drawn into a care he already has. The Spirit himself, Paul says, “maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Romans 8:26, ASV). Hyde’s groans in the room on the hillside were, in his friends’ understanding, a small echo of those. “It Is Not Our Broken Heart” There is a danger here, and Paterson saw it. If intercession is measured by how much the intercessor suffers, then prayer becomes a kind of spiritual athletics. Those who can stay up longest and weep most will be counted the best at it, and ordinary Christians will despair. McGaw preserves a conversation from the end of one of the conventions that addresses this directly. A Christian was praying aloud, asking God for “Thy heart of love for sinners, Thy broken heart for their sins, Thy tears with which to admonish night and day.” Then he went on, “But, O Lord, I feel so cold. My heart is so hard and dead. I am so lukewarm!” A friend interrupted him. “Why are you looking down at your poor self, brother? Of course your heart is cold and dead. But you have asked for the broken heart of Jesus, his love, his burden for sin, his tears. Is he a liar? Has he not given what you asked for? Then why look away from his heart to your own?” Paterson drew the lesson clearly: “It is not our broken heart, it is God’s we need. It is not our sufferings, it is Christ’s we are partakers of. It is not our tears with which we should admonish night and day — it is all Christ’s. The fellowship of his sufferings is his free gift — free for the taking in simple faith, never minding our feelings.” This is an important corrective. The burden that Hyde carried was not something he manufactured. It was given. And the secret of his prayer life, Paterson insisted, was not his own effort but Christ’s intercession: “I confess my ever failing prayers … and plead his never failing intercession.” Not a Hermit One more detail from the summer of 1908 deserves to be remembered. For all the intensity of those weeks, Hyde did not become a recluse. His host’s children loved “Uncle John,” who had often played with them, and they greeted him with smiles. They seemed to understand that this was “no time for play,” and were hushed and gentle in his presence. Yet “there was nothing of the hermit about him,” Paterson wrote. “People were more than ever attracted to him, and freely asked for his prayers. He always had leisure to speak to them of spiritual things, and entered even more patiently than ever into their trials and disappointments.” That is the test of genuine intercession. Prayer that makes a person impatient with the people he prays for, or too spiritual to be interrupted, has gone wrong somewhere. Hyde’s prayer made him more available, not less. For Reflection Few of us will pray as Hyde prayed in the hills in 1907 and 1908, and later chapters will ask honestly whether he himself should have prayed quite so hard. But all of us can ask whether we have ever longed for the salvation of others as Rachel longed for children, or as Paul longed for his people. We can ask whether we have ever prayed for them until it cost us something. And if our hearts feel cold, Paterson’s word is for us. We are not asked to produce a broken heart. We are invited to ask for Christ’s, and to trust that he gives it, “never minding our feelings.”

fields.title: A Soul a Day, and “What About That One?”
fields.body_html:
“What man of you, having a hundred sheep, and having lost one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?”

— Luke 15:4, ASV

The Most Famous Claim

If people know one thing about Praying Hyde besides his name, it is usually this. In 1908 he asked God for one soul a day, and by the end of the year more than four hundred had been won. The next year he asked for two a day, and got them. The year after that he asked for four a day, and on any day when four did not come, he could neither eat nor sleep until he found out why.

It is a stirring story. It has been preached in countless sermons and printed in countless books. And because it is so famous, it is worth taking more care over it than over almost anything else in Hyde’s life: what exactly the sources say, where they got it, and what we can confirm.

What McGaw Records

The story comes from McGaw’s book, in a section from his unnamed informant, almost certainly Paterson. The key passage describes what followed the burden of the summer of 1908:

It was about this time that John Hyde laid hold of God in a very definite covenant. This was for one soul a day — not less, not enquirers simply but a soul saved — ready to confess Christ in public and be baptized in his name. Then the stress and strain was relieved. His heart was filled with the peace of full assurance.

Hyde returned to his district with this confidence, the account says. It meant long journeys, nights of prayer, and cold dews and exhausting heat, “yet victory always crowning this.” And then comes the figure: “By the end of that year more than four hundred were gathered in.” The account for 1909 says that he asked for two souls a day. The next section speaks of “the eight hundred souls gathered in since last year’s convention,” that is, between the conventions of 1909 and 1910. For 1910 it says that he “at length got the assurance of four souls a day.”

Notice two things about this account. First, the definition of a “soul” is strict: not an enquirer, not someone who had shown interest, but a person ready to confess Christ publicly and be baptized. Second, the numbers come without any source. The memoir does not say who counted, or whether the figures are Hyde’s own estimate, a mission return, or a friend’s impression.

What the Records Show

No mission report yet found gives Hyde’s personal baptisms for 1908, 1909, or 1910. That does not mean the figures are wrong. The Presbyterian mission reported by station and district, not by individual missionary. But it means that the famous numbers rest, as far as we know, on this one memoir.

What the records do show is that something remarkable was happening in Hyde’s district. The women’s missionary magazine of his church reported in October 1911 that the Ferozepore training school had moved to Moga, and added: “Moga is where Rev. J. N. Hyde has been burying the good seed, and baptisms have steadily increased for five years past. They numbered 685 in 1910.” Griswold’s obituary says that Hyde “was marvelously used of God during his last few years at Moga in bringing very many to decision and baptism,” and that “rarely a day passed without the winning of trophies of grace.”

Most valuable of all is a line from Hyde himself. McGaw quotes a letter Hyde wrote to his old seminary classmates near the end of his time in India:

For three full years now God has given us decisions and baptisms every day when we have been out in our district — over a thousand the past two years … never a day if we were right with God without souls.

This is the closest we come to Hyde’s own account of the soul-a-day years, and it is worth reading carefully. He says “us,” not “me.” The baptisms belonged to the whole team of missionary and Indian evangelists working the district together. He says “when we have been out in our district”, meaning on the days of touring, not every calendar day of the year. And he gives a round figure, over a thousand in two years, which fits well with the 685 baptisms the mission recorded at Moga in 1910. His emphasis falls not on the arithmetic but on the condition: “never a day if we were right with God without souls.”

Read this way, the story is both more modest and more believable than the legend. Hyde did not personally lead four people a day to Christ for a year. What happened was this. In the middle of a great movement toward Christ among the poorest people of the Punjab, Hyde and his Indian fellow workers prayed specifically and expectantly for daily fruit, and for three years they saw it. That is extraordinary enough.

A Covenant, Not a Quota

There is a danger in the soul-a-day story, and it is not only the danger of exaggeration. Numbers can take over. A missionary who has asked God for a certain number of converts every day may be tempted to count people rather than love them. He may baptize too quickly, or treat a day without results as a personal failure. The critics of the Punjab mass movements worried about exactly this: converts baptized with little teaching, and churches full of people whom no one had time to instruct.

Hyde was not immune to the pressure. Paterson remembered him saying that “if on any day four souls were not brought into the fold, at night there would be such a weight on his heart that it was positively painful, and he could not eat nor sleep.” There is something admirable in that, and something troubling.

But the sources also show what kept Hyde’s covenant from becoming a quota. First, its motive was love, not success. Paterson insists that no number satisfied him: “No matter if he won the one a day or two a day or four a day, he had an unsatisfied longing, an undying passion for lost souls.” He seemed always to be hearing the Good Shepherd’s words, “And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring” (John 10:16, ASV). Second, when a day passed without fruit, he looked first at himself, not at the people. As we will see in a later chapter, what he usually found was that he had lost the spirit of praise. Third, his definition of a convert was demanding. He was not counting hands raised or cards signed, but people willing to confess Christ publicly and be baptized. In the villages of the Punjab that often meant persecution from employers and family.

And the numbers did not make him hurry. The most famous story of those years is about a day when Hyde refused to leave a village because one person was missing.

“What About That One?”

Paterson heard this story from one of Hyde’s Indian evangelists, who told it “with shame.” It is the most vivid scene in all the memoirs, and it has the ring of a true story partly because it makes the storyteller look bad.

One morning, after prayer, Hyde and two Indian evangelists felt assured that God would give them ten souls that day. They set out in a country cart to a distant village. The road ran along a river bank and was dangerous after dark. They reached the village. They sang, and preached, and sang again, and preached again. The day wore on. Not one person showed the slightest interest. The evangelists grew hungry and thirsty. As Paterson put it, echoing the parable of the prodigal son, “No man gave unto them.” They began to want to go home. Hyde would not move. He was waiting for the ten.

At last, near a humble cottage, they asked for a drink. The man offered them milk as well as water, and invited them in. As they talked, he showed a surprising knowledge of Jesus Christ. Yes, he said, the family had been thinking about following him. Then why not now? He called his wife and children. They understood what they were doing, and they decided together, there and then, to take their stand on the Lord’s side. Hyde baptized them all, nine people in all.

By now it was getting dark. The short winter day was ending, and the dangerous road lay ahead. Surely now they could go. The father of the family urged it too. Hyde left the house reluctantly. One of the evangelists went for the cart. The other took Hyde by the arm and hurried him toward it. When it came, they tried to lift him in. He would not get in. He looked pleadingly at the evangelist and asked, “What about that one?”

The evangelist lost his temper. It was all very well for the Sahib, he thought, if he broke his neck on the road in the dark. He had no wife or family to think of. It was a different matter for them. He said something sharp about their wives and children waiting anxiously at home. The two of them almost used force to get Hyde into the cart. And each time, “the same cry” came from him: “What about that one?”

After a while the father of the family came up, wondering why the Padri Sahib was still standing in the road. Hyde told him that one soul was still missing. “Why, there he is!” said the man. “My nephew, whom I have adopted. He has been living with the rest of us, but has been out playing.” He brought the boy forward, a bright and intelligent lad. Hyde asked him about his faith, and the boy answered clearly. There could be no doubt about him, and he too was baptized.

“That is the ten,” said Hyde, with what the evangelist called “a weary sigh of heart’s ease,” and climbed into the cart. They reached home safely in the dark, tired but content.

The Shepherd’s Arithmetic

It is possible to read this story as a lesson in stubborn faith: Hyde asked for ten, and would not settle for nine. That is part of it. But the heart of the story is not the number. It is the one.

The verse at the head of this chapter describes a shepherd who has ninety-nine sheep safe and goes after the one that is lost, “until he find it” (Luke 15:4, ASV). By any sensible reckoning, ninety-nine is a good day’s result. But the shepherd does not reckon sensibly. He reckons by love, and love counts differently. Jesus concludes, “I say unto you, that even so there shall be joy in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine righteous persons, who need no repentance” (Luke 15:7, ASV).

Paterson saw the same thing. Hyde, he wrote, “knew that the good Shepherd was Himself searching for that one still outside the Fold.” Hyde’s stubbornness in the road was not the obstinacy of a man chasing a target. It was the stubbornness of a man who believed he was standing beside the Good Shepherd, who had not stopped searching.

And the story ends with rest. Paterson wrote that the “rest of soul” the Lord gives his faithful under-shepherds is also the rest they give him, “for in their passion and longing for the lost He sees of the travail of His soul and is satisfied.” The phrase is from Isaiah’s great prophecy of the suffering servant: “He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied” (Isaiah 53:11, ASV). The joy of the village road in the dark was not finally Hyde’s. It belonged to Christ.

Preach and Baptize on the Spot

One more feature of these years deserves notice, because it troubles some readers today. Hyde baptized quickly. He told his mission in 1907 that the ideal was to “preach and baptize on the spot.” McGaw’s sources remember him baptizing people “in the village, by the roadside, or anywhere.”

This can look reckless. But it was not unbiblical. When Philip explained the gospel to the Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza, the man said, “Behold, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?” Philip baptized him at once (Acts 8:36, 38, ASV). On the day of Pentecost about three thousand were baptized (Acts 2:41, ASV). The New Testament knows nothing of years-long waiting periods for people who have confessed Christ.

What made quick baptism responsible in the Punjab was what came after it. Hyde’s own method insisted on following up converts in their places of work, and trying “every time we visit a convert … to leave some lesson or some influence on his life.” He founded the Ferozepore training school, later moved to Moga, to prepare village preachers and teachers. Baptism was the beginning of discipleship, not the end of evangelism. Whether the mission always managed that follow-up well is another question. It was stretched very thin by the sheer size of the movement. But Hyde did not treat baptism as a finishing line.

For Reflection

The soul-a-day story is often told to make Christians feel that they pray too little and expect too little. It may do that. But its real challenge lies in the question Hyde asked in the dark: “What about that one?”

Most churches are content with the ninety-nine. Most of us, if we have seen nine people come to faith, would call it a remarkable day and head home before dark. Hyde’s question will not let us settle so easily. Somewhere near us, playing in the lane or sitting at the back or living in the next house, there is probably one person no one has yet thought to ask about. The Good Shepherd has not stopped searching for them. We might pray, like Hyde, to be standing where he is searching.

fields.title: The Accuser of the Brethren
fields.body_html:
“For thus saith Jehovah of hosts: After glory hath he sent me unto the nations which plundered you; for he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye.”

— Zechariah 2:8, ASV

A Rebuke in the Middle of a Prayer

Of all the stories told about John Hyde, the one that has done the most good may be the one that shows him at his worst.

It comes from McCheyne Paterson, whose reminiscences in Carré’s book tell it, and it appears again, in almost the same words, in the account McGaw compiled. Carré’s version places it when Hyde was “up in the hills resting for a short time,” praying in his “inner chamber.” McGaw’s leaves out the hills and dates it about 1910. They agree on everything else, and Paterson said Hyde himself used to speak of it “as one of the most direct and solemn lessons God had ever taught him.”

Hyde had been burdened about an Indian pastor. The man’s spiritual life seemed to have gone cold, and his congregation had become as lifeless as their minister. Hyde resolved to give time to definite intercession for him. He went into his room, knelt, and began to pour out his heart to God about the pastor. In Carré’s version his first words were something like, “O God! Thou knowest that brother how —” In McGaw’s they were, “O Father, thou knowest how cold —”

He never finished the sentence. “Cold” was the word he was about to say. But, as McGaw’s version has it, “a finger seemed to be laid on his lips, so that the word was not uttered”, a “Hand,” in Paterson’s telling, and a voice said to him in stern reproach: “He that toucheth him, toucheth the apple of mine eye.”

A great horror came over Hyde. He cried out, “Forgive me, Father, in that I have been an accuser of the brethren before thee!”

The Apple of His Eye

The words that stopped Hyde are adapted from the verse at the head of this chapter. In Zechariah, God speaks of the nations that have plundered his people: “he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye” (Zechariah 2:8, ASV). The “apple of the eye” is the pupil, the most sensitive and carefully guarded part of the body. The phrase occurs elsewhere too. Moses sang of how God found Israel in the wilderness and “kept him as the apple of his eye” (Deuteronomy 32:10, ASV). David prayed, “Keep me as the apple of the eye; hide me under the shadow of thy wings” (Psalm 17:8, ASV).

In Zechariah the warning is addressed to Israel’s enemies. What shook Hyde was that it had been turned on him. He was not an enemy of the pastor. He was praying for him. He meant well. But in the very act of intercession he had begun to list the man’s faults to God, and God had treated it as an attack on someone he held precious.

The phrase Hyde used in his confession, “an accuser of the brethren,” makes the point even more sharply. It comes from the book of Revelation, and it is a name for Satan: “the accuser of our brethren is cast down, who accuseth them before our God day and night” (Revelation 12:10, ASV). Hyde had come to God to do the work of an intercessor. He found that he had been doing the work of the accuser.

The Oldest Sin of the Praying Person

This is a sin that belongs especially to people who pray. It is easy to criticise others in conversation, and most of us know it is wrong. It is much harder to notice when we are doing it in prayer, because prayer feels like a holy activity. We bring someone before God “in concern,” and before we know it we are telling God what is wrong with them. We describe their coldness, their failures, their bad influence, and we ask him to deal with it. The prayer has a spiritual shape. Its content is accusation.

Jesus’ parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector shows the same danger. The Pharisee stood and “prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as the rest of men” (Luke 18:11, ASV). His prayer was full of comparison and quietly full of contempt. James warns, “Speak not one against another, brethren. He that speaketh against a brother, or judgeth his brother, speaketh against the law, and judgeth the law” (James 4:11, ASV). Jesus himself warns against seeing the speck in a brother’s eye while ignoring the beam in one’s own (Matthew 7:3-5, ASV).

Hyde was one of the most prayerful men of his generation. That did not protect him from this sin. If anything it exposed him to it, because intercessors spend so much time thinking about the spiritual condition of others. Yet his friends were unanimous that criticism of people was not in his character. Jones wrote that he “never heard him criticizing any persons, though he could vehemently denounce sin.” This story is the key to that. The gentleness his friends admired was not natural to him. He had been taught it, abruptly, in the middle of a prayer.

“Show Me What Things Are Lovely”

What Hyde did next is the most important part of the story.

He confessed his sin and claimed, in Paterson’s phrase, “the precious blood of Christ that cleanseth from all sin.” Then he remembered a verse from Philippians: “whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things” (Philippians 4:8, ASV). And he prayed a new prayer: “Father, show me what things are lovely and of good report in my brother’s life.”

The answer came, Paterson says, “like a flash.” Hyde remembered that the pastor had given up everything for Christ, and had endured much suffering from relatives he had left behind for the gospel. He remembered the man’s years of hard work, the tact with which he managed a difficult congregation, the many quarrels he had healed, and what a good husband he was. One thing after another rose up in his mind. And Hyde spent the whole of his time of prayer, which he had set apart for intercession, in thanksgiving for his brother instead. “He could not recall a single petition,” Paterson wrote, “nothing but thanksgiving!”

McGaw’s version adds a further lesson that Hyde drew. He had wanted, he said, to keep the rule of Philippians 4:8 by looking at whatever was lovely in his brother, without giving up his commitment to whatever was true. Surely, he thought, the pastor’s coldness was true? What he came to see was that the sins of God’s children, though real, are passing. They are not their true nature. The true thing about a believer is what he is in Christ, and what he will be when God has finished the work he has begun. Paul wrote to the same Philippians, “he who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ: even as it is right for me to be thus minded on behalf of you all, because I have you in my heart” (Philippians 1:6-7, ASV). To see a fellow believer truly is to see him as God sees him, in the light of what grace will make him.

The Pastor Revived

The story has an epilogue. When Hyde went down from the hills, he heard that the pastor had just then received a great spiritual uplift. According to McGaw’s version, the pastor was preaching again “with fire.” Paterson believed it had happened at the very time Hyde was praising God for him. “While he was praising, God was blessing.”

Paterson made this into a general principle: “While we bless God for any child of His, He delights to bless that one!” We should be careful not to turn that into a mechanism, as though praise were a lever that forces God’s hand. The Bible gives no such formula, and Hyde would not have claimed one. But there is a deep truth here. Criticism, even criticism offered to God in prayer, tends to see people as problems. Thanksgiving sees them as God’s work in progress. And the attitude we take toward people in private prayer shapes, sooner or later, the way we treat them in public.

The Carpenter’s Shop

Paterson told a small parable to explain what Hyde had learned, and it is worth passing on.

Suppose, he said, you walk into a carpenter’s workshop and start pointing out faults in the half-made furniture. “How rough this is! What an ugly corner that is!” The carpenter will be annoyed, and rightly. “Bear in mind,” he will say, “that I am still making these things. They are not yet finished. Come and see the Pattern after which they are being fashioned.” And he will show you finished chairs and tables, perfectly shaped and polished. Who is right, the critic or the carpenter? The critic looks at what is rough and passing. The carpenter looks at what will be.

“Let us remember above all else,” Paterson wrote, “that God’s people on this earth are in the making. This is His workshop and souls are being fashioned and formed in it.” He pointed to the Carpenter of Nazareth, of whom Isaiah prophesied, “A bruised reed will he not break, and a dimly burning wick will he not quench” (Isaiah 42:3, ASV). Jesus, Paterson said, looked at the faint light in his erring disciples rather than at the smoke, and by doing so blew them into flame until they became the light of the world.

Does This Mean Never Correcting Anyone?

Paterson anticipated an objection. “Then should we shut our eyes to the faults of all? Should we never reprove sin?” He answered that our Lord did reprove sin at times, and so must we. The New Testament is full of correction. Paul rebuked Peter to his face. Jesus spoke sternly to the Pharisees and to his own disciples. The church is told to “reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all longsuffering and teaching” (2 Timothy 4:2, ASV). Hyde himself, Jones says, “could vehemently denounce sin.” And in private, during the dispute over public confession at Sialkot, he told Jones plainly that hidden immorality among Christians was more common than anyone imagined.

The lesson Hyde learned was not that sin should be ignored. It was about where correction begins and in what spirit. It begins with honest confession of our own sin. It proceeds with thankfulness for what God is doing in the other person. And any rebuke that follows comes from someone who has first seen his brother as the apple of God’s eye. Galatians gives the order: “Brethren, even if a man be overtaken in any trespass, ye who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1, ASV). Criticism that has not passed through thanksgiving is usually just accusation.

For Reflection

Most of us pray for people whose faults we know well: a difficult colleague, a disappointing pastor, a wayward relative, a church member who irritates us. It is worth listening, next time, to what we actually say about them to God. Do our prayers sound more like intercession or more like a charge sheet?

Hyde’s remedy is simple enough to try today. Stop in the middle of the complaint. Confess it. Then pray his prayer: “Father, show me what things are lovely and of good report in my brother’s life.” Stay with that prayer until something comes to mind, and then give thanks for it. It may be that, as Hyde found, the whole time of prayer turns into praise. And it may be that, while we are praising, God is blessing.

fields.title: The Garment of Praise
fields.body_html:
“to appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of Jehovah, that he may be glorified.”

— Isaiah 61:3, ASV

A Man Not Naturally Happy

The popular image of Praying Hyde is a sorrowful one: a gaunt figure on his face in the dark, sobbing for souls. There is truth in that image, and earlier chapters have not hidden it. But it is only half the truth, and the friends who knew him best were anxious that it should not be taken for the whole.

McCheyne Paterson began his chapter on Hyde’s joy with an admission that he thought would comfort many readers. “Mr. John Hyde was not naturally a bright and happy man. On the contrary he was in himself inclined to be morose, retiring, shy and silent. Yet he became one of the most joyous souls I have ever met.”

That sentence holds a whole gospel. Temperament is real, and Hyde’s was gloomy. Grace did not erase his temperament. He remained shy, and in public he often looked burdened. But grace gave him a joy that his temperament could never have produced. Jones noticed the same thing. People who did not know Hyde well thought him “a morose, melancholy person,” but in the company of those who understood him “how bright and cheerful he was.” Jones said he had what some called “sanctified humour,” kept “under perfect control.”

The Great Exchange

Paterson says Hyde was “very fond” of the verse at the head of this chapter. In Isaiah 61, the anointed servant of the Lord announces good news to the afflicted. Among other things, he comes “to give unto them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness” (Isaiah 61:3, ASV). Hyde read this as an exchange. We hand over to Christ what we have: ashes, mourning, and a spirit of heaviness. He hands us what he has: his beauty, his oil of joy, his garment of praise. Paterson added a pointed remark about the ashes: “what is our past life but ‘ashes’?”

The joy, in other words, is not produced by the one who receives it. It is Christ’s own joy, given. Jesus said, “These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be made full” (John 15:11, ASV). Hyde, Paterson wrote, received “our Lord’s Double Gift of Joy … freely from his Master’s Hand, and then would burst out into joyful praise. For no one can be filled with the Divine Joy and not sing His Praise!”

This is why the image of a garment matters. A garment is put on. It does not grow from within. A man with a heavy spirit does not wait until he feels praise before he praises. He accepts the garment Christ offers and puts it on, and the feeling follows.

“Praising God Through Shut Teeth”

Paterson says that no one he ever knew obeyed Paul’s command more faithfully than Hyde: “giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father” (Ephesians 5:20, ASV). It was, he said, “one great source of his joy and therefore of his attractive power.”

Hyde would say again and again that if we want to know why trials are sent to us, we should begin by thanking God for them, and we will soon see why. His circle of friends had a private phrase for this: “Praising God through shut teeth.” It meant praising God in the face of the worst troubles and darkest hours, not because the troubles felt good but because God was still Father. “We can never doubt that He is our Father in Heaven,” Paterson wrote, “and so all must be well for us at all times and in all circumstances.”

Hyde had a story he liked to tell about how he learned this. He and his catechists were touring the villages in the hot weather, when preaching had to begin very early. One morning he woke with one of his worst headaches, so painful that he could not lift his head from the pillow. He could not preach. But he could look up to his Father and thank him “for the love that had permitted that headache.” At his insistence, the evangelists carried his bed out to a shady place and went off to preach without him.

In that village, work among the women had been at a standstill. Some of the men had been baptized, but their wives had never come forward. Whenever anyone spoke to them about it, they said they had never talked it over among themselves. Now the women heard that the Padri Sahib was ill, and they came in a body to sympathise with him. As he lay there, he spoke to them of the claims of Christ. Yes, they said, they believed he had died for them. Then why had they not confessed him? They had never discussed it among themselves, they said. There was no time like the present, said Hyde, so why not discuss it now? They agreed, and after some talk among themselves they told him it was plain to them that they ought to be baptized. To the great joy of their husbands and the evangelists, it was done. “And John Hyde saw why the headache had been sent,” Paterson wrote. He always said afterwards that it had taught him to give thanks for all things at all times.

Singing Villages

Two more stories, both from Paterson, show how often praise went before fruit in Hyde’s work.

Once Hyde was travelling in a country cart to a distant village with one of his Punjabi evangelists and two of the evangelist’s small children. The men were talking gloomily about their destination. The gospel had been preached there for a long time, and hardly anyone had shown any interest. The children had no such worries. They were happy, and they sang, psalm after psalm and hymn after hymn. Their singing was infectious. Soon the two men were singing too, and they sang all the way to the village. When they arrived they found the people unexpectedly interested and eager. Before they left, more than a dozen had shown such living faith that Hyde “felt he dared not refuse them baptism then and there.” It was the first gospel breakthrough in that village, and Hyde was convinced it had been “heralded and brought about … by the spirit of praise which the children had evinced.” The psalm says, “Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou established strength” (Psalm 8:2, ASV).

Another time Hyde and a party of evangelists were camped in a village where the mission had worked for thirty years. The farm labourers there had for years been putting off a decision for Christ. Their excuse never changed: “Not now during the harvest, but afterwards when it is over.” But every year ended the same way, and Paterson could not help quoting Jeremiah: “The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved” (Jeremiah 8:20, ASV). The mission party was so discouraged that they decided to leave the next morning. That night someone suggested they go into the village and sing the gospel. They did, and they were so carried away that they sang on until after midnight.

Next morning, as they were packing up, a young man came running from the village. He begged them not to go. The panchayat, the village council, had been called and was meeting at that moment. No one had gone to work. They were considering whether to decide for Christ at once. The missionaries waited. Soon the young man came running back: they had all decided to serve Christ. Hyde found some fifteen men, mostly heads of families, ready for baptism, and baptized them before everyone. Afterwards the young man, himself a new convert, said to Hyde, “This is the result of your singing last night.” He reminded them of one of the songs: “Lift up your heads, O ye gates … And the King of glory will come in” (Psalm 24:7, ASV). “Has he not entered in this morning?”

No one in the missionary party had noticed the connection until the new convert pointed it out.

Praise Before the Answer

The Bible is full of this pattern. When King Jehoshaphat faced an invading army, he “appointed them that should sing unto Jehovah, and give praise in holy array, as they went out before the army.” And “when they began to sing and to praise, Jehovah set liers-in-wait” against the enemy (2 Chronicles 20:21-22, ASV). Paul and Silas, beaten and chained in the prison at Philippi, did not wait for release before they praised God. “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns unto God, and the prisoners were listening to them” (Acts 16:25, ASV). The earthquake came after the singing.

Paterson believed this was one of the deepest secrets of Hyde’s work. He remembered Hyde telling him that on the days when fewer souls were brought in than he had asked for, he would ask the Lord to show him what obstacle in himself was hindering the blessing. “He invariably found that it was the want of praise in his life.” Then he would confess it as sin, accept forgiveness, and ask for the spirit of praise “as for any other gift of God.” He would exchange “his ashes for Christ’s garland, his mourning for Christ’s oil of joy, his spirit of heaviness for Christ’s garment of praise,” praising God “beforehand for what he was going to do.” And, Paterson says, “as he praised God souls would come to him.”

Paterson offered a simple explanation. “No fisher can possibly throw his line lightly when he is dull and sad. It is only the bright and joyous soul that can win souls to Christ.” He noted how Paul, in the chapter of Philippians where he speaks of his fellow workers, immediately adds, “Rejoice in the Lord always: again I will say, Rejoice” (Philippians 4:4, ASV).

Holy Laughter

One more memory of Hyde’s joy comes from a friend who spent a holiday with him in the hills in the summer of 1907. There had been “seasons of great conflict” in prayer, and at times the friend feared Hyde would break down completely. But after whole nights of prayer and praise he would appear “fresh and smiling in the morning.”

The friend credited much of this joy to a poor Punjabi Christian of low-caste origin, whom he calls only “G—.” This brother, he said, had “been used of God to teach us all how to make such times of prayer a very heaven upon earth.” After most awful crying in prayer, G— would seem to break through into the presence of the Father. “You could see the smile of God reflected in his face. Then he would laugh aloud in the midst of his prayer. It was the joy of a son revelling in the delight of his Father’s smile.”

It is fitting that the lesson came from him. The missionaries had come to teach the villagers of the Punjab, and here a villager whose name we do not even know taught the missionaries how to laugh before God. The friend connected it with a verse from Proverbs about divine Wisdom at the creation: “I was daily his delight, Rejoicing always before him” (Proverbs 8:30, ASV). God, he said, had been teaching Hyde and him that he is “the God of Isaac,” a name that means laughter. Such laughter, he thought, “seemed to relieve the tension and give heaven’s own refreshment to wrestling spirits.”

The same friend quoted Nehemiah’s words to the weeping people of Jerusalem: “neither be ye grieved; for the joy of Jehovah is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10, ASV). He also recorded a claim that Hyde himself seems to have believed at the time: that since he had learned to draw on God’s strength, he had scarcely ever felt tired, though he had had little sleep for weeks. “No man need ever break down,” the friend added, “through overstrain in this ministry of intercession.” Hyde’s later history would not bear that confident claim out. We will come back to it honestly in a later chapter. But the joy was real, and it was the true secret of how he kept going as long as he did.

For Reflection

In his last weeks, in his sister’s home in Massachusetts in the winter of 1912, Hyde did not lament. A colleague later reported that after his worst spasms of pain he would say, “Praise the Lord,” or quote Paul’s words, “In every thing give thanks” (1 Thessalonians 5:18, in the older wording he knew). He had been learning that lesson for twenty years, from headaches in village huts, from singing children in a cart, and from a low-caste brother laughing in prayer. At the end it had become his native language.

Many of us, like Hyde, are not naturally joyful. The garment of praise is still offered. We do not have to feel like praising before we put it on. We can hand over our ashes and our heaviness, thank God through shut teeth if we must, and begin to sing. And we may find, as Hyde did, that the King of glory comes in.
fields.body_text: “to appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of Jehovah, that he may be glorified.” — Isaiah 61:3, ASV A Man Not Naturally Happy The popular image of Praying Hyde is a sorrowful one: a gaunt figure on his face in the dark, sobbing for souls. There is truth in that image, and earlier chapters have not hidden it. But it is only half the truth, and the friends who knew him best were anxious that it should not be taken for the whole. McCheyne Paterson began his chapter on Hyde’s joy with an admission that he thought would comfort many readers. “Mr. John Hyde was not naturally a bright and happy man. On the contrary he was in himself inclined to be morose, retiring, shy and silent. Yet he became one of the most joyous souls I have ever met.” That sentence holds a whole gospel. Temperament is real, and Hyde’s was gloomy. Grace did not erase his temperament. He remained shy, and in public he often looked burdened. But grace gave him a joy that his temperament could never have produced. Jones noticed the same thing. People who did not know Hyde well thought him “a morose, melancholy person,” but in the company of those who understood him “how bright and cheerful he was.” Jones said he had what some called “sanctified humour,” kept “under perfect control.” The Great Exchange Paterson says Hyde was “very fond” of the verse at the head of this chapter. In Isaiah 61, the anointed servant of the Lord announces good news to the afflicted. Among other things, he comes “to give unto them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness” (Isaiah 61:3, ASV). Hyde read this as an exchange. We hand over to Christ what we have: ashes, mourning, and a spirit of heaviness. He hands us what he has: his beauty, his oil of joy, his garment of praise. Paterson added a pointed remark about the ashes: “what is our past life but ‘ashes’?” The joy, in other words, is not produced by the one who receives it. It is Christ’s own joy, given. Jesus said, “These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be made full” (John 15:11, ASV). Hyde, Paterson wrote, received “our Lord’s Double Gift of Joy … freely from his Master’s Hand, and then would burst out into joyful praise. For no one can be filled with the Divine Joy and not sing His Praise!” This is why the image of a garment matters. A garment is put on. It does not grow from within. A man with a heavy spirit does not wait until he feels praise before he praises. He accepts the garment Christ offers and puts it on, and the feeling follows. “Praising God Through Shut Teeth” Paterson says that no one he ever knew obeyed Paul’s command more faithfully than Hyde: “giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father” (Ephesians 5:20, ASV). It was, he said, “one great source of his joy and therefore of his attractive power.” Hyde would say again and again that if we want to know why trials are sent to us, we should begin by thanking God for them, and we will soon see why. His circle of friends had a private phrase for this: “Praising God through shut teeth.” It meant praising God in the face of the worst troubles and darkest hours, not because the troubles felt good but because God was still Father. “We can never doubt that He is our Father in Heaven,” Paterson wrote, “and so all must be well for us at all times and in all circumstances.” Hyde had a story he liked to tell about how he learned this. He and his catechists were touring the villages in the hot weather, when preaching had to begin very early. One morning he woke with one of his worst headaches, so painful that he could not lift his head from the pillow. He could not preach. But he could look up to his Father and thank him “for the love that had permitted that headache.” At his insistence, the evangelists carried his bed out to a shady place and went off to preach without him. In that village, work among the women had been at a standstill. Some of the men had been baptized, but their wives had never come forward. Whenever anyone spoke to them about it, they said they had never talked it over among themselves. Now the women heard that the Padri Sahib was ill, and they came in a body to sympathise with him. As he lay there, he spoke to them of the claims of Christ. Yes, they said, they believed he had died for them. Then why had they not confessed him? They had never discussed it among themselves, they said. There was no time like the present, said Hyde, so why not discuss it now? They agreed, and after some talk among themselves they told him it was plain to them that they ought to be baptized. To the great joy of their husbands and the evangelists, it was done. “And John Hyde saw why the headache had been sent,” Paterson wrote. He always said afterwards that it had taught him to give thanks for all things at all times. Singing Villages Two more stories, both from Paterson, show how often praise went before fruit in Hyde’s work. Once Hyde was travelling in a country cart to a distant village with one of his Punjabi evangelists and two of the evangelist’s small children. The men were talking gloomily about their destination. The gospel had been preached there for a long time, and hardly anyone had shown any interest. The children had no such worries. They were happy, and they sang, psalm after psalm and hymn after hymn. Their singing was infectious. Soon the two men were singing too, and they sang all the way to the village. When they arrived they found the people unexpectedly interested and eager. Before they left, more than a dozen had shown such living faith that Hyde “felt he dared not refuse them baptism then and there.” It was the first gospel breakthrough in that village, and Hyde was convinced it had been “heralded and brought about … by the spirit of praise which the children had evinced.” The psalm says, “Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou established strength” (Psalm 8:2, ASV). Another time Hyde and a party of evangelists were camped in a village where the mission had worked for thirty years. The farm labourers there had for years been putting off a decision for Christ. Their excuse never changed: “Not now during the harvest, but afterwards when it is over.” But every year ended the same way, and Paterson could not help quoting Jeremiah: “The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved” (Jeremiah 8:20, ASV). The mission party was so discouraged that they decided to leave the next morning. That night someone suggested they go into the village and sing the gospel. They did, and they were so carried away that they sang on until after midnight. Next morning, as they were packing up, a young man came running from the village. He begged them not to go. The panchayat, the village council, had been called and was meeting at that moment. No one had gone to work. They were considering whether to decide for Christ at once. The missionaries waited. Soon the young man came running back: they had all decided to serve Christ. Hyde found some fifteen men, mostly heads of families, ready for baptism, and baptized them before everyone. Afterwards the young man, himself a new convert, said to Hyde, “This is the result of your singing last night.” He reminded them of one of the songs: “Lift up your heads, O ye gates … And the King of glory will come in” (Psalm 24:7, ASV). “Has he not entered in this morning?” No one in the missionary party had noticed the connection until the new convert pointed it out. Praise Before the Answer The Bible is full of this pattern. When King Jehoshaphat faced an invading army, he “appointed them that should sing unto Jehovah, and give praise in holy array, as they went out before the army.” And “when they began to sing and to praise, Jehovah set liers-in-wait” against the enemy (2 Chronicles 20:21-22, ASV). Paul and Silas, beaten and chained in the prison at Philippi, did not wait for release before they praised God. “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns unto God, and the prisoners were listening to them” (Acts 16:25, ASV). The earthquake came after the singing. Paterson believed this was one of the deepest secrets of Hyde’s work. He remembered Hyde telling him that on the days when fewer souls were brought in than he had asked for, he would ask the Lord to show him what obstacle in himself was hindering the blessing. “He invariably found that it was the want of praise in his life.” Then he would confess it as sin, accept forgiveness, and ask for the spirit of praise “as for any other gift of God.” He would exchange “his ashes for Christ’s garland, his mourning for Christ’s oil of joy, his spirit of heaviness for Christ’s garment of praise,” praising God “beforehand for what he was going to do.” And, Paterson says, “as he praised God souls would come to him.” Paterson offered a simple explanation. “No fisher can possibly throw his line lightly when he is dull and sad. It is only the bright and joyous soul that can win souls to Christ.” He noted how Paul, in the chapter of Philippians where he speaks of his fellow workers, immediately adds, “Rejoice in the Lord always: again I will say, Rejoice” (Philippians 4:4, ASV). Holy Laughter One more memory of Hyde’s joy comes from a friend who spent a holiday with him in the hills in the summer of 1907. There had been “seasons of great conflict” in prayer, and at times the friend feared Hyde would break down completely. But after whole nights of prayer and praise he would appear “fresh and smiling in the morning.” The friend credited much of this joy to a poor Punjabi Christian of low-caste origin, whom he calls only “G—.” This brother, he said, had “been used of God to teach us all how to make such times of prayer a very heaven upon earth.” After most awful crying in prayer, G— would seem to break through into the presence of the Father. “You could see the smile of God reflected in his face. Then he would laugh aloud in the midst of his prayer. It was the joy of a son revelling in the delight of his Father’s smile.” It is fitting that the lesson came from him. The missionaries had come to teach the villagers of the Punjab, and here a villager whose name we do not even know taught the missionaries how to laugh before God. The friend connected it with a verse from Proverbs about divine Wisdom at the creation: “I was daily his delight, Rejoicing always before him” (Proverbs 8:30, ASV). God, he said, had been teaching Hyde and him that he is “the God of Isaac,” a name that means laughter. Such laughter, he thought, “seemed to relieve the tension and give heaven’s own refreshment to wrestling spirits.” The same friend quoted Nehemiah’s words to the weeping people of Jerusalem: “neither be ye grieved; for the joy of Jehovah is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10, ASV). He also recorded a claim that Hyde himself seems to have believed at the time: that since he had learned to draw on God’s strength, he had scarcely ever felt tired, though he had had little sleep for weeks. “No man need ever break down,” the friend added, “through overstrain in this ministry of intercession.” Hyde’s later history would not bear that confident claim out. We will come back to it honestly in a later chapter. But the joy was real, and it was the true secret of how he kept going as long as he did. For Reflection In his last weeks, in his sister’s home in Massachusetts in the winter of 1912, Hyde did not lament. A colleague later reported that after his worst spasms of pain he would say, “Praise the Lord,” or quote Paul’s words, “In every thing give thanks” (1 Thessalonians 5:18, in the older wording he knew). He had been learning that lesson for twenty years, from headaches in village huts, from singing children in a cart, and from a low-caste brother laughing in prayer. At the end it had become his native language. Many of us, like Hyde, are not naturally joyful. The garment of praise is still offered. We do not have to feel like praising before we put it on. We can hand over our ashes and our heaviness, thank God through shut teeth if we must, and begin to sing. And we may find, as Hyde did, that the King of glory comes in.

fields.title: Tears at a Train Window
fields.body_html:
“Wherefore watch ye, remembering that by the space of three years I ceased not to admonish every one night and day with tears.”

— Acts 20:31, ASV

A Boy from the Mission School

Most of the people John Hyde led to Christ are nameless in the records. They appear only as numbers in a mission report, or as “souls” in a friend’s memoir. One of them is known by his initials, and his story, told by McCheyne Paterson, is the most human in all the accounts of Hyde’s life. It does not end neatly. That is one reason to trust it.

Paterson calls him “J. N.” He was a young Brahman, from the highest Hindu caste, who had attended the mission school in Paterson’s town. As he grew up the teaching of Christ drew him, and he also attended the Sunday school of one of the women missionaries. When he left school and began to earn his living, he publicly confessed Christ as his Saviour, in the face of what Paterson calls “the bitterest opposition” of his widowed mother and his relatives.

His family then changed tactics. Instead of opposing him, they began to please him. Their kindness won his heart, and he went back home. There he fell in with young men who led him into drink. Paterson thought the weakness might have run in the family. He fell, and he denied his Lord.

But he was miserable. He went to Mr. Hyde, “who received him as did the father his prodigal son.” The young man came to live with Hyde. Once again he was won from his old ways and confessed his faith. And once again the drink would take hold of him. More than once he stole Hyde’s clothes and sold them to buy liquor.

Paterson met Hyde around that time. With a smile Hyde told him, “I may not get up to you to the hills this summer, the Father evidently desires me to spend my hot weather in the plains, for I have no warm clothes left!” He took the loss, Paterson says, cheerfully, and thought his clothes “a small price to pay in exchange for an immortal soul.” The letter to the Hebrews commends believers who “took joyfully the spoiling of your possessions, knowing that ye have for yourselves a better possession and an abiding one” (Hebrews 10:34, ASV). Hyde would point out how the Lord had borne with Judas, and how he never sent away anyone who wanted to stay with him. So Hyde bore with the young man.

The Train to Lahore

Paterson heard the next part of the story from a stranger. He was travelling by train when a Christian woman who worked as a ticket collector at a station told him about a remarkable man she had just seen.

A missionary had been talking to a young man sitting in a train bound for Lahore. The young man was loud and almost abusive. “I am tired of this sort of thing,” he said. “I am going to my boon companions and shall have a good time.” The missionary leaned forward and, in a low voice, begged him not to go away from him. He got only a rude answer. The ticket collector, disgusted, walked away. When she came back, the missionary was leaning into the carriage window, still pleading. He was imploring the young man in Christ’s name, and she saw tears running down his cheeks as he reasoned with him. The young man would not listen. The train pulled out. The missionary, Paterson later learned, went on alone and sad to stay with friends at Gujrat.

The next day the ticket collector saw the same young man coming back from Lahore. “You have come back very soon again,” she said. He looked up at her with a pale face. “I am going back to him,” he said. “I have not been able to sleep all night — I could not forget his tears.”

The missionary was John Hyde, and the young man was J. N.

Years later J. N. told Paterson what happened when he got back. He went to the mission house where Hyde was staying and found him in his room, praying. Hyde opened his eyes, saw him, took him in his arms, and said, “I have just been praying that God would send you back to me, and see, He has answered me!”

“I Could Not Forget His Tears”

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from Paul’s farewell to the elders of the church at Ephesus. Looking back on three years among them, Paul reminded them that “I ceased not to admonish every one night and day with tears” (Acts 20:31, ASV). Tears were not a sign of weakness in Paul’s ministry. They were one of its instruments. He told the Corinthians, “I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls” (2 Corinthians 12:15, ASV).

Paterson drew the obvious lesson. “I often feel that if souls could say the same of us, that we wept over them — our tears would bring them to a proper frame of mind.” He reminded his readers that Jesus himself wept at the grave of Lazarus, and that those who saw him said, “Behold how he loved him!” (John 11:36, ASV).

There is no technique in this. Tears cannot be produced to order, and tears produced to manipulate someone are a kind of lie. What moved J. N. was not the tears themselves but what they revealed: that this man really loved him, cared more for his soul than for his own dignity, and would lean out of a train window in front of strangers to plead with him. Many people have heard the gospel explained correctly. Fewer have seen someone weep for them.

A Waiting Shed at Moga

J. N. also told Paterson how he had first come to know Hyde, and his account shows Hyde’s way with people very clearly.

He had seen Hyde on the platform of the railway station at Moga. He went up to him, mentioned the name of another missionary, and said that he himself had been baptized but had fallen away. “Why did you deny Christ?” Hyde asked him. The young man began to make excuses. Hyde did not argue. He took him into the third-class waiting shed, and there, with two other Christians, knelt down and prayed with him. A crowd gathered to stare. The young man’s own relatives came and saw him kneeling with the Christians. Then the train came in. Hyde said goodbye and added, “We will meet again in a week’s time or so, God will arrange it.”

The encounter so affected the young man that he set out to find Hyde. He heard that Hyde was holding meetings in a Christian village some distance inland. With a Christian friend he walked for two days to get there, and arrived exhausted. He was told Hyde was in his room praying. Hyde looked up, saw the Brahman lad, and took him in his arms “in good Punjabi style.” Then, seeing how tired he was, he made him lie down and began to rub and press his swollen feet. The young man protested. A Brahman did not expect a European missionary to touch his feet. Hyde insisted on serving him with his own hands. Years later, J. N. told Paterson about it with tears in his eyes, and said, “I often see him in my dreams before me as of old.”

Jesus, having washed his disciples’ feet, told them: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, ye also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14, ASV). Hyde had never needed to be told twice.

An Island in a Pool

In the same Christian village J. N. saw something he never forgot. One day he missed Hyde and went looking for him. He found him on a small island in a pool, surrounded by Christian children, all of them praying. The young man waded across to join them. Hyde was praying aloud, a phrase at a time, and the children were repeating what he said. They were praying that God’s Holy Spirit might fill all their hearts. Afterwards Hyde crossed back through the water with them all, and said to J. N. that God had told him from his Word to go into the valley and pray. He saw that this place was the valley, and as he went, the children had followed him.

That evening, while they were eating dinner, news came that the village’s Indian pastor had suddenly fallen ill and that his house was on fire. Everyone ran to help. While the others fought the flames, Hyde went to the pastor and found him crying out in pain and fear of death, with some unconfessed sin evidently weighing on his conscience. Hyde talked and prayed with him. Then he said, “I think it is God’s will that you confess your sin in church before your congregation.” The pastor agreed, and he was carried to the church on his bed. Lying on it, weeping, he confessed that he had committed a great sin against God in that very church, and prayed for forgiveness. According to the story, a great peace came over him and his pain left him. About twenty members of the congregation, conscience-stricken, confessed their own sins too. The firefighters joined them, and the service went on for an hour and a half. Then everyone went back to their half-eaten dinner.

From that village Hyde and his companions went on to a hill station where he had been urgently asked to hold meetings. They travelled third class in the heat, with only enough money for one pony and one porter between them, so they took turns riding. One night the Indian preacher, riding ahead, felt his pony freeze. A tiger had sprung from the roadside and landed just behind him. The terrified pony bolted and leapt a ditch, and the tiger was left on the road. When Hyde came up later there was no sign of it. He made them go back by moonlight to see the paw marks in the dust. They stayed a week in the hill station, and J. N., who was with them, was convicted of having denied his Lord, confessed, and was received back into fellowship. “So they went like beggars and returned like kings!” Paterson remarked, and the young man laughed and agreed. A missionary, he said, had lent him his own pony for the journey home.

An Unfinished Story

It would be pleasant to end J. N.’s story there. Paterson did not. When he wrote his reminiscences, about ten years after Hyde’s death, J. N. was still coming to see him. He was “much chastened,” but he had still not given up drink, and he admitted he had not kept his promise. He was working for a lawyer in a job Paterson disliked. His aged mother was still alive, and the old Brahman friend who came with him whispered that the young man would come back to the Christians “whenever his mother dies.” The young man smiled and did not deny it. He spoke of Hyde, pointing upward, as the one “Up there.” Paterson reminded him that Hyde was praying for him, and asked his readers to pray too. “It is not for nothing,” he wrote, “that God has sent the lad back to me and he is sitting by my side as I write.”

That is where the record ends. We do not know what became of J. N. His story is a reminder that even the most loving intercession does not guarantee a tidy result, and that Hyde’s tears did not end his friend’s struggle. They kept him coming back. Love, Paul says, “beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7, ASV). Sometimes that is all it can do, and it is not nothing.

Blankets and a Stick

J. N. was not the only one who took advantage of Hyde. Jones heard repeatedly that people stole Hyde’s belongings. He saw men wearing clothes they had taken from him, and would not call them to account “lest the men should be driven further away from Christ.” Some of his fellow missionaries blamed him for it.

One of Hyde’s Indian evangelists, who shared a village mud house with him for a time, told Paterson a story against himself. One cold winter night Hyde knocked at his door, late. The evangelist did not want to open it. Hyde called his name and asked, “Can you lend me a sheet for the night?” “Where are your own blankets?” the evangelist snapped through the closed door. Then he answered his own question: “Oh yes! that drunken sot that was with you has gone off with them. He will sell them, get drink and make a beast of himself. Do you know that you put us all about by doing things like this and then shivering yourself in the cold?”

The evangelist asked Paterson, with tears, whether he could imagine Hyde’s answer. Hyde called him by name and said: “If the prodigal had come back to you, you would have taken a stick to him!”

It is the gentlest possible rebuke, and it goes to the heart of the parable. In Jesus’ story, the father sees his son “while he was yet afar off” and “was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20, ASV). It is the elder brother who stands outside, angry, counting the cost. Hyde knew which character he wanted to be.

“He Has No Fault”

Jones heard another story from an Indian doctor in the Punjab shortly after Hyde’s death. The Arya Samaj, the Hindu reform movement that was working hard against Christian conversions, had been troubled by Hyde’s influence and by the number of people baptized under his preaching. Its members decided to send a man to live near Hyde, watch for his faults, and publish them, so as to break his influence.

Their man went to Hyde pretending to be an enquirer who wanted to know all about Christianity. Hyde welcomed him kindly and invited him to stay. He stayed for three or four days, watching Hyde day and night. Then he ran away, went back to the men who had sent him, and said: “He has no fault, the man has no fault, he is a God and not man.”

McGaw records a similar remark by a young Hindu: “Mr. Hyde seems to me like God.” Hyde would have been appalled by such words. He was painfully aware of his own sins, and he hid when he thought people were admiring him rather than Christ. We should read these stories as the tribute of people who had never seen anything like the Christ-like love they saw in him, and who reached for the only word they had. But the stories point to something real. Jesus told his disciples, “Give to every one that asketh thee; and of him that taketh away thy goods ask them not again” (Luke 6:30, ASV). Very few Christians take that literally. Hyde seems to have done so, and it made even his enemies wonder.

Given Altogether

One more fact about Hyde belongs here. He never married. Jones once asked him why, pointing out that a wife could look after his comforts. Hyde smiled, paused, and then answered “just as if he were betraying a secret”:

Years ago I felt that I wanted to give something to Jesus Christ who loved me so, and I gave myself to Him absolutely and promised Him that no one should come into my life and share my affection for Him. I told the Lord that I would not marry but be His altogether.

Scripture honours such a choice without requiring it. Jesus spoke of some who make themselves celibate “for the kingdom of heaven’s sake,” and added, “He that is able to receive it, let him receive it” (Matthew 19:12, ASV). Paul wrote that “he that is unmarried is careful for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:32, ASV), while insisting that marriage is good and that each person has “his own gift from God” (1 Corinthians 7:7, ASV). Hyde’s vow was his own gift and calling, not a pattern for others. But it explains a good deal. He had no household to protect, no family to worry about on a dark road, and no children to feed. He could give away his blankets and wait in a village until dark for one more soul. His angry evangelist, on the dark road, had thought that the Sahib had no wife or family to think of. He meant it as a complaint. Hyde would have heard it as a description of what he had freely given.

For Reflection

Hyde’s love for people was not sentimental. It cost him his clothes, his blankets, his sleep, his dignity at a railway window, and, as we will see, his health. And it did not always succeed. J. N. was still struggling ten years after Hyde’s death.

But it made the gospel visible. A drunken Brahman could not forget his tears. An enemy sent to spy on him could find no fault. An evangelist who slammed the door on him remembered his answer for the rest of his life. Most of us will never be asked to love as extravagantly as Hyde did. But each of us can ask whether anyone has ever been unable to forget our love for them, and whether there is someone we should be leaning out of a window to plead with today.
