Paterson drew the obvious lesson. “I often feel that if souls could say the same of us, that we wept over them — our tears would bring them to a proper frame of mind.” He reminded his readers that Jesus himself wept at the grave of Lazarus, and that those who saw him said, “Behold how he loved him!” (John 11:36, ASV). There is no technique in this. Tears cannot be produced to order, and tears produced to manipulate someone are a kind of lie. What moved J. N. was not the tears themselves but what they revealed: that this man really loved him, cared more for his soul than for his own dignity, and would lean out of a train window in front of strangers to plead with him. Many people have heard the gospel explained correctly. Fewer have seen someone weep for them. A Waiting Shed at Moga J. N. also told Paterson how he had first come to know Hyde, and his account shows Hyde’s way with people very clearly. He had seen Hyde on the platform of the railway station at Moga. He went up to him, mentioned the name of another missionary, and said that he himself had been baptized but had fallen away. “Why did you deny Christ?” Hyde asked him. The young man began to make excuses. Hyde did not argue. He took him into the third-class waiting shed, and there, with two other Christians, knelt down and prayed with him. A crowd gathered to stare. The young man’s own relatives came and saw him kneeling with the Christians. Then the train came in. Hyde said goodbye and added, “We will meet again in a week’s time or so, God will arrange it.” The encounter so affected the young man that he set out to find Hyde. He heard that Hyde was holding meetings in a Christian village some distance inland. With a Christian friend he walked for two days to get there, and arrived exhausted. He was told Hyde was in his room praying. Hyde looked up, saw the Brahman lad, and took him in his arms “in good Punjabi style.” Then, seeing how tired he was, he made him lie down and began to rub and press his swollen feet. The young man protested. A Brahman did not expect a European missionary to touch his feet. Hyde insisted on serving him with his own hands. Years later, J. N. told Paterson about it with tears in his eyes, and said, “I often see him in my dreams before me as of old.” Jesus, having washed his disciples’ feet, told them: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, ye also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14, ASV). Hyde had never needed to be told twice. An Island in a Pool In the same Christian village J. N. saw something he never forgot. One day he missed Hyde and went looking for him. He found him on a small island in a pool, surrounded by Christian children, all of them praying. The young man waded across to join them. Hyde was praying aloud, a phrase at a time, and the children were repeating what he said. They were praying that God’s Holy Spirit might fill all their hearts. Afterwards Hyde crossed back through the water with them all, and said to J. N. that God had told him from his Word to go into the valley and pray. He saw that this place was the valley, and as he went, the children had followed him. That evening, while they were eating dinner, news came that the village’s Indian pastor had suddenly fallen ill and that his house was on fire. Everyone ran to help. While the others fought the flames, Hyde went to the pastor and found him crying out in pain and fear of death, with some unconfessed sin evidently weighing on his conscience. Hyde talked and prayed with him. Then he said, “I think it is God’s will that you confess your sin in church before your congregation.” The pastor agreed, and he was carried to the church on his bed. Lying on it, weeping, he confessed that he had committed a great sin against God in that very church, and prayed for forgiveness. According to the story, a great peace came over him and his pain left him. About twenty members of the congregation, conscience-stricken, confessed their own sins too. The firefighters joined them, and the service went on for an hour and a half. Then everyone went back to their half-eaten dinner. From that village Hyde and his companions went on to a hill station where he had been urgently asked to hold meetings. They travelled third class in the heat, with only enough money for one pony and one porter between them, so they took turns riding. One night the Indian preacher, riding ahead, felt his pony freeze. A tiger had sprung from the roadside and landed just behind him. The terrified pony bolted and leapt a ditch, and the tiger was left on the road. When Hyde came up later there was no sign of it. He made them go back by moonlight to see the paw marks in the dust. They stayed a week in the hill station, and J. N., who was with them, was convicted of having denied his Lord, confessed, and was received back into fellowship. “So they went like beggars and returned like kings!” Paterson remarked, and the young man laughed and agreed. A missionary, he said, had lent him his own pony for the journey home. An Unfinished Story It would be pleasant to end J. N.’s story there. Paterson did not. When he wrote his reminiscences, about ten years after Hyde’s death, J. N. was still coming to see him. He was “much chastened,” but he had still not given up drink, and he admitted he had not kept his promise. He was working for a lawyer in a job Paterson disliked. His aged mother was still alive, and the old Brahman friend who came with him whispered that the young man would come back to the Christians “whenever his mother dies.” The young man smiled and did not deny it. He spoke of Hyde, pointing upward, as the one “Up there.” Paterson reminded him that Hyde was praying for him, and asked his readers to pray too. “It is not for nothing,” he wrote, “that God has sent the lad back to me and he is sitting by my side as I write.” That is where the record ends. We do not know what became of J. N. His story is a reminder that even the most loving intercession does not guarantee a tidy result, and that Hyde’s tears did not end his friend’s struggle. They kept him coming back. Love, Paul says, “beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7, ASV). Sometimes that is all it can do, and it is not nothing. Blankets and a Stick J. N. was not the only one who took advantage of Hyde. Jones heard repeatedly that people stole Hyde’s belongings. He saw men wearing clothes they had taken from him, and would not call them to account “lest the men should be driven further away from Christ.” Some of his fellow missionaries blamed him for it. One of Hyde’s Indian evangelists, who shared a village mud house with him for a time, told Paterson a story against himself. One cold winter night Hyde knocked at his door, late. The evangelist did not want to open it. Hyde called his name and asked, “Can you lend me a sheet for the night?” “Where are your own blankets?” the evangelist snapped through the closed door. Then he answered his own question: “Oh yes! that drunken sot that was with you has gone off with them. He will sell them, get drink and make a beast of himself. Do you know that you put us all about by doing things like this and then shivering yourself in the cold?” The evangelist asked Paterson, with tears, whether he could imagine Hyde’s answer. Hyde called him by name and said: “If the prodigal had come back to you, you would have taken a stick to him!” It is the gentlest possible rebuke, and it goes to the heart of the parable. In Jesus’ story, the father sees his son “while he was yet afar off” and “was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20, ASV). It is the elder brother who stands outside, angry, counting the cost. Hyde knew which character he wanted to be. “He Has No Fault” Jones heard another story from an Indian doctor in the Punjab shortly after Hyde’s death. The Arya Samaj, the Hindu reform movement that was working hard against Christian conversions, had been troubled by Hyde’s influence and by the number of people baptized under his preaching. Its members decided to send a man to live near Hyde, watch for his faults, and publish them, so as to break his influence. Their man went to Hyde pretending to be an enquirer who wanted to know all about Christianity. Hyde welcomed him kindly and invited him to stay. He stayed for three or four days, watching Hyde day and night. Then he ran away, went back to the men who had sent him, and said: “He has no fault, the man has no fault, he is a God and not man.” McGaw records a similar remark by a young Hindu: “Mr. Hyde seems to me like God.” Hyde would have been appalled by such words. He was painfully aware of his own sins, and he hid when he thought people were admiring him rather than Christ. We should read these stories as the tribute of people who had never seen anything like the Christ-like love they saw in him, and who reached for the only word they had. But the stories point to something real. Jesus told his disciples, “Give to every one that asketh thee; and of him that taketh away thy goods ask them not again” (Luke 6:30, ASV). Very few Christians take that literally. Hyde seems to have done so, and it made even his enemies wonder. Given Altogether One more fact about Hyde belongs here. He never married. Jones once asked him why, pointing out that a wife could look after his comforts. Hyde smiled, paused, and then answered “just as if he were betraying a secret”: Years ago I felt that I wanted to give something to Jesus Christ who loved me so, and I gave myself to Him absolutely and promised Him that no one should come into my life and share my affection for Him. I told the Lord that I would not marry but be His altogether. Scripture honours such a choice without requiring it. Jesus spoke of some who make themselves celibate “for the kingdom of heaven’s sake,” and added, “He that is able to receive it, let him receive it” (Matthew 19:12, ASV). Paul wrote that “he that is unmarried is careful for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:32, ASV), while insisting that marriage is good and that each person has “his own gift from God” (1 Corinthians 7:7, ASV). Hyde’s vow was his own gift and calling, not a pattern for others. But it explains a good deal. He had no household to protect, no family to worry about on a dark road, and no children to feed. He could give away his blankets and wait in a village until dark for one more soul. His angry evangelist, on the dark road, had thought that the Sahib had no wife or family to think of. He meant it as a complaint. Hyde would have heard it as a description of what he had freely given. For Reflection Hyde’s love for people was not sentimental. It cost him his clothes, his blankets, his sleep, his dignity at a railway window, and, as we will see, his health. And it did not always succeed. J. N. was still struggling ten years after Hyde’s death. But it made the gospel visible. A drunken Brahman could not forget his tears. An enemy sent to spy on him could find no fault. An evangelist who slammed the door on him remembered his answer for the rest of his life. Most of us will never be asked to love as extravagantly as Hyde did. But each of us can ask whether anyone has ever been unable to forget our love for them, and whether there is someone we should be leaning out of a window to plead with today.

fields.title: The Cross He Could Not Stop Preaching
fields.body_html:
“but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, yea, the death of the cross.”

— Philippians 2:7-8, ASV

A Whole Day on His Knees

At one of the Sialkot Conventions, the European visitors slept in the dormitory of the mission boarding school, a long, narrow building crowded with beds. Pengwern Jones found that his bed had been placed between Hyde’s and Dr. Griswold’s. He also noticed that Hyde’s bed was never slept in. Hyde spent his nights in the prayer room.

One morning, soon after dawn, Hyde rushed into the dormitory, went down on his knees beside his bed, and began to pray. Jones went to have an early breakfast, came back, and found him still praying. He went out to the prayer meeting and the morning service and came back at eleven. Hyde was still on his knees. Jones went to lunch, returned at half past twelve, lay down on his cot to rest, and watched him. The dormitory was noisy all day. People came in and out between the services, talking, looking for things, and resting. Jones went to the afternoon service, then to tea, then to the five o’clock meeting, coming back each time. At six o’clock Hyde was still kneeling. He had been there all day.

Jones decided to wait. If Hyde rose, he would ask him how he could pray all day amid such noise. Half an hour later Hyde looked up and smiled. Jones sat on his bed and asked him the secret. He offered to fetch him a cup of tea. Hyde refused the tea and asked only for a glass of water. Then he said, “Let me tell you what a vision I had — a new vision of Christ!”

Lower and Lower

Jones wrote down what Hyde said that evening as best he could remember it. He confessed that he could not do it justice. His account falls into three stages. It is a meditation on the verse at the head of this chapter, Paul’s great hymn about the self-emptying of Christ.

First, Hyde spoke of what it cost Christ to become a man. Jones had never seen it this way. Christ left his glory to live in a sinful world, and breathed its air every day. No wonder, Hyde said, that he often escaped from the crowds to the mountains, as though for a breath of the fresh air of heaven. Hyde described the holy Son of God living surrounded by sin until Jones felt that “even the Incarnation was an Infinite Sacrifice, even if the Death on Calvary had never taken place.” Then Hyde stopped, and said quietly, “and He took this place — became man — for me.”

After a while he went on. Second, Christ became a slave. He washed his disciples’ feet, which was the work of a slave. He did not merely act like a servant. He, the King of kings, whom the hosts of heaven worshipped, “became a bond-servant, a slave.” Paul’s word in Philippians 2:7 means exactly that. Hyde wept as he spoke, and Jones wept with him.

Then Hyde said something that shocked Jones so much that he hesitated, years later, to write it down. “I saw more,” Hyde said. “I saw that my Jesus became a dog.”

“My Jesus Became a Dog”

It is a startling phrase, and it needs careful reading. Hyde explained what he meant. He had been thinking about the Syrophoenician woman who begged Jesus to heal her daughter. Jesus answered her, “it is not meet to take the children’s bread and cast it to the dogs,” and she replied, “Yea, Lord; even the dogs under the table eat of the children’s crumbs” (Mark 7:27-28, ASV). Jesus used the contemptuous word of his day for Gentiles, and the woman accepted it. But Christ died for the Gentiles, for the “dogs.” It must be, Hyde reasoned, that to save them he took the dog’s place.

“At first,” he told Jones, “this was too awful to think of.” But when he thought of Christ’s life, he saw how much of it resembled the life of the pariah dogs that roamed every Indian town. Those dogs had no home. Christ said, “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the heaven have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20, ASV). Those dogs were constantly kicked and beaten. Christ was driven away, mocked, struck, and at last killed. “And that is what I have been doing,” Hyde said, “worshipping Him and praising Him for this.”

Hyde was not saying that Christ became less than human, or that he ceased to be God. He was reaching, in the language of the Indian streets, for a way to express how low Christ stooped. His Punjabi listeners knew exactly what it meant to be treated like a dog. Many of the village Christians he served had been treated that way all their lives by their higher-caste neighbours. Psalm 22, which Christ quoted on the cross, says, “For dogs have compassed me” (Psalm 22:16, ASV). Hyde saw the Saviour not only surrounded by dogs but numbered among the despised. It was his way of saying what Paul says in Philippians: Christ “humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, yea, the death of the cross.”

Jones never forgot that evening. “I remember nothing of dinner that night,” he wrote. “My impression is that we both sat on that bed for hours speaking of Christ … I shall never forget the vision I had of the love of Christ going lower and lower, suffering more and more and all for me.”

A Sermon on the Cross

At another convention Hyde gave an address to the European visitors, most of them missionaries, on the Cross. Jones called it “one of the most inspiring messages I ever heard.”

Hyde began by saying that from whatever side we look at Christ on the cross, we see wounds. From above we see the marks of the crown of thorns, and from behind, the furrows of the scourging. He went on to show that in the crucified Christ there is sufficiency for every need. Jones felt, as he listened, that he had enough “for time and for eternity.” But the climax came when Hyde spoke of Christ’s cry, “It is finished” (John 19:30, ASV).

To the disciples, Hyde said, it seemed that Jesus had failed. To his enemies it seemed they had finally overcome him. To all appearances the struggle was over and his life had ended in tragedy. And at that moment he cried out in triumph. “It is finished” was not a groan of defeat but a shout of victory, raised in the darkest hour.

Then Hyde applied it. United to Christ, he said, we too can shout in triumph when everything points to despair. Our work may seem to have failed and the enemy to have won. All our friends may blame us and our colleagues pity us. Even then we can take our stand with Christ on the cross and shout, “Victory, Victory, Victory!” “This,” Hyde said, “is real Victory: to shout triumphantly though all around is dense darkness.”

Jones said that from that day he never despaired about his work. Whenever he felt discouraged, he seemed to hear Hyde’s voice shouting “Victory,” and it took him straight to Calvary. Among the listeners was the Hon. M. Waldegrave, son of the English evangelical peer Lord Radstock. Waldegrave told Jones afterwards that he usually went to his tent after each meeting to write the message down for his wife, “but Mr. Hyde’s message just delivered seems so sacred and appealing that I dare not try to write it.”

When Jones talked with Hyde afterwards, Hyde told him that for a whole year he had been “fascinated by the Cross.” “I cannot speak on any other subject now,” he said. Paul had written the same thing: “For I determined not to know anything among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2, ASV).

Silence Instead of a Sermon

Paterson remembered an evening at Sialkot that shows Hyde’s devotion to the cross in a different way. The committee had decided not to announce the names of speakers, so that people would attend to the message rather than the messenger. But word had got out that Hyde was to speak, and the hall was full and expectant. A close friend of Hyde’s was in the chair that evening. The subject of Christ’s sufferings was heavy on his heart, and when he was asked what psalm should be sung, he suggested Psalm 22. To his surprise, the song leader announced that they would sing Psalm 22 “at Mr. Hyde’s request.” The two men had not spoken about it.

Hyde sat on the platform behind the pulpit, deep in prayer. When he did not move, the chairman read from Zechariah 13, where the prophet asks, “What are these wounds between thine arms?” and the answer comes, “Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends” (Zechariah 13:6, ASV). He spoke about the loneliness of Christ in his sufferings. Then, during another hymn, he laid his hand on Hyde’s shoulder and said, “If God has a message for you to give, will you give it now?” Hyde did not move. The convention’s chairman, the Rev. John Forman, leaned over to ask whether Hyde was going to speak, and was told that he had been asked. When the singing stopped, the chairman asked whether he might give two messages that God had laid on his own heart, and did so. The meeting went on to its close, and Hyde slipped away to the prayer room without saying a word.

Later Paterson asked him about it. Hyde said he had been full of a subject, “The Glory of Christ’s Kingdom.” But when the chairman laid a hand on his shoulder, the gesture seemed to press him down. The words “If God has a message” made him doubt whether God wanted him to speak just then. So he waited in prayer, and received no clear leading to speak. He kept silent. Paterson thought it took both a man closely in touch with his Father and a man who cared more for God’s approval than for other people’s to keep silent in front of a crowd that had come to hear him.

A Letter About Psalm 22

Psalm 22 seems to have been especially dear to Hyde, and we have a rare piece of his own writing about it. In a letter to his sister Mary he wrote a set of notes on the psalm, verse by verse. McGaw printed them in 1923. He added the text of the psalm and slightly rearranged the notes, but he insisted that “the notes are from the hand of dear John himself.”

The psalm begins with the cry Jesus uttered on the cross: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1, ASV). Hyde saw David “praying in some deep and terrible trial,” an agony “so real and awful as to reveal to David Christ’s prayer.” He described the opening cry as “the cry, the voice of the sufferings of hell, but by a person with the praise of heaven in his heart.” And he noticed how quickly the psalm turns from forsakenness to worship: “But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel” (Psalm 22:3, ASV).

On the verse “But I am a worm, and no man; A reproach of men, and despised of the people” (Psalm 22:6, ASV), Hyde wrote that the speaker is “taking the sinner’s place and enduring what came to him on the Cross of Calvary. The sinner’s place and reproach, yet himself without sin.” On the verses about trust from birth, he noticed that there is “no cry for mercy — just help which is his by right — the sinless Christ. Yet in his greatest sufferings, ‘There is none to help.’”

His longest note is on a line from verse 17: “I may count all my bones. They look and stare upon me” (Psalm 22:17, ASV). Hyde saw in the first half a picture of Christ worn thin: “How this tells of three years — yes, a lifetime, but especially of three years of sorrow over our, my, sin, of prayer and fasting and watching, sometimes whole nights; and then days and nights of work — teaching, healing, preaching, and of grief as he saw sin and its hold and havoc.” And on the second half: “How this tells of a human soul, sensitive and shrinking from the gaze of men. This tells of the indignities heaped upon him which only the most refined and holy can feel in all their power!”

Finally, on the psalm’s great turn, “Yea, from the horns of the wild-oxen thou hast answered me” (Psalm 22:21, ASV), Hyde wrote: “Here again is a cry for help unheard, yet in faith heard. Thou hast ‘answered me.’” The rest of the psalm, he noted, reveals “the glory that shall follow.”

McGaw, reading these notes, said something that anyone who has read this far will understand. “It has seemed to me that in no other writings have I seen such a likeness of the dear brother himself. I have said, ‘John Hyde has here unconsciously given us a portrait of John Hyde.’” The man who prayed whole nights, grew thin with grief over sin, shrank from people’s gaze, and cried for help “unheard, yet in faith heard”, and who would die with a shout of victory, was describing his Lord. In the process, without meaning to, he described what his Lord had made of him.

“Dead and Buried”

McGaw’s informant (almost certainly Paterson) preserved one of Hyde’s sayings that sums up what the cross meant for his daily life. “When we keep near to Jesus,” Hyde used to say, “it is he who draws souls to himself through us, but he must be lifted up in our lives; that is, we must be crucified with him.” It is “self,” he said, that comes between us and him. So self must be dealt with as Christ was dealt with: “crucified, dead and buried with Christ.” And he added a sentence that his friends never forgot: if self is not buried, “the stench of the old man will frighten souls away.” But if those three steps downward are taken, then the new man will be “revived, raised, and seated,” the corresponding steps upward.

This is the language of Paul: “I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I that live, but Christ liveth in me” (Galatians 2:20, ASV), and, “far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world hath been crucified unto me, and I unto the world” (Galatians 6:14, ASV). For Hyde, the cross was not only the place where his sins were forgiven. It was the pattern of the life he was called to live, lower and lower, and always, in the end, lifted up.

For Reflection

Hyde’s friends remembered many things about his prayers: their length, their intensity, their tears. But what they remembered most about his preaching was that he could not stop talking about the cross. “I cannot speak on any other subject now.”

That is the right order. The prayer came from the cross, not the other way round. A man who has seen Christ go “lower and lower … all for me” will pray, and weep, and give away his blankets, not in order to earn anything but because he has seen what he has been given. If our own prayer is thin, the remedy may not be more effort at praying. It may be more time at the foot of the cross, looking, until we too can say, “and He took this place — for me.”

All our friends may blame us and our colleagues pity us. Even then we can take our stand with Christ on the cross and shout, “Victory, Victory, Victory!” “This,” Hyde said, “is real Victory: to shout triumphantly though all around is dense darkness.” Jones said that from that day he never despaired about his work. Whenever he felt discouraged, he seemed to hear Hyde’s voice shouting “Victory,” and it took him straight to Calvary. Among the listeners was the Hon. M. Waldegrave, son of the English evangelical peer Lord Radstock. Waldegrave told Jones afterwards that he usually went to his tent after each meeting to write the message down for his wife, “but Mr. Hyde’s message just delivered seems so sacred and appealing that I dare not try to write it.” When Jones talked with Hyde afterwards, Hyde told him that for a whole year he had been “fascinated by the Cross.” “I cannot speak on any other subject now,” he said. Paul had written the same thing: “For I determined not to know anything among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2, ASV). Silence Instead of a Sermon Paterson remembered an evening at Sialkot that shows Hyde’s devotion to the cross in a different way. The committee had decided not to announce the names of speakers, so that people would attend to the message rather than the messenger. But word had got out that Hyde was to speak, and the hall was full and expectant. A close friend of Hyde’s was in the chair that evening. The subject of Christ’s sufferings was heavy on his heart, and when he was asked what psalm should be sung, he suggested Psalm 22. To his surprise, the song leader announced that they would sing Psalm 22 “at Mr. Hyde’s request.” The two men had not spoken about it. Hyde sat on the platform behind the pulpit, deep in prayer. John Forman, leaned over to ask whether Hyde was going to speak, and was told that he had been asked. When the singing stopped, the chairman asked whether he might give two messages that God had laid on his own heart, and did so. The meeting went on to its close, and Hyde slipped away to the prayer room without saying a word. Later Paterson asked him about it. Hyde said he had been full of a subject, “The Glory of Christ’s Kingdom.” But when the chairman laid a hand on his shoulder, the gesture seemed to press him down. The words “If God has a message” made him doubt whether God wanted him to speak just then. So he waited in prayer, and received no clear leading to speak. He kept silent. Paterson thought it took both a man closely in touch with his Father and a man who cared more for God’s approval than for other people’s to keep silent in front of a crowd that had come to hear him. In a letter to his sister Mary he wrote a set of notes on the psalm, verse by verse. McGaw printed them in 1923. He added the text of the psalm and slightly rearranged the notes, but he insisted that “the notes are from the hand of dear John himself.” The psalm begins with the cry Jesus uttered on the cross: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1, ASV). Hyde saw David “praying in some deep and terrible trial,” an agony “so real and awful as to reveal to David Christ’s prayer.” He described the opening cry as “the cry, the voice of the sufferings of hell, but by a person with the praise of heaven in his heart.” And he noticed how quickly the psalm turns from forsakenness to worship: “But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel” (Psalm 22:3, ASV). On the verse “But I am a worm, and no man; A reproach of men, and despised of the people” (Psalm 22:6, ASV), Hyde wrote that the speaker is “taking the sinner’s place and enduring what came to him on the Cross of Calvary. The sinner’s place and reproach, yet himself without sin.” On the verses about trust from birth, he noticed that there is “no cry for mercy — just help which is his by right — the sinless Christ. Yet in his greatest sufferings, ‘There is none to help.’” His longest note is on a line from verse 17: “I may count all my bones. They look and stare upon me” (Psalm 22:17, ASV). Hyde saw in the first half a picture of Christ worn thin: “How this tells of three years — yes, a lifetime, but especially of three years of sorrow over our, my, sin, of prayer and fasting and watching, sometimes whole nights; and then days and nights of work — teaching, healing, preaching, and of grief as he saw sin and its hold and havoc.” And on the second half: “How this tells of a human soul, sensitive and shrinking from the gaze of men. This tells of the indignities heaped upon him which only the most refined and holy can feel in all their power!” Finally, on the psalm’s great turn, “Yea, from the horns of the wild-oxen thou hast answered me” (Psalm 22:21, ASV), Hyde wrote: “Here again is a cry for help unheard, yet in faith heard. Thou hast ‘answered me.’” The rest of the psalm, he noted, reveals “the glory that shall follow.” McGaw, reading these notes, said something that anyone who has read this far will understand. “It has seemed to me that in no other writings have I seen such a likeness of the dear brother himself. In the process, without meaning to, he described what his Lord had made of him. “Dead and Buried” McGaw’s informant (almost certainly Paterson) preserved one of Hyde’s sayings that sums up what the cross meant for his daily life. “When we keep near to Jesus,” Hyde used to say, “it is he who draws souls to himself through us, but he must be lifted up in our lives; that is, we must be crucified with him.” It is “self,” he said, that comes between us and him. So self must be dealt with as Christ was dealt with: “crucified, dead and buried with Christ.” And he added a sentence that his friends never forgot: if self is not buried, “the stench of the old man will frighten souls away.” But if those three steps downward are taken, then the new man will be “revived, raised, and seated,” the corresponding steps upward. This is the language of Paul: “I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I that live, but Christ liveth in me” (Galatians 2:20, ASV), and, “far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world hath been crucified unto me, and I unto the world” (Galatians 6:14, ASV). For Hyde, the cross was not only the place where his sins were forgiven. It was the pattern of the life he was called to live, lower and lower, and always, in the end, lifted up. For Reflection Hyde’s friends remembered many things about his prayers: their length, their intensity, their tears. But what they remembered most about his preaching was that he could not stop talking about the cross. “I cannot speak on any other subject now.” That is the right order. The prayer came from the cross, not the other way round. A man who has seen Christ go “lower and lower … all for me” will pray, and weep, and give away his blankets, not in order to earn anything but because he has seen what he has been given. If our own prayer is thin, the remedy may not be more effort at praying. It may be more time at the foot of the cross, looking, until we too can say, “and He took this place — for me.”

fields.title: A Heart on the Wrong Side
fields.body_html:
“And he saith unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while. For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.”

— Mark 6:31, ASV

The Last Convention

The Sialkot Convention of 1910 was John Hyde’s last. McGaw’s sources remember it as the climax of his ministry there. The burden he had carried for five years, they said, pressed heavier each year. Before the convention he spent long nights in prayer, and “the long sleepless nights and weary days of watching with prayer” were “written on every feature of his face.” Yet when he stood up to speak, “his figure was almost transformed,” and he spoke “with such fire and such force that many hardly recognized the changed man.”

That year, the memoirs say, Hyde was called to help at revival meetings and conferences far beyond the Punjab, in Calcutta, Bombay, and other large cities. In the same year, the same sources add, he “was never more misjudged and misunderstood.” They do not say by whom. It may have been fellow missionaries who thought his piety extreme, or churches that found his preaching on sin uncomfortable. Hyde was now forty-four, and he had been in India for eighteen years. He did not know it, but he had little more than a year of health left.

A Fortnight in Calcutta

After the convention Hyde went to Calcutta to hold meetings. He stayed nearly a fortnight with a friend there, and McGaw printed the friend’s account. The friend was probably the Mr. F. Kehl of Calcutta whom McGaw thanks in his acknowledgements.

Hyde had fever the whole time. “Yet he took the meetings regularly, and how God spoke to us, though he was bodily unfit to do any work!” The host was himself unwell with a pain in his chest that kept him awake at night. From his dark room he could see the flash of Hyde’s electric light across the passage whenever Hyde got up and switched it on. He watched it come on at twelve, at two, at four, and at five. From five it stayed on until sunrise.

Hyde grew worse, and the annual meeting of his mission was calling him back to the Punjab. The friend grew anxious and persuaded Hyde to see a doctor. The next morning, the friend wrote, the doctor gave his verdict:

The heart is in an awful condition. I have never come across such a bad case as this. It has been shifted out of its natural position on the left side to a place over on the right side. Through stress and strain it is in such a bad condition that it will require months and months of strictly quiet life to bring it back again to anything like its normal state. What have you been doing with yourself?

“Dear Hyde said nothing,” the friend wrote. “He only smiled. But we who knew him knew the cause; his life of incessant prayer day and night, praying exceedingly with many tears for his converts, for his fellow-laborers, for his friends, and for the church in India!”

What Was Wrong with His Heart?

This is the origin of one of the most famous claims about Praying Hyde: that prayer physically moved his heart from one side of his chest to the other. The story has been retold countless times, and it usually loses its source along the way. It deserves careful handling, because it is precisely the kind of story that devotion embroiders.

First, what we actually have is a friend’s report, written down years later, of what a Calcutta doctor said after one examination. We do not have the doctor’s name or his notes. We do not know what instruments he used or what he meant by “shifted.” The friend then added his own interpretation of the cause. The doctor, according to the friend’s own account, did not know the cause. He asked Hyde, “What have you been doing with yourself?”

Second, a heart found on the right side of the chest has well-known medical explanations. Some people are born with the heart on the right side, a condition called dextrocardia. It often causes no trouble and may go unnoticed for years until a doctor listens in the right place. In other cases a heart in the normal position is pushed or pulled to the right by disease in the chest, such as fluid around the lungs, a collapsed or scarred lung, or a growth. Doctors call that dextroposition. Either might explain what the Calcutta doctor found. A man who had lived for eighteen years in the Punjab, often in poor village conditions, and who was feverish at the time of the examination, could easily have had some such illness.

Third, Hyde’s final illness gives us another clue. Within a year and a half he would die of a malignant tumour. For years before that he had suffered from severe headaches. The memoirs mention them several times, and the headache that sent him to Clifton Springs was, McGaw says, one he had “suffered much before leaving India.” We cannot diagnose a man a century after his death. But it is at least possible that the illness that killed him had been at work in his body for some time. Serious illness can affect the heart and lungs in ways that a doctor of 1910 might describe as a heart “shifted” and “in an awful condition.”

None of this means that Hyde’s way of life did him no harm. It almost certainly did. A man who slept very little for years, often missed meals, and kept long vigils while carrying fever would wear his body down. But the notion that prayer itself moved a healthy heart across the chest is a devotional interpretation laid on top of a medical report we do not fully have. The honest course is to tell the story as Hyde’s friends told it, and to leave the miracle unclaimed.

“The Man Who Never Sleeps” Pays the Price

There is a harder question behind the medical one, and Hyde’s friends did not avoid it. Was it right for him to live as he did?

The Calcutta friend put the question sharply: “We have heard of martyrs who were kept in prison, and in the end were put to death. But have we ever heard of one who was so given up to the ministry of prayer that the strain of a daily burden brought him to a premature grave?” Another missionary in India answered: “No, friend, not a premature grave; it was the grave of Jesus Christ. John Hyde laid down his life calmly and deliberately for the Church of God in India.”

That is a moving answer, and there is truth in it. Paul described his own ministry as one of “labor and travail, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness” (2 Corinthians 11:27, ASV). He did not treat his body’s decline as failure: “though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16, ASV). Christians are called to “present your bodies a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1, ASV). Some are called to spend themselves in ways that shorten their lives, and the church rightly honours them.

But other voices in the story should also be heard. Griswold, who admired Hyde, noted that he “was sometimes criticised by his brethren for the rigorous and ascetic nature of his piety, for the way in which he seemed to deny to the flesh even its just claims.” The phrase “its just claims” matters. The body has claims that are just. It needs food and sleep, and it has limits. The teenage servant who cried because his master would not eat or sleep at the conventions was not lacking in spirituality. He was seeing clearly. And the confident claim a friend made in 1907, that since Hyde had learned to draw on God’s strength he scarcely felt tired, and that “no man need ever break down through overstrain in this ministry of intercession”, did not survive the events of 1910 and 1911.

The Lord Who Said “Rest a While”

The verse at the head of this chapter is easy to overlook in a book about a man of prayer. The apostles had returned from a mission. They were so busy that “they had no leisure so much as to eat.” And Jesus did not tell them to pray harder or work longer. He told them to “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while” (Mark 6:31, ASV).

The Bible has a great deal to say about the body’s limits, and it says it without embarrassment. When Elijah collapsed in exhaustion and despair under a juniper tree, God did not rebuke him or send him to pray. An angel woke him and said, “Arise and eat.” He ate, and slept again. Then the angel came a second time: “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for thee” (1 Kings 19:5-7, ASV). The psalmist says that rising early, staying up late, and eating the bread of anxious toil is vain, “For so he giveth unto his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2, ASV). Jesus himself, in the middle of a storm, was “asleep on the cushion” (Mark 4:38, ASV). And Paul, who fasted often, also warned against practices that have “a show of wisdom … and severity to the body” but are “not of any value against the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23, ASV).

None of this condemns Hyde. His long nights were not a technique for earning God’s favour or displaying piety. By every account they were a response to burdens he believed God had laid on him. His friends say he regularly asked God whether he should eat or sleep, and obeyed when he was told to. The story of the lunch bell shows that. And a man should be judged by the light he had. Many devout Christians of Hyde’s era, formed by the holiness teaching of the time, saw the neglect of the body as a sign of devotion. Hyde’s Indian neighbours, many of whom revered their own ascetic holy men, may have been especially moved by it. Griswold noted that his “simple, mystical and ascetic type of piety powerfully impressed the Indian people.”

But it does mean that Hyde’s way of praying should not be copied as a pattern. His closest friends were clear about this. Jones remembered how Hyde himself dreaded that anyone should try to imitate him, and he urged readers to follow Hyde’s spirit of prayer, “but not necessarily in the ‘form’ that he manifested it.” Many Christians, Jones said, “cannot spend weeks in prayer and fasting as he did, they are physically unfit for it.” But everyone can make prayer “their very breath.” Hyde’s form of prayer was his calling, and it cost him his life. The spirit of that prayer is for everyone, and it need not cost anyone their health.

Leaving India

Hyde did not follow the Calcutta doctor’s advice to live quietly for months. The mission’s annual meeting was calling him back to the Punjab, and he seems to have gone. He had founded the Ferozepore training school for village preachers and teachers, and it was about to move to Moga. Moga itself was the district where the baptisms had been increasing for five years. There was much to hold him.

But his health was failing. In March 1911 he left India for the last time. McGaw wrote that he started home “as the physicians would say, a ‘dying man.’” He had arrived in India in the autumn of 1892, “less than twenty years before.” McGaw added: “But surely they were nineteen beautiful years!”

For Reflection

It is right to honour John Hyde’s sacrifice, and right to be moved by a man who loved the church in India so much that he would not spare himself. It is also right to say that God does not usually ask his servants to destroy their health in prayer, and that rest, food, and sleep are gifts from him, not concessions to weakness.

Hyde’s life does not settle that tension, and we should not pretend it does. But it gives us a question worth asking. Are we more at risk of sparing ourselves too much in God’s service, or too little? Most of us, if we are honest, know the answer to that. Those who are the exception, who are already spending themselves beyond their strength, should hear the Lord who said, “Come ye yourselves apart … and rest a while.”

fields.title: Wales, Shrewsbury, and a Hymn That Sang Him Down
fields.body_html:
“Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.”

— Galatians 6:2, ASV

A Guest on Good Friday

Pengwern Jones had gone home to Wales on furlough in December 1910. Before he left India he had seen Hyde, who told him he expected to take his own furlough early in 1911. Jones gave Hyde his address and begged him to visit on his way through Britain. Hyde answered, as he usually did, that he would come if the Lord opened the way. Then he lost the address.

Jones later pieced together how Hyde found him anyway, and he told the story as a small chain of providences. The day before Hyde’s steamer reached Liverpool, Hyde asked a missionary of the Church Missionary Society on board whether he had any idea what part of Wales Jones came from. Jones barely knew the man and had never met his wife. But the man said his wife had Jones’s address, went down to her cabin, and brought it up. Jones never discovered how she came to have it.

The ship docked on Good Friday, 14 April 1911. Hyde crossed the Mersey to Birkenhead to catch a train for Llangollen, in north Wales, where Jones’s family lived. At the station he was told that only one train ran on Good Friday, and it had gone. A bystander overheard and told him that a cheap excursion train was going direct to Llangollen. But excursion passengers could not take luggage, and Hyde had all his belongings in a large American trunk. He stood there, Jones was sure, and prayed. Then the guard came up and said, “Go and secure your seat and leave your trunk with me, I shall bring it in my van.”

Meanwhile, in Llangollen, Jones had been surprised to find himself free. A deputation tour he had been booked for had been cancelled at the last minute because the district was busy preparing for the investiture of the Prince of Wales at Caernarfon. He wondered what the free fortnight was for. On Good Friday morning he walked round the little town as he had as a boy. When he got home his wife met him at the door, greatly excited. “Guess who has come,” she said. “Go to the bedroom and see who is there having a wash.” Jones rushed upstairs, and there was Hyde, “with his face beaming with joy.”

A Little Heaven in Llangollen

Jones called the following weeks “a little Heaven on earth.” A doctor and his wife who lived nearby begged to have Hyde to stay, and Jones, knowing Hyde needed medical care, gladly agreed. But Hyde came to Jones’s house for most of his meals. He and Mrs. Jones understood each other “from the very first hour.” Grace before meals often turned into a long prayer, and the food went cold.

They walked together on the hills around the town. They sat on the rustic benches set out for visitors, or lay in the shade of the trees, and prayed. On these walks, Jones says, Hyde gave him “some of his early history” and spoke often of his mother. It may have been on these walks, too, that he told Jones the stories of the letter on the ship and the open-air meeting recorded in the early chapters of this book.

One visit that spring became a small classic. Jones took Hyde to see an elderly Christian woman who was very deaf. She told them loudly that she missed the church services terribly, “for I cannot hear anything when I go.” To her astonishment, Hyde answered, “You ought to praise God for that.” She thought he had misheard, and repeated, “I cannot hear, I tell you.” “That is why I tell you that you should praise the Lord,” he said. Then he explained. He himself could rarely hear anything at services. But it was a wonderful opportunity to pray. He would look at the preacher and pray for him. Then he would look at the people one by one and pray for each of them as he looked, until he found himself praising God for his deafness because it gave him such an opportunity for prayer and worship. The old woman laughed heartily and said she would try it. Two or three years later she wrote to Jones that Hyde’s advice had made a wonderful difference to her life.

The deafness that had troubled him as a young missionary, and that he had carried for twenty years, had become a gift he could pass on to someone else.

Shrewsbury

Jones heard that the American evangelist J. Wilbur Chapman and his song leader Charles M. Alexander were about to hold a mission at Shrewsbury, just over the border in England. Chapman and Alexander were near the end of a long evangelistic tour around the world. Hyde had never met Chapman, but they were both Presbyterians, and he wanted to. So he and Jones took small rooms in a quiet hotel in Shrewsbury for three days. They were joined for the first afternoon by a couple who had been deeply blessed in the revival of 1904 and 1905.

The mission opened in the Music Hall on Thursday, 20 April 1911. Jones was disappointed to find the streets almost empty as they walked to the first service. Near the hall they met Chapman and his party, and Hyde introduced himself. Very few people came. The evening meeting was larger, but there was no enthusiasm. Chapman and his team were clearly discouraged. That night an elder of one of the local churches, an old friend of Jones’s, joined them for supper. He was surprised that they had come all the way to attend a mission. He had heard of it but had not bothered to go.

The next day Chapman called the ministers and church leaders of the town together to discuss how to rouse the people. Hyde and Jones were invited. Chapman spoke with intensity. But some of the ministers treated the whole mission “as some little side-show,” and their remarks showed “a state of appalling indifference.” At last Chapman, with a sad face, said that if that was the spirit in which the town’s leaders faced the mission, he had nothing more to say, and he left the room. That sobered the most flippant, and the few earnest people carried the meeting.

Jones watched Hyde. “I noticed Hyde’s head getting lower and lower, and his face wore that burdened look he always had when the burden of prayer was coming on him.” Hyde said little to anyone that night. Both men had preaching engagements elsewhere on the Sunday, and they left the next afternoon. But Hyde asked Jones to book his hotel room for the following week, because he meant to come back early on Monday morning. “I cannot leave a brother minister to bear this burden alone,” he said.

The verse at the head of this chapter was the whole of Hyde’s reasoning. “Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2, ASV). Chapman was a stranger, and a famous one. Hyde owed him nothing and was himself seriously ill. But a brother was carrying a heavy load, and the law of Christ said to help carry it.

“Here Is a Minister Who Sorely Needs Thy Help”

Jones was worried about Hyde’s health. Without telling him, he wrote to Chapman asking whether someone could be found to help Hyde in his intercession. Chapman arranged for a Mr. Davis of the Pocket Testament League (probably George T. B. Davis), a man of like spirit, to be with him, and the two became friends. Hyde went back on Monday, 24 April, and stayed the rest of the week.

What happened next has been told in two quite different ways, and it is worth setting them side by side.

The famous version is a letter printed in both memoirs of 1923, without a date or an addressee. In Carré’s copy Chapman says he had received “a letter from a missionary”, which fits the note Jones had quietly sent him. In it Chapman describes a mission in England where the audience was extremely small, until he received a note saying that an American missionary known as “the Praying Hyde” was coming to pray. “Almost instantly the tide turned. The hall was packed, and my first invitation meant fifty men for Jesus Christ.” Then Chapman asked Hyde to pray for him. Hyde, in this version, came to Chapman’s room, “turned the key in the door, dropped on his knees, waited five minutes without a single syllable coming from his lips.” Chapman could hear both their hearts beating, and felt hot tears running down his face. Then Hyde said, “Oh God!”, was silent for at least five more minutes, and then prayed for men as Chapman had never heard anyone pray. “I rose from my knees,” Chapman says, “to know what real prayer was.”

But Chapman himself published an account of the same prayer in 1917, in a book of his own called When Home Is Heaven, and it reads differently. He names the town: “We were in Shrewsbury, England, and our work was not going well, when a message came to me that an American missionary had heard of our difficulties and was coming over to pray for us.” He was told not to provide for the missionary’s entertainment or give him any consideration at all. He was told that the missionary might not even attend the meetings, “but he would pray.” The missionary came, and “instantly the tide turned in our work, and the victory was remarkable.” Then, as Chapman was leaving Shrewsbury, he sent for Hyde and asked him to pray for him:

He knelt beside me, he was still for several moments, I was tempted to open my eyes, and I saw his face lighted up with the light of heaven, his lips trembling, and his tears starting, and then he said something like this: “My Father, here is a minister who sorely needs Thy help, do bless him, I beseech Thee, may his life be precious in Thy sight. May he be girded anew with strength for service; may Jesus Christ become more real to him,” and then he was still again for a little while, and when the closing words of the prayer were said we arose from our knees and I had learned a never-to-be-forgotten lesson concerning intercession.

Chapman’s authorised biographer, writing in 1920 with Chapman’s papers in front of him, printed the 1917 version and recorded that on the very day the missionary arrived “at least fifty people” responded to the invitation.

The two versions agree on the essentials. The mission was struggling. Word came that Hyde was coming to pray. The tide turned, and fifty people responded. And when Hyde prayed for Chapman personally, Chapman learned something about intercession that he never forgot. They differ in the drama. The locked door, the five-minute silences, and the single cry of “Oh God!” are found only in the undated letter. The printed account, which Chapman himself put his name to, has a stillness of “several moments” and a simple, tender prayer. Perhaps Chapman told the story differently on different occasions, as preachers do. Perhaps the letter was embellished by someone who copied it. We cannot know. But the version Chapman published is quieter, and it may be the more moving of the two. What struck him was not a spectacular silence but a man who knelt beside him, with trembling lips, and asked God to make Jesus Christ more real to a tired evangelist.

“My Dear Saviour’s Burden”

Jones heard afterwards that the mission had been a great success, that the churches were revived and many were converted. The elder who had not bothered to go to the first meetings attended later, was “gloriously blessed,” and a few weeks afterwards stirred his whole presbytery with an account of what he had seen.

But the week had cost Hyde dearly. He returned to Jones’s home, as Jones put it, “crawled back to us.” The next day he was so weak he could hardly speak. As Jones bent over him, Hyde smiled and whispered: “The burden was very heavy, but my dear Saviour’s burden for me took Him down to the grave.”

Jones was struck most by what Hyde did not say. “Not one word of criticism did I hear.” Hyde did not blame the indifferent ministers or mention his own part. He spoke only of “the glory of Christ manifested,” of Chapman’s and Alexander’s powerful messages, and of the gift of intercession his companion Davis had received. “Instead of criticizing and blaming the men,” Jones wrote, “he took their burden and carried it to the Lord.”

A Hymn That Sang Him Down

Two more episodes from that spring show the same spirit, and Jones found them harder to bear than Hyde did.

Hyde and Jones were invited to a two-day prayer meeting at the home of the Rev. Evan Hopkins, one of the founders of the Keswick Convention, held about a month before Keswick each year for its speakers and friends. About forty people were there. Toward the middle of the second day a discussion began about whether Keswick should have a prayer room like Sialkot’s, and the two Indian missionaries were asked to describe their experience. Jones spoke briefly, wanting to leave Hyde as much time as possible. Hyde began to speak, slowly and quietly, and Jones could tell that he was carrying a heavy message. After three or four minutes one of the women present began to sing a popular hymn. Others joined in. The message was never delivered.

Hyde closed his eyes and prayed. Jones was afraid he would be hurt, “but there was not a word of resentment or even displeasure.” The burden of the undelivered message was so great that Hyde was prostrated with a violent headache and could not leave with the others that evening. He stayed on as Hopkins’s guest, and told Jones afterwards what blessed fellowship they had had. He never mentioned being sung down.

On another occasion that spring Hyde went to a meeting of a presbytery in north Wales. He had spoken with great power in many of its churches, and people there had urged him to come. He made a long journey early in the morning, suffering from headache and from the illness that would kill him within a year. The presbytery was unusually large because word had got round that he would be there. Messages were sent up to the moderator more than once. But the meeting closed without anyone welcoming him. It was conducted in Welsh, which he did not understand. He was too deaf to have heard it anyway, so he sat through it with his eyes closed, praying for everyone there. Afterwards many people crowded round to say how sorry they were that he had not been asked to speak. He smiled on them all. When Jones, alone with him, expressed his indignation, Hyde gently rebuked him. The Lord knew everything, he said, and “it was not our place to criticize the Lord’s people.”

Jones remembered him saying something similar when urged to defend himself against a bitter and unjust attack: “They do not understand. I know they do not want to be unkind.” When a friend offered to write and explain the situation for him, Hyde answered, “This is my cross which He wants me to take up and carry for Him.” Peter wrote of Christ, “who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1 Peter 2:23, ASV). Hyde had been learning that for twenty years. In the spring of 1911, in the land of his friend’s birth, it was very visible.

For Reflection

Hyde’s last season in Britain gathered up all the lessons of his life. The deafness he had carried was turned to praise. A struggling evangelist he did not know was carried in prayer, at great cost. And an interrupted message, a slight from a presbytery, and an unjust attack were all met without resentment.

Burden-bearing is not only for people who can pray all week in a hotel room. It is the ordinary law of Christ, and it is open to anyone who notices that someone else is struggling and says, as Hyde did, “I cannot leave a brother to bear this burden alone.” And the meekness that refuses to criticise the Lord’s people, even when they have been thoughtless or unkind, is within reach of anyone who has looked long enough at the cross.

fields.title: “Victory, Victory, Victory”
fields.body_html:
“but thanks be to God, who giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

— 1 Corinthians 15:57, ASV

A Summer of Doctors

Hyde had hoped to stay in Britain through the summer of 1911 and attend the Keswick Convention in July. He had a plan for it. He and McCheyne Paterson, who was also in Britain, would join Pengwern Jones to form a trio and hold a prayer room at Keswick, praying day and night through the convention, as they had at Sialkot. It never happened. When Keswick week came, both Hyde and Paterson were ill. Jones went alone. He suggested a prayer room to the organisers, but nothing came of it. Years later he still wondered what might have happened if his two friends had been well enough to come.

Charles Alexander, Chapman’s song leader, had not forgotten the missionary who had prayed for Shrewsbury. He took Hyde to his own doctor in England, and a consultation with two other physicians followed. The doctors tried to make Hyde understand how serious his condition was. Alexander, listening, was sure Hyde understood that he was dying. Both Alexander and the doctor were amazed at his composure. He had long ago ceased to fear death, McGaw writes. For him, as for Paul, “to depart and be with Christ … is very far better” (Philippians 1:23, ASV).

Clifton Springs

Hyde sailed for America in the summer. The missionary magazine of his church recorded his arrival among the month’s missionary movements: “Rev. J. N. Hyde, from Lodiana, India,” landing at New York on 8 August 1911, with a forwarding address at Clifton Springs, New York. Clifton Springs, in western New York, was the site of a large sanitarium much used by returning missionaries, many of whom arrived home exhausted and ill. Hyde went there at once, McGaw says, hoping to find relief from “a severe headache from which he had suffered much before leaving India.”

The doctors found a tumour. It was operated on and proved malignant. McGaw calls it a sarcoma. Later accounts say it was in the brain. The records do not allow us to be more precise than that. Hyde rallied after the operation, and for some weeks he was able to sit up.

From Clifton Springs he sent a postcard to one of his sisters, dated 27 October 1911. McGaw quoted it. It is one of the very few pieces of Hyde’s own writing to survive from his last months, and it is characteristic:

Am still in bed or wheel chair getting a fine rest and doing a lot of the ministry of intercession, and having not a few opportunities of personal work. How the radiance of holiness shone out in Jesus’ every word and deed!

Even in a wheelchair in a sanitarium, he was praying for others and talking to the people around him about Christ. And his thoughts were not on his own suffering but on the holiness of Jesus.

Northampton

On 19 December 1911 Hyde left Clifton Springs to stay with his sister in Northampton, Massachusetts. She was married to a professor there, E. H. Mensel. Soon after the New Year he began to have pains in his back and side. He thought it was rheumatism. His doctor knew that the tumour had returned.

The weeks that followed were, as the missionary magazine of his church put it, “days of unutterable suffering.” But the same magazine recorded what his friends remembered most: “the remembrance of his heroic, uncomplaining endurance, his splendid Christian fortitude.” In the midst of his agony, it reported, he said: “Thank God for pain, thank God for everything!”

H. D. Griswold, writing the obituary for the Presbyterian mission magazine, added more. “After his worst paroxysms of pain he would say: ‘Praise the Lord,’ or ‘In every thing give thanks.’” And, Griswold wrote, “to his sister he said shortly before his death: ‘It’s just victory, victory, victory.’”

John Nelson Hyde died at his sister’s home in Northampton on 17 February 1912. He was forty-six years old. Griswold’s obituary says forty-seven, and so does McGaw, but he was born in November 1865 and had turned forty-six only three months before.

This correction is worth making plainly, because popular accounts of Hyde’s life have repeated a mistake about his death for a century. Many say he died at Clifton Springs. That is not true. The mission magazine of his church, the obituary in its foreign missions journal, and the catalogue of his seminary all agree: he died on 17 February 1912, at Northampton, Massachusetts, in his sister’s home. Clifton Springs was where he had gone for treatment, not where he died.

“Shout the Victory of Jesus Christ!”

Griswold wrote that Hyde’s “last words were uttered in the Punjabi tongue, thereby indicating that his heart was in the Punjab.” He added, in a phrase that echoes Paul, that Hyde “was led in triumph even unto the end.” Paul wrote, “thanks be unto God, who always leadeth us in triumph in Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:14, ASV).

What were those last Punjabi words? The answer comes from W. B. Anderson, the United Presbyterian missionary who had helped to found the Sialkot Convention. He wrote a tribute to Hyde in his church’s magazine, and McGaw closed his book with it. The words mean, roughly, “Shout the victory of Jesus Christ!” or “Say, Victory to Jesus the Messiah!” Anderson explained why they mattered. After hours of agonising prayer for people in bondage to sin, Hyde would often rise with those around him and shout that cry. Anderson’s tribute preserved one more memory, and it helps explain that shout. About four years before Hyde’s death, Anderson said, Hyde had spoken to a few close friends about something that happened to him on a day of prayer for India:

And Hyde had drawn a practical conclusion: “We must exercise the greatest care to be utterly obedient to Him who sees all the battle field all the time. It is only He who can put each man in the place where his life can count for the most.”

That was how Hyde saw his own life, and his death. He was one soldier in a great campaign whose outcome was certain, placed by a Commander who could see the whole field. His own place had been a few hundred villages in the Punjab, a prayer room at Sialkot, a hotel room in Shrewsbury, and now a sickbed in Massachusetts. Hyde’s brother Will and his sister Mary brought his body home to Carthage, Illinois. Young, Hyde’s seminary classmate, now pastor of the church in Carthage, and he preached. Francis McGaw assisted.

McGaw stood on the platform and looked down into the coffin. The face was “greatly emaciated,” he wrote, “but it was the same sweet, peaceful, gentle yet strong, resolute face that I had known in 1901 — the last time I saw him alive.” The day was “cloudy and chill and gloomy.” In Moss Ridge Cemetery they laid him beside his father, his mother, and his brother Edmund.

McGaw ended his account of the burial with the Christian hope. The clouds and shadows would flee away, “the chill and gloom of the grave be dispelled, and that man of prayer and praise come forth in the likeness of the Risen Son of God!” At the front of his little book he printed Paul’s words from the end of his own life: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith: henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give to me at that day; and not to me only, but also to all them that have loved his appearing” (2 Timothy 4:7-8, ASV).

For Reflection

Hyde’s death was not easy. The records do not soften that, and neither should we. It was weeks of “unutterable suffering,” far from the Punjab he loved, from an illness no one could cure. Yet everyone who was near him remembered the same things: thanksgiving in the middle of pain, a shout of victory in Punjabi, and the words “It’s just victory, victory, victory.”

That is the fruit of a whole life. A man does not learn to say “Thank God for pain” on his deathbed. He learns it through twenty years of headaches in village huts, thanks offered through shut teeth, and seeing the cross as a victory. John Hyde had been practising that shout of triumph for a long time. At the end it came naturally. “But thanks be to God, who giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57, ASV).

fields.title: The Legacy of Praying Hyde
fields.body_html:
“By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, through which he had witness borne to him that he was righteous, God bearing witness in respect of his gifts: and through it he being dead yet speaketh.”

— Hebrews 11:4, ASV

A Stone in a Pond

Near the end of his book, Francis McGaw recalled a scene from his boyhood. There was a pond near his father’s house. He would stand on the bank and throw a stone into the middle, then watch the ripples spread in widening circles, until every part of the surface was moving and the little waves lapped at the bank by his feet. “Sialkot started circles and waves of blessing,” he wrote, “that are even now beating in the secret recesses and inlets of many human hearts.”

It is a good image, and a modest one. A stone thrown into a pond disappears at once. Its effect is seen only in the ripples, and the farther they travel, the harder it is to say which ripple came from which stone. That is how it is with the influence of a life like John Hyde’s. He wrote no books, founded no great institution, held no office of importance, and died at forty-six. What he left was a disturbance in the water that is still spreading.

This last chapter asks what that legacy is. It asks what is truly his, and what is ours to take up.

What He Left in the Punjab

Hyde’s first legacy belongs to the church he served, and it is the one the devotional books say least about.

In the villages of the Moga district there were hundreds of Christian families who had been baptized in the years when Hyde was “burying the good seed,” as the missionary magazine put it. The Ferozepore training school, later moved to Moga, which Griswold says Hyde founded, went on training village preachers and teachers. The humble village evangelists with whom he had lived “as a brother” carried on his work, and something of his zeal went with them. Griswold closed his obituary with a sentence that was, in its way, a prophecy: “His memory will constitute a precious heritage for the Punjab Church.”

The Sialkot Convention continues to this day. It is now a gathering of the churches of Pakistan, long since led by Pakistani Christians. The descendants of the villagers who came to Christ in the mass movements of Hyde’s time make up much of the Christian community of Pakistan and the Indian Punjab. They are often poor, and they have often been persecuted. Their faith has been tested in ways that Hyde’s generation could not have imagined. W. B. Anderson wrote that the Punjabi cry of victory Hyde loved, “Bol, Yisu Masih, ki jai!”, had become “the great war cry of the Punjab Church.” Hyde would have wanted to be remembered, if at all, as one voice in that shout.

What He Left in His Friends

Hyde’s second legacy is in the people who knew him, and here the memoirs are eloquent.

Pengwern Jones wrote, ten years after Hyde’s death: “I owe to him more than I owe to any man, for showing me what a ‘prayer-life’ is, and what a real consecrated life is.” Jones said that after every visit with Hyde he vowed to pray more than ever before, “and Christ always seemed more real to me.” He believed that Hyde, in his last years, “created a new era of prayer in the Punjab,” and that he had been “given to India to teach men how to pray.”

Paterson went on praying and preaching at Sialkot, and others carried on the prayer rooms Hyde had helped to begin. The Calcutta friend who watched Hyde’s light go on through the night began asking God to wake him for prayer too, and found that he woke at two, then at four, “with striking regularity.” J. Wilbur Chapman, who knew Hyde for only a week, wrote years afterwards that he had learned from him “a never-to-be-forgotten lesson concerning intercession.” An old deaf woman in Llangollen learned to praise God for her deafness. A drunken Brahman boy could not forget his tears.

McGaw collected other testimonies. A pastor in Illinois wrote that Hyde’s example had moved at least one member of his congregation to go to China as a missionary. A woman missionary in India read an account of Hyde’s prayer life and was so convicted by it that she resolved to give the best hours of every day to prayer and Bible study. She found it very hard. She had always been busy, and “to hear others going around hard at work while I stayed quietly in my room, as it were inactive” was a constant struggle. But in her district, where years of work had produced little, fifteen people were baptized in the first months, then more than a hundred. Two years later she reported that the Christians there numbered six hundred, where before there had been a hundred. “The stress and the strain have gone out of my life,” she wrote. “I could not go back to the old life, and God grant that it may always be impossible.”

That is the kind of legacy Hyde would have wanted. It is not admiration for him, but people praying.

What He Left in Print

Hyde’s third legacy is the one that has travelled farthest, and it is a strange one for a man who wrote almost nothing. It is the story of his life.

The two small books of 1923 were printed and reprinted. Later biographers built on them, and later preachers built on the biographers. A century on, the name “Praying Hyde” is known to many who could not say what country he worked in or what church sent him. That fame has done real good. Countless Christians have been stirred to pray by it. It has also, as this book has tried to show, carried a good deal of legend along with it.

Some readers may feel that the careful sorting in these chapters, between the documented, the remembered, and the legendary, takes something away from Hyde. It does not. The man who comes through the testing is more believable than the legend, and more helpful. The legendary Hyde, with his heart moved by prayer and his four converts every day, is a figure few of us can relate to. The real Hyde was a shy, deaf, slow-speaking, ambitious young man. He threw away a letter in anger, struggled with a besetting sin, and spent ten years in unfruitful work. His colleagues thought him odd, and God had to correct him in the middle of a prayer. He is a man we can recognise. And what God did through him is therefore something God might do through us.

What Is Not Ours to Take

Before we ask what to take from Hyde’s life, it is worth saying clearly what we should leave.

We should not copy his neglect of his body. His closest friends said so, and he said so himself. His form of prayer, the sleepless nights, the missed meals, the weeks of fasting, was his particular calling, and it cost him his life. Most of us are not called to it, and we would be wrong to make it a standard.

We should not turn his story into a formula. The soul-a-day covenant, the long repetitions of a single word in prayer, the dancing in the prayer room: these belonged to a particular man, time, and place. They are not techniques that produce revival if they are used correctly.

And we should not make him a hero to be admired from a distance. He hated that. When he thought people were looking at him rather than at Christ, Jones said, “he would run away and remain away in some hiding place praying for them.”

What Is Ours

What remains, when all that is set aside, is still a great deal. Each of the chapters of this book has drawn out one lesson. Together they make a short summary of what John Hyde has to teach.

Faithfulness in small and hidden things matters, because God answers a father’s prayers for labourers. Honesty before God matters more than reputation, and a settled call comes from time on one’s knees, not from more arguments. A wounding letter from a friend may be the voice of God. A besetting sin is not something to live with. Slow years are not wasted years. The despised are those God chooses. The messenger needs preparing as much as the message. A small daily discipline of prayer, kept “till the awakening comes,” can prepare the way for revival. The Holy Spirit must be first. A prayer room behind a meeting is as important as a pulpit in front of it. Travail in prayer is Christ’s burden shared, not a burden we manufacture. The one who is missing matters as much as the ninety-nine. Accusing a brother, even in prayer, is the work of the accuser, and thanksgiving is its cure. Praise is a garment we can put on before we feel it. Love may cost us our blankets. The cross is victory even in the darkness. Rest is a gift, not a failure. Other people’s burdens are ours to bear. And death, for a Christian, is not defeat but a shout of triumph.

None of these lessons is new. Every one is in Scripture. What Hyde’s life adds is a picture of them being lived, imperfectly, by a real man.

He Being Dead Yet Speaketh

The verse at the head of this chapter speaks of Abel, the first person in the Bible to die. The writer to the Hebrews says of him that “through it he being dead yet speaketh” (Hebrews 11:4, ASV). Abel left no words at all. What speaks is his faith, and the sacrifice it offered.

Carré applied the phrase to Hyde in the foreword of his book in 1923. Jones used it again: “‘He being dead yet speaketh’ is true of him. It is now ten years since he was called Home, but he is not forgotten, he is speaking to us to-day, and throwing light on the Prayer-Life of Christ.”

That last phrase is the key. Hyde’s friends did not think that his life pointed to himself. They thought it threw light on Christ, and in particular on the prayer life of Christ, who “ever liveth to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25, ASV). The deepest thing Hyde’s life teaches is not about Hyde at all. It is that the risen Lord is still praying. He still longs for the lost, still carries his people’s burdens, and still invites his friends to watch with him. In the Punjab, one of those friends said yes.

The writer to the Hebrews, having listed the faithful who had died, turns to his readers: “Therefore let us also, seeing we are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus the author and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:1-2, ASV). John Hyde is one of that cloud now. He is not watching us to be admired, but cheering us on toward the One he looked at all his life.

For Reflection

The man the Punjab called “the man who never sleeps” has been at rest for more than a century. “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from henceforth: yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labors; for their works follow with them” (Revelation 14:13, ASV).

The question his life puts to us is the one Jesus asked his sleeping friends in Gethsemane, the question at the head of this book’s preface: “What, could ye not watch with me one hour?” It is not asked in anger. It is asked by a Lord who knows our weakness, who is still praying for us, and who still, in his kindness, wants our company. Hyde answered it with his life. We are invited to answer it in ours, not in his form, but in his spirit. Perhaps that means half an hour at noon. Perhaps it means a thanksgiving instead of an accusation, or a person no one has thought to ask about. But in some way it means watching with Christ, and praying “till the awakening comes.”
