Most of us are not called to it, and we would be wrong to make it a standard. We should not turn his story into a formula. The soul-a-day covenant, the long repetitions of a single word in prayer, the dancing in the prayer room: these belonged to a particular man, time, and place. They are not techniques that produce revival if they are used correctly. And we should not make him a hero to be admired from a distance. He hated that. When he thought people were looking at him rather than at Christ, Jones said, “he would run away and remain away in some hiding place praying for them.” What Is Ours What remains, when all that is set aside, is still a great deal. Each of the chapters of this book has drawn out one lesson. Together they make a short summary of what John Hyde has to teach. Faithfulness in small and hidden things matters, because God answers a father’s prayers for labourers. Honesty before God matters more than reputation, and a settled call comes from time on one’s knees, not from more arguments. A wounding letter from a friend may be the voice of God. A besetting sin is not something to live with. Slow years are not wasted years. The despised are those God chooses. The messenger needs preparing as much as the message. A small daily discipline of prayer, kept “till the awakening comes,” can prepare the way for revival. The Holy Spirit must be first. A prayer room behind a meeting is as important as a pulpit in front of it. Travail in prayer is Christ’s burden shared, not a burden we manufacture. The one who is missing matters as much as the ninety-nine. Accusing a brother, even in prayer, is the work of the accuser, and thanksgiving is its cure. Praise is a garment we can put on before we feel it. Love may cost us our blankets. The cross is victory even in the darkness. Rest is a gift, not a failure. Other people’s burdens are ours to bear. And death, for a Christian, is not defeat but a shout of triumph. None of these lessons is new. Every one is in Scripture. What Hyde’s life adds is a picture of them being lived, imperfectly, by a real man. He Being Dead Yet Speaketh The verse at the head of this chapter speaks of Abel, the first person in the Bible to die. The writer to the Hebrews says of him that “through it he being dead yet speaketh” (Hebrews 11:4, ASV). Abel left no words at all. What speaks is his faith, and the sacrifice it offered. Carré applied the phrase to Hyde in the foreword of his book in 1923. Jones used it again: “‘He being dead yet speaketh’ is true of him. It is now ten years since he was called Home, but he is not forgotten, he is speaking to us to-day, and throwing light on the Prayer-Life of Christ.” That last phrase is the key. Hyde’s friends did not think that his life pointed to himself. They thought it threw light on Christ, and in particular on the prayer life of Christ, who “ever liveth to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25, ASV). The deepest thing Hyde’s life teaches is not about Hyde at all. It is that the risen Lord is still praying. He still longs for the lost, still carries his people’s burdens, and still invites his friends to watch with him. In the Punjab, one of those friends said yes. The writer to the Hebrews, having listed the faithful who had died, turns to his readers: “Therefore let us also, seeing we are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus the author and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:1-2, ASV). John Hyde is one of that cloud now. He is not watching us to be admired, but cheering us on toward the One he looked at all his life. For Reflection The man the Punjab called “the man who never sleeps” has been at rest for more than a century. “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from henceforth: yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labors; for their works follow with them” (Revelation 14:13, ASV). The question his life puts to us is the one Jesus asked his sleeping friends in Gethsemane, the question at the head of this book’s preface: “What, could ye not watch with me one hour?” It is not asked in anger. It is asked by a Lord who knows our weakness, who is still praying for us, and who still, in his kindness, wants our company. Hyde answered it with his life. We are invited to answer it in ours, not in his form, but in his spirit. Perhaps that means half an hour at noon. Perhaps it means a thanksgiving instead of an accusation, or a person no one has thought to ask about. But in some way it means watching with Christ, and praying “till the awakening comes.”

fields.title: Appendix A: Twenty-Five Lessons from Hyde’s Prayer Life
fields.body_html:
The lessons below are not a system of prayer, and John Hyde would not have wanted them to become one. They gather the themes woven through this book so that readers can return to them. Each is drawn from his life as the sources record it, and each rests on Scripture, not on his example alone.

1. Prayer Begins at Home

Hyde’s life of prayer grew from a father who prayed daily for labourers in the harvest. Faithful, repeated prayer in an ordinary home is never wasted. Jesus’ instruction comes before any sending: “Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he send forth laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:38, ASV). Those who pray it honestly should be ready for God to answer through their own children, or through themselves.

2. Some Questions Are Settled Only on Our Knees

When Hyde asked a classmate for arguments about the mission field, the classmate sent him to pray until the question was settled. There is a place for counsel. But some decisions wait on our willingness to hear God, not on more information. “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10, ASV).

3. Receive Correction From Those Who Love You

Hyde crumpled the letter that told him he was not yet filled with the Spirit, then went back on his knees to find it. Pride throws away a hard word. Grace reads it again. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6, ASV).

4. Ask for the Holy Spirit

The remedy for Hyde’s spiritual unreadiness was not a technique but a request. “How much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?” (Luke 11:13, ASV). He asked in anger, in misery, and at last in surrender. He was answered.

5. Do Not Preach a Saviour You Have Not Trusted

A stranger’s question at an open-air meeting exposed a besetting sin in Hyde’s life. He would not go on preaching until it was dealt with. “Take heed to thyself, and to thy teaching” (1 Timothy 4:16, ASV). The promise is not freedom from temptation but freedom from sin’s rule: “For sin shall not have dominion over you” (Romans 6:14, ASV).

6. Weakness Is Not a Disqualification

Hyde was deaf, slow of speech, and shy. God did not remove these things. He worked through them. “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9, ASV).

7. Unfruitful Years Are Not Wasted Years

Griswold described Hyde’s first decade in India as “steady, patient, but not especially fruitful.” The years of listening, Bible study, and hidden faithfulness were the soil of everything that followed. “Let us not be weary in well-doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Galatians 6:9, ASV).

8. God Chooses the Despised

Hyde served in a movement that brought the poorest and most despised people of the Punjab to Christ. He embraced them, lived among them, and baptized them. “God chose the foolish things of the world, that he might put to shame them that are wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27, ASV).

9. Prepare the Messenger as Well as the Message

Hyde’s nights of prayer began when he realised he had spent a night preparing a talk and none preparing himself. “The preparation of the Messenger is quite as important as the preparation of the message.” The apostles guarded both: “we will continue stedfastly in prayer, and in the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4, ASV).

10. Keep the Bible Open When You Pray

Jones remembered Hyde kneeling with his hands resting on an open Bible, “face to face with the Lord and resting on the promises.” Prayer fed by Scripture has somewhere to stand. Daniel prayed after reading Jeremiah (Daniel 9:2-3).

11. A Small Promise Kept Daily

The Punjab Prayer Union asked for half an hour a day, as soon after noon as possible, “till the awakening comes.” A modest discipline kept faithfully can outlast great resolutions. “Evening, and morning, and at noonday, will I complain, and moan; and he will hear my voice” (Psalm 55:17, ASV).

12. Pray Until

The prayer union’s pledge and Isaiah’s watchmen share one word: till. “Take ye no rest, and give him no rest, till he establish” (Isaiah 62:6-7, ASV). Jesus taught “that they ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luke 18:1, ASV).

13. Put the Holy Spirit First

Hyde asked pastors whether the Holy Spirit was first in their pulpits, and then showed what he meant by having “no message” and giving the meeting to the Spirit. “He shall bear witness of me: and ye also bear witness” (John 15:26-27, ASV).

14. Someone Must Do the Hidden Work

“Go in and speak, that is your work. I shall go back to the Prayer Room to pray for you, that is my work.” Preaching and praying are two parts of one work. Every ministry needs someone doing the hidden part. “Thy Father who seeth in secret shall recompense thee” (Matthew 6:6, ASV).

15. Enlarge Your Expectation

Hyde prayed “Wide, Lord, wide” over one verse, because God’s complaint in the psalm is that his people would not open their mouths. “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm 81:10, ASV).

16. The Burden Is Given, Not Manufactured

Hyde’s travail for souls was real and costly. But his friends insisted that the broken heart we need is Christ’s, not our own, “free for the taking in simple faith, never minding our feelings.” “The Spirit himself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Romans 8:26, ASV).

17. The One Still Matters

Nine people had been baptized, the road was dangerous, and the evangelists were angry. Hyde still asked, “What about that one?” The Good Shepherd goes after the lost one “until he find it” (Luke 15:4, ASV).

18. Numbers Serve Love, Not the Reverse

Hyde asked God for a definite number of souls a day. What kept this from becoming a quota was love for people, a strict definition of conversion, and the habit of searching his own heart when fruit was lacking. Joy in heaven is over “one sinner that repenteth” (Luke 15:7, ASV).

19. Do Not Accuse the Brethren, Even in Prayer

God stopped Hyde in the middle of a prayer that listed a pastor’s faults. Hyde confessed that he had been “an accuser of the brethren” and spent the rest of the time giving thanks. “He that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye” (Zechariah 2:8, ASV).

20. Look for What Is Lovely

“Father, show me what things are lovely and of good report in my brother’s life.” God’s people are in the workshop, not yet finished. “Whatsoever things are lovely … think on these things” (Philippians 4:8, ASV).

21. Put On the Garment of Praise

Hyde was not naturally joyful. He found that the obstacle to fruitfulness was usually “the want of praise” and learned to put on praise before he felt it. “The garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness” (Isaiah 61:3, ASV). “In everything give thanks” (1 Thessalonians 5:18, ASV).

22. Love Will Cost Something

Hyde gave away his clothes and blankets, wept at a train window, and rubbed a tired convert’s feet. He answered an angry fellow worker: “If the prodigal had come back to you, you would have taken a stick to him!” “I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls” (2 Corinthians 12:15, ASV).

23. The Cross Is Victory

Hyde was “fascinated by the Cross” and could speak of nothing else. He taught that Christ’s cry “It is finished” was a shout of triumph in the darkest hour, and that those united to Christ can shout it too. “For I determined not to know anything among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2, ASV).

24. Honour the Body’s Just Claims

Hyde’s way of praying cost him his health. His friends urged others to follow his spirit, not his form. The Lord who called his disciples to watch also told them, “Come ye yourselves apart … and rest a while” (Mark 6:31, ASV). God “giveth unto his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2, ASV).

25. Bear Burdens, Refuse Resentment, and Die Giving Thanks

Hyde carried a stranger’s burden at Shrewsbury. He was sung down and ignored without complaint. He said of unkindness, “This is my cross which He wants me to take up and carry for Him.” And he died saying, “Thank God for pain,” and, “It’s just victory, victory, victory.” “Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2, ASV). “But thanks be to God, who giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57, ASV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.”

— James 1:22, ASV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a twenty-week reading course. Its purpose is not to make John Hyde an object of admiration, but to let his life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own prayer and discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse, and to end with a few minutes of actual prayer, not only talk about prayer.

Chapter 1 - A Minister’s Son from Carthage

Central idea

Hyde’s life of prayer grew from a father who prayed daily for labourers in the harvest, a mother’s quiet holiness, and a brother’s unfinished life. Faith can be modelled and prayed over in an ordinary home.

Scriptures to revisit

Matthew 9:36-38; 2 Timothy 1:5; Deuteronomy 6:6-7; Matthew 10:5.

Reflection

1. Who prayed for you before you could pray for yourself? 2. Is there a prayer you have prayed faithfully for years without seeing the answer? 3. Are you willing for God to answer your prayers for labourers through your own family?

Chapter 2 - “It Is Settled”

Central idea

Hyde did not settle his call by collecting arguments but by staying on his knees until the question was settled. Mixed motives do not disqualify a real call.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 6:1-8; Luke 6:12; Psalm 46:10; Philippians 1:15-18.

Reflection

1. Is there a question in your life that you keep reopening with fresh arguments? 2. What would it mean to bring it to God and wait until it is settled? 3. Where is “self” mixed into your service for God, and are you willing for him to purify it?

Chapter 3 - The Letter on the Ship

Central idea

A friend’s letter wounded Hyde’s pride and led him to seek the filling of the Holy Spirit, and to become willing to work “quietly out of sight.”

Scriptures to revisit

Luke 11:9-13; Acts 1:8; Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 27:6.

Reflection

1. Have you ever thrown away a hard word that was actually from God? 2. What does it mean to you to be filled with the Spirit? 3. Are you willing to be useful without being seen?

Chapter 4 - The Sin That Had Not Been Taken Away

Central idea

A stranger’s question exposed a besetting sin, and Hyde refused to preach a Saviour whose power he had not experienced. Deliverance was real, and it was also a beginning.

Scriptures to revisit

Hebrews 12:1-2; Romans 6:14; Romans 7:24-25; 1 John 1:8-9; 1 Timothy 4:16.

Reflection

1. What sin “so easily besets” you? 2. Have you made a kind of peace with it? 3. How would you answer the stranger’s question: has the Saviour you speak of saved you?

Chapter 5 - Slow of Speech and Hearing

Central idea

Hyde’s deafness, slowness, and shy temperament were never removed. God gave him “the tongue of them that are taught” through a listening ear, and grace to be misunderstood without bitterness.

Scriptures to revisit

Exodus 4:10-12; 2 Corinthians 12:9; 1 Corinthians 2:1-5; Isaiah 50:4; Matthew 6:33.

Reflection

1. What limitation do you wish God would remove? 2. How might he be working through it instead? 3. How do you respond when colleagues misunderstand you?

Chapter 6 - The Punjab He Entered

Central idea

Hyde’s prayers belonged to a great movement of the poor and despised toward Christ. He lived among them as a brother.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Corinthians 1:26-29; Luke 4:18; James 2:5; Galatians 3:28.

Reflection

1. Who are the despised people in your community? 2. Does your church resemble the church in Corinth, or does it avoid them? 3. How specific are your prayers for real people and places?

Chapter 7 - Preparing the Messenger

Central idea

“The preparation of the Messenger is quite as important as the preparation of the message.” Hyde’s nights of prayer grew from that conviction, and his daily prayer was anchored in Scripture.

Scriptures to revisit

Luke 6:12; Mark 1:35; Acts 6:4; Isaiah 40:31; 2 Chronicles 14:11.

Reflection

1. How do you prepare yourself, not just your work? 2. Do you pray with your Bible open? 3. Hyde asked, “Have we ever wept for souls? Have you? Have I?” How would you answer?

Chapter 8 - The Half-Hour Rule

Central idea

The Punjab Prayer Union’s five questions and daily half-hour prepared the way for revival. A small promise kept daily is powerful.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 62:6-7; Luke 18:1-8; Mark 8:38; Romans 1:16; Psalm 55:17; Daniel 6:10.

Reflection

1. Answer the five questions of the Punjab Prayer Union honestly. 2. Could you keep a half-hour of prayer each day, “till the awakening comes”? 3. With whom could you make such a covenant?

Chapter 9 - Sialkot: “Is the Holy Spirit First?”

Central idea

Hyde urged pastors to put the Holy Spirit first and themselves behind, then did it himself by having “no message” and giving the meeting to the Spirit.

Scriptures to revisit

John 15:26-27; John 16:13-14; 1 John 1:7; Ephesians 3:14-19.

Reflection

1. Is the Holy Spirit first in your ministry, conversations, and plans? 2. What would it cost you to step back publicly? 3. What kept Hyde from testifying about his struggles, and what keeps you?

Chapter 10 - The Prayer Room

Central idea

At Sialkot the prayer room was the secret of the convention. “Go in and speak, that is your work. I shall go back to the Prayer Room to pray for you, that is my work.”

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 81:10-16; Acts 1:14; Acts 4:31; Genesis 28:16-17.

Reflection

1. Who is doing the hidden work of prayer for your church? 2. Is your expectation of God “wide” or narrow? 3. How do you handle disagreements in your church, and have you tried meeting to pray first?

Chapter 11 - “Give Me Souls, or I Die”

Central idea

Hyde’s travail in prayer echoed Rachel’s longing and Paul’s labour. It was a sharing in Christ’s grief, not an addition to his work, and the broken heart it needs is Christ’s own.

Scriptures to revisit

Galatians 4:19; Genesis 30:1; Romans 9:1-3; Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24; Romans 8:26.

Reflection

1. Have you ever longed for someone’s salvation enough to lose sleep? 2. How do you understand “the fellowship of his sufferings”? 3. When your heart feels cold, do you look at it, or at Christ’s?

Chapter 12 - A Soul a Day, and “What About That One?”

Central idea

The famous numbers are less certain than the legend, but the reality was remarkable, and its heart was the one person still missing.

Scriptures to revisit

Luke 15:1-7; John 10:16; Isaiah 53:11; Acts 8:26-40.

Reflection

1. Is there “one” near you whom no one has asked about Christ? 2. How do you keep evangelism from becoming a numbers game? 3. What does it mean to stand where the Good Shepherd is searching?

Chapter 13 - The Accuser of the Brethren

Central idea

God stopped Hyde mid-prayer for accusing a pastor. Confession and thanksgiving turned the prayer into praise, and the pastor was revived.

Scriptures to revisit

Zechariah 2:8; Revelation 12:10; Philippians 4:8; Philippians 1:6-7; Isaiah 42:3; Galatians 6:1.

Reflection

1. Listen to your prayers for difficult people. Are they intercession or accusation? 2. Pray Hyde’s prayer about someone: “Father, show me what things are lovely and of good report in my brother’s life.” 3. How can correction pass through thanksgiving first?

Chapter 14 - The Garment of Praise

Central idea

A naturally gloomy man learned to put on praise before he felt it. Praise so often went before fruit that he treated its absence as sin.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 61:1-3; Ephesians 5:20; 2 Chronicles 20:21-22; Acts 16:25; Nehemiah 8:10; Psalm 24:7-10.

Reflection

1. What would “praising God through shut teeth” look like in your present troubles? 2. Is there a trial you could begin to thank God for? 3. Where has your spirit of heaviness become a habit?

Chapter 15 - Tears at a Train Window

Central idea

Hyde’s love for people cost him his possessions, dignity, and sleep. It did not always succeed, but it made the gospel visible.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 20:31; 2 Corinthians 12:15; Luke 15:11-32; John 13:14; 1 Corinthians 13:4-7; Matthew 19:12.

Reflection

1. Has anyone ever been unable to forget your love for them? 2. Are you more like the father or the elder brother toward those who fail repeatedly? 3. What would it cost you to love someone as Hyde loved J. N.?

Chapter 16 - The Cross He Could Not Stop Preaching

Central idea

Hyde’s prayer flowed from a long gaze at the cross: Christ becoming man, slave, and despised “for me,” and “It is finished” as a shout of victory.

Scriptures to revisit

Philippians 2:5-11; Psalm 22; Mark 7:24-30; John 19:30; 1 Corinthians 2:2; Galatians 2:20.

Reflection

1. Spend time with Hyde’s three steps: Christ became man, slave, despised, “for me.” 2. Where do you need to shout “Victory” in apparent defeat? 3. Is self in your life “crucified, dead and buried”?

Chapter 17 - A Heart on the Wrong Side

Central idea

Hyde’s health broke under his way of life. His sacrifice is to be honoured, but his form is not a pattern, and rest is God’s gift.

Scriptures to revisit

Mark 6:30-32; 1 Kings 19:4-8; Psalm 127:2; 2 Corinthians 4:16; Romans 12:1.

Reflection

1. Are you more likely to spare yourself too much in God’s service, or too little? 2. How do you tell a burden given by God from a burden you have taken up yourself? 3. What would obedience to “rest a while” look like for you?

Chapter 18 - Wales, Shrewsbury, and a Hymn That Sang Him Down

Central idea

Hyde carried a stranger’s burden at great cost and met slights without resentment. The two versions of Chapman’s story agree on what matters.

Scriptures to revisit

Galatians 6:2; 1 Peter 2:21-23; Romans 12:10; Philippians 2:3-4.

Reflection

1. Whose burden could you help carry in prayer this week? 2. How do you respond when you are overlooked or interrupted? 3. What does “This is my cross” mean in your situation?

Chapter 19 - “Victory, Victory, Victory”

Central idea

Hyde died in pain, giving thanks and shouting the victory of Christ in Punjabi. Twenty years of praise had become his native language.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Corinthians 15:54-58; 2 Corinthians 2:14; Philippians 1:21-23; John 16:33; 2 Timothy 4:6-8.

Reflection

1. What habits of thanksgiving are you building now for your own last days? 2. How does the certainty of Christ’s victory change how you face suffering? 3. What “place” has Christ given you in the great battle?

Chapter 20 - The Legacy of Praying Hyde

Central idea

Hyde’s legacy is in the Punjab church, in the people he taught to pray, and in a story that, told honestly, throws light on the prayer life of Christ.

Scriptures to revisit

Hebrews 11:4; Hebrews 12:1-2; Hebrews 7:25; Revelation 14:13; Matthew 26:40-41.

Reflection

1. Which lesson from Hyde’s life is most needed in yours? 2. What would it mean to follow his spirit and not his form? 3. How will you answer Jesus’ question, “Could ye not watch with me one hour?”
fields.body_text: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.” — James 1:22, ASV This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a twenty-week reading course. Its purpose is not to make John Hyde an object of admiration, but to let his life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own prayer and discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse, and to end with a few minutes of actual prayer, not only talk about prayer. Chapter 1 - A Minister’s Son from Carthage Central idea Hyde’s life of prayer grew from a father who prayed daily for labourers in the harvest, a mother’s quiet holiness, and a brother’s unfinished life. Faith can be modelled and prayed over in an ordinary home. Scriptures to revisit Matthew 9:36-38; 2 Timothy 1:5; Deuteronomy 6:6-7; Matthew 10:5. Reflection 1. Who prayed for you before you could pray for yourself? 2. Is there a prayer you have prayed faithfully for years without seeing the answer? 3. Are you willing for God to answer your prayers for labourers through your own family? Chapter 2 - “It Is Settled” Central idea Hyde did not settle his call by collecting arguments but by staying on his knees until the question was settled. Mixed motives do not disqualify a real call. Scriptures to revisit Isaiah 6:1-8; Luke 6:12; Psalm 46:10; Philippians 1:15-18. Reflection 1. Is there a question in your life that you keep reopening with fresh arguments? 2. What would it mean to bring it to God and wait until it is settled? 3. Where is “self” mixed into your service for God, and are you willing for him to purify it? Chapter 3 - The Letter on the Ship Central idea A friend’s letter wounded Hyde’s pride and led him to seek the filling of the Holy Spirit, and to become willing to work “quietly out of sight.” Scriptures to revisit Luke 11:9-13; Acts 1:8; Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 27:6. Reflection 1. Have you ever thrown away a hard word that was actually from God? 2. What does it mean to you to be filled with the Spirit? 3. Are you willing to be useful without being seen? Chapter 4 - The Sin That Had Not Been Taken Away Central idea A stranger’s question exposed a besetting sin, and Hyde refused to preach a Saviour whose power he had not experienced. Deliverance was real, and it was also a beginning. Scriptures to revisit Hebrews 12:1-2; Romans 6:14; Romans 7:24-25; 1 John 1:8-9; 1 Timothy 4:16. Reflection 1. What sin “so easily besets” you? 2. Have you made a kind of peace with it? 3. How would you answer the stranger’s question: has the Saviour you speak of saved you? Chapter 5 - Slow of Speech and Hearing Central idea Hyde’s deafness, slowness, and shy temperament were never removed. God gave him “the tongue of them that are taught” through a listening ear, and grace to be misunderstood without bitterness. Scriptures to revisit Exodus 4:10-12; 2 Corinthians 12:9; 1 Corinthians 2:1-5; Isaiah 50:4; Matthew 6:33. Reflection 1. What limitation do you wish God would remove? 2. How might he be working through it instead? 3. How do you respond when colleagues misunderstand you? Chapter 6 - The Punjab He Entered Central idea Hyde’s prayers belonged to a great movement of the poor and despised toward Christ. He lived among them as a brother. Scriptures to revisit 1 Corinthians 1:26-29; Luke 4:18; James 2:5; Galatians 3:28. Reflection 1. Who are the despised people in your community? 2. Does your church resemble the church in Corinth, or does it avoid them? 3. How specific are your prayers for real people and places? Chapter 7 - Preparing the Messenger Central idea “The preparation of the Messenger is quite as important as the preparation of the message.” Hyde’s nights of prayer grew from that conviction, and his daily prayer was anchored in Scripture. Scriptures to revisit Luke 6:12; Mark 1:35; Acts 6:4; Isaiah 40:31; 2 Chronicles 14:11. Reflection 1. How do you prepare yourself, not just your work? 2. Do you pray with your Bible open? 3. Hyde asked, “Have we ever wept for souls? Have you? Have I?” How would you answer? Chapter 8 - The Half-Hour Rule Central idea The Punjab Prayer Union’s five questions and daily half-hour prepared the way for revival. A small promise kept daily is powerful. Scriptures to revisit Isaiah 62:6-7; Luke 18:1-8; Mark 8:38; Romans 1:16; Psalm 55:17; Daniel 6:10. Reflection 1. Answer the five questions of the Punjab Prayer Union honestly. 2. Could you keep a half-hour of prayer each day, “till the awakening comes”? 3. With whom could you make such a covenant? Chapter 9 - Sialkot: “Is the Holy Spirit First?” Central idea Hyde urged pastors to put the Holy Spirit first and themselves behind, then did it himself by having “no message” and giving the meeting to the Spirit. Scriptures to revisit John 15:26-27; John 16:13-14; 1 John 1:7; Ephesians 3:14-19. Reflection 1. Is the Holy Spirit first in your ministry, conversations, and plans? 2. What would it cost you to step back publicly? 3. What kept Hyde from testifying about his struggles, and what keeps you? Chapter 10 - The Prayer Room Central idea At Sialkot the prayer room was the secret of the convention. “Go in and speak, that is your work. I shall go back to the Prayer Room to pray for you, that is my work.” Scriptures to revisit Psalm 81:10-16; Acts 1:14; Acts 4:31; Genesis 28:16-17. Reflection 1. Who is doing the hidden work of prayer for your church? 2. Is your expectation of God “wide” or narrow? 3. How do you handle disagreements in your church, and have you tried meeting to pray first? Chapter 11 - “Give Me Souls, or I Die” Central idea Hyde’s travail in prayer echoed Rachel’s longing and Paul’s labour. It was a sharing in Christ’s grief, not an addition to his work, and the broken heart it needs is Christ’s own. Scriptures to revisit Galatians 4:19; Genesis 30:1; Romans 9:1-3; Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24; Romans 8:26. Reflection 1. Have you ever longed for someone’s salvation enough to lose sleep? 2. How do you understand “the fellowship of his sufferings”? 3. When your heart feels cold, do you look at it, or at Christ’s? Chapter 12 - A Soul a Day, and “What About That One?” Central idea The famous numbers are less certain than the legend, but the reality was remarkable, and its heart was the one person still missing. Scriptures to revisit Luke 15:1-7; John 10:16; Isaiah 53:11; Acts 8:26-40. Reflection 1. Is there “one” near you whom no one has asked about Christ? 2. How do you keep evangelism from becoming a numbers game? 3. What does it mean to stand where the Good Shepherd is searching? Chapter 13 - The Accuser of the Brethren Central idea God stopped Hyde mid-prayer for accusing a pastor. Confession and thanksgiving turned the prayer into praise, and the pastor was revived. Has anyone ever been unable to forget your love for them? 2. Are you more like the father or the elder brother toward those who fail repeatedly? 3. What would it cost you to love someone as Hyde loved J. N.? fields.title: Appendix C: Chronology of the Life and Times of John Hyde
fields.body_html:
“So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom.”

— Psalm 90:12, ASV

The dates below are meant as orientation. Where a date comes from an independent record, such as the seminary catalogue, the missionary magazines of Hyde’s church, a mission report, or a contemporary obituary, it is given plainly. Where it rests on the devotional memoirs of 1923, it is marked as such. Events in the wider history of the Punjab and of revival are included for context.

1834 - The Lodiana Mission

American Presbyterian missionaries begin work at Ludhiana in the Punjab. The mission, later called the Punjab Mission of the Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A., becomes Hyde’s mission.

1855-1857 - The Sialkot Mission

The United Presbyterian Church of North America opens a mission centred on Sialkot. It will host the Sialkot Convention from 1904.

1863 - Edmund Hyde Born

John’s elder brother, Edmund Harris Hyde, is born.

1865 - Birth

John Nelson Hyde is born on 9 November 1865 at Carrollton, Greene County, Illinois, to the Rev. Smith Harris Hyde, a Presbyterian minister, and his wife. He is one of six children who grow to adulthood. His father later serves seventeen years as pastor of the Presbyterian church at Carthage, Illinois.

1873 - Ditt and the Beginning of the Mass Movement

Ditt, a lame hide-dealer of the Chuhra community near Sialkot, is baptized and returns to his village. In August he brings his wife, daughter, and two neighbours for baptism. From this beginning, the people movement among the Punjab’s lowest castes gradually spreads.

1881 - Census

The Punjab census counts 3,912 Indian Christians.

1886 - Mount Hermon

At a student conference called by D. L. Moody, one hundred students volunteer for foreign missions. The Student Volunteer Movement follows.

1887 - College

Hyde graduates from Carthage College, Illinois. He then teaches for a time.

1888 - Edmund Graduates

Edmund Hyde graduates from Lake Forest University. He later spends a year at McCormick Seminary. McGaw says he was a Student Volunteer.

1889 - Seminary

Hyde enters McCormick Theological Seminary, Chicago.

1891 - Edmund’s Death

Edmund dies in August 1891 after contracting fever during summer mission work in Montana (the place and illness per McGaw). John is between his second and final years of seminary.

1891-1892 - The Decision

During his final year, after a night on his knees, Hyde tells a classmate, “It is settled” (McGaw).

1892 - Ordination and Sailing

Hyde graduates from McCormick. He is ordained by the Presbytery of Schuyler on 26 April 1892 and appointed to the Punjab (Lodiana) Mission. He sails from New York on 15 October 1892. On the voyage he receives the letter urging him to seek the filling of the Spirit (McGaw; Carré). Soon after arriving in India he faces the question at the open-air meeting (Carré).

1892-1901 - Early Years

Language study and village work in the Ferozepore and Ludhiana districts. Griswold later calls these years “steady, patient, but not especially fruitful.” Hyde neglects language study for Bible study and is reprimanded (McGaw). His colleagues begin to notice, and some to criticise, his long hours of prayer.

1896 - “The Life on Wings”

Hyde speaks on “The Life on Wings” at a Student Volunteer conference in Lahore, with John R. Mott present. The address is printed in Madras the same year.

1901 - Census; First Furlough

The Punjab census counts 38,513 Indian Christians. Hyde arrives in New York on 15 May 1901 “from Ferozepore.”

1902 - Return to India

Hyde speaks at the Presbyterian women’s board meeting in Omaha in the spring. He sails from New York on 17 September 1902.

1904 - The Prayer Union and the First Convention

The Punjab Prayer Union is begun, “about April” (Carré), with Hyde “one of the moving spirits.” The first Sialkot Convention “for the deepening of the spiritual life” is held. Hyde leads Bible studies, testifies to his own struggles at a men’s meeting (McGaw), and says at its close, “Oh, I must not lose this blessing” (Griswold). The Welsh revival begins in the autumn.

1905 - The Second Convention

Revival at Pandita Ramabai’s Mukti mission and in the Khasi Hills. The Prayer Union’s spring meeting feels “the burden of a world plunged in sin.” The Sialkot Convention of 25 August to 3 September, with nearly 300 attending, sees deep conviction and confession. The appointed speaker on the Holy Spirit, identified by the memoirs as Hyde, has “no message,” and the chairman declares, “The Holy Ghost is leader of this meeting” (official mission report).

1906 - The Convention Opened to All

The convention is opened to Christians generally. Hyde, Paterson, and Turner are said to have prayed for weeks beforehand (McGaw). Pengwern Jones first meets Hyde, probably this year, at the Punjab Mission’s meeting in Ludhiana.

1907 - Moga; Murree

By 1907 the Ludhiana district has been reorganised. Hyde becomes superintendent of the Moga circle of 275 villages. The mission report quotes his method: “Begin the day in prayer and praise with your helpers.” In the summer he spends a week of prayer at Murree with Paterson and Jones (Carré). A letter he writes on 9 May about political unrest is quoted in Woman’s Work.

1908 - One Soul a Day

After a summer of travail in the hills with friends (very probably the Patersons), Hyde asks God for one soul a day. The memoirs report more than four hundred won that year (McGaw; no independent record found).

1909 - Two a Day

The memoirs report a request for two souls a day, and eight hundred “gathered in” between the 1909 and 1910 conventions (McGaw; no independent record found).

1910 - Four a Day; The Last Convention; Calcutta

The memoirs report four souls a day (McGaw). The Moga district records 685 baptisms in 1910 (Woman’s Work, 1911). Hyde’s last Sialkot Convention. Meetings in Calcutta and elsewhere. A Calcutta doctor reports his heart displaced to the right side (McGaw). The Ferozepore training school for village preachers and teachers, founded by Hyde, is in operation (Griswold).

1911 - Leaving India; Britain

Hyde leaves India in March 1911. He lands at Liverpool on Good Friday, 14 April, and stays with Pengwern Jones at Llangollen (Carré). He prays for the Chapman-Alexander mission at Shrewsbury, 20-28 April. He is at Evan Hopkins’s pre-Keswick prayer meeting, but illness keeps him from Keswick in July. The Punjab census counts 163,994 Indian Christians. That summer the training school moves from Ferozepore to Moga.

1911 - Clifton Springs

Hyde arrives in New York on 8 August 1911 and goes to Clifton Springs, New York, for treatment. A tumour is found and operated on. He writes a postcard to his sister on 27 October. On 19 December he moves to his sister’s home in Northampton, Massachusetts.

1912 - Death

John Nelson Hyde dies on 17 February 1912 at the home of his sister, Mrs. E. H. Mensel, in Northampton, Massachusetts, aged forty-six. His last words are spoken in Punjabi (Griswold), remembered as “Bol, Yisu Masih, ki jai!” (W. B. Anderson). He is buried on 20 February 1912 in Moss Ridge Cemetery, Carthage, Illinois, beside his parents and his brother Edmund. Griswold’s obituary, “The Man Who Never Sleeps,” appears in The Assembly Herald in April.

1921-1923 - The Memoirs

Pengwern Jones publishes his reminiscences month by month in The Remembrancer, with a further series by McCheyne Paterson. In 1923 they are gathered by E. G. Carré as A Present-Day Challenge to Prayer (Madras). In the same year Francis McGaw publishes Praying Hyde (Philadelphia).

fields.title: Appendix D: Notes on Sources and Method
fields.body_html:
“it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write unto thee in order … that thou mightest know the certainty concerning the things wherein thou wast instructed.”

— Luke 1:3-4, ASV

This appendix explains where the story told in this book comes from, how the sources were weighed, and which popular claims about John Hyde have been corrected. It is written for readers who want to check the story for themselves, and for anyone who will retell it.

The Two Memoirs of 1923

Nearly everything vivid about Hyde’s inner life comes from two books published in 1923, eleven years after his death.

A Present-Day Challenge to Prayer, edited by Captain E. G. Carré, was published by the S.P.C.K. Depository in Madras. A London edition titled Praying Hyde was later published by Pickering & Inglis (1931). It gathers two series of reminiscences that first appeared month by month in The Remembrancer, the prayer circular of the Bengal and Assam Prayer Union. Part One is by the Rev. J. Pengwern Jones of the Welsh Presbyterian Mission, the circular’s editor. Part Two, “A Master Fisher for Souls,” is by the Rev. R. McCheyne Paterson of the Punjab. Carré insists that he only arranged the articles into chapters and gave them “practically word for word.” Jones wrote from close friendship. He shared rooms with Hyde at Sialkot and Murree, and Hyde stayed with him in Wales in 1911. Paterson was Hyde’s closest companion in prayer.

Praying Hyde, by Francis A. McGaw, was published by the Sunday School Times Company in Philadelphia. McGaw, a Presbyterian minister in Akron, Ohio, had known the Hyde family in Carthage. He describes himself as a compiler, not an author. His acknowledgements thank Paterson, Jones, W. B. Anderson, F. Kehl of Calcutta, officials of the Presbyterian Board, Hyde’s sisters, and others. Much of his account of the Sialkot years is Paterson’s testimony, sometimes in the first person. McGaw does not name the narrator of most of his Sialkot passages, “a brother” or “I”. Some of those passages match Paterson’s chapters in Carré almost word for word, so this book treats the narrator as almost certainly Paterson. Some stories appear in both books in almost identical words.

Both books are sincere and in many details precise. Both were written to inspire prayer rather than to record history. They rarely give dates. They sometimes place the same event differently. They report numbers without saying where they come from. They sometimes interpret events in ways that go beyond what their witnesses could know. This book has used them throughout, and has tried in the text to say which of them each story comes from.

Independent Records

The following sources are independent of the memoirs and were written close to the events:

General Catalogue of the McCormick Theological Seminary (Chicago, 1912). This gives Hyde’s birth date and place, college, seminary course, ordination, station (“Ferozepore, India, ‘92-’12”), and date and place of death. It also records his brother Edmund.

Woman’s Work for Woman, later Woman’s Work, the magazine of the Presbyterian women’s boards of foreign missions. Its monthly columns record Hyde’s sailings and arrivals (1892, 1901, 1902, 1911), his death, a brief tribute noting his words “Thank God for pain, thank God for everything!”, and the report of 685 baptisms at Moga in 1910.

H. D. Griswold, “Obituary: The Man Who Never Sleeps,” The Assembly Herald, April 1912. This is the single most valuable document for an honest biography. It was written by a colleague who admired Hyde but did not idealise him.

The President’s Report on the Work of the Punjab Mission (Ludhiana Mission Press, 1907). It records Hyde’s superintendence of the Moga circle and quotes his observations and his method of village work.

W. B. Anderson and C. R. Watson, Far North in India (1909). The history of the United Presbyterian mission includes Andrew Gordon’s account of Ditt and the mission’s official report of the 1905 Sialkot Convention. That report independently confirms the scene in which the appointed speaker had “no message” and the chairman gave the meeting to the Holy Spirit.

J. Wilbur Chapman, When Home Is Heaven (1917), and Ford C. Ottman, J. Wilbur Chapman: A Biography (1920). These give Chapman’s own printed account of Hyde’s prayer at Shrewsbury and the dates of the mission.

J. Waskom Pickett, Christian Mass Movements in India (1933), and the published Punjab census figures, as analysed by later historians of Punjabi Christianity. They supply the context of the mass movement.

Hyde’s Own Words

Hyde wrote very little that survives. The following are the passages in which we come closest to his own voice:

His account of the letter on the voyage, quoted by McGaw from “an Indian publication,” and a fuller version told to Pengwern Jones in conversation.

His account of the open-air meeting and his besetting sin, as told to Jones.

An extract from his 1896 address “The Life on Wings,” reprinted by Carré.

His observations on village work and his method (“Begin the day in prayer and praise with your helpers …”), quoted in the mission report of 1907.

A sentence from a letter of 9 May 1907 about political unrest, quoted in Woman’s Work.

A passage from his last class letter to his seminary classmates (“over a thousand the past two years …”), quoted by McGaw.

His notes on Psalm 22, from a letter to his sister Mary, printed by McGaw with some rearrangement.

A postcard to his sister dated 27 October 1911, quoted by McGaw.

Many sayings reported by friends, such as “First things first,” “What about that one?”, “That is your work … that is my work,” and “It’s just victory, victory, victory.” These are memories of speech, not transcripts.

Corrections to the Popular Story

The following popular claims have been corrected or qualified in this book:

Place and date of death. Hyde died on 17 February 1912 at his sister’s home in Northampton, Massachusetts. He did not die at Clifton Springs, New York, where he had been treated. Three independent Presbyterian sources agree.

Age at death. He was forty-six, not forty-seven as Griswold and McGaw say.

His station. Sialkot was the United Presbyterian mission’s town, not Hyde’s. His station was Ferozepore, and from 1907 he superintended the Moga circle of the Ludhiana district.

Founding the convention and the prayer union. The early sources call Hyde one of the “moving spirits” of the Punjab Prayer Union and name him among the leaders of the Sialkot Convention. No independent record names him as the founder of either. Griswold says he was closely associated with the convention from its beginning.

The soul-a-day figures. The figures of four hundred in 1908 and eight hundred between the 1909 and 1910 conventions appear only in McGaw. The independent record shows steadily increasing baptisms in the Moga district, 685 in 1910, and Hyde’s own report of “over a thousand the past two years” for his team.

The displaced heart. The report comes from a friend’s memory of one doctor’s examination. The claim that prayer moved Hyde’s heart is an interpretation. A heart on the right side may be congenital (dextrocardia) or the result of chest disease (dextroposition).

Chapman at Shrewsbury. The dramatic version, with the locked door and the five-minute silences, comes from an undated letter printed in both memoirs. Chapman’s own published account (1917) is quieter. Both agree on the turning of the mission and on Chapman’s lesson in intercession.

Last words. Griswold records that Hyde’s last words were in Punjabi. W. B. Anderson gives them as “Bol, Yisu Masih, ki jai!”, a phrase whose spelling and translation vary. Griswold also records that he said to his sister, “It’s just victory, victory, victory.”

Inferences Offered With Caution

Two suggestions in this book go slightly beyond the sources and are offered as probable, not proven. First, Jones states in passing that the friend who wrote the letter on the ship was the man “preparing a short account of Hyde,” which suggests that the letter-writer was Francis McGaw himself. Second, the unnamed speaker in the official report of the 1905 convention is identified with Hyde because the memoirs tell the same story about him.

Later Books

Many later books about Hyde exist, including popular biographies from the 1940s onward and modern compilations of his supposed letters. This book has not relied on them. Where they add details not found in the 1923 memoirs or the contemporary records, those details could not be verified.

Where More May Be Found

The records of the Punjab Mission and of the Presbyterian Board of Foreign Missions, held at the Presbyterian Historical Society in Philadelphia, may contain letters and reports by Hyde that have not been published. Local newspapers in Illinois and Massachusetts from February 1912 may contain further obituaries. A future biographer with access to those archives may be able to answer questions this book has had to leave open.

Scripture

All Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901, checked against its published text. Where Hyde or his friends quoted another version, such as the King James or the Revised Version, their wording has been kept and marked, and the ASV has been used for the book’s own quotations.
